‘It exists, it will be’ means that (the path leading to liberation from Saṃsāra) clearly exists and will come to be. ‘Not for non-existence’ means it cannot but happen (it will certainly occur). ‘In this very way’ means just like this. ‘Does not seek’ means not wishing to go or not going. ‘Washes’ refers to (the pool of the Deathless) which is being cleansed. ‘One who acts according to one's own will’ (Serī) means one who is self-dependent. ‘One who is self-mastered’ (Sayaṃvasī) means one who can act according to one's own will. ‘Like a great robber’ is because one destroys the treasure of merit through misconduct and wrong livelihood due to excessive attachment to the body. ‘Refuge’ (Nāthā) refers to those who have a refuge. Since the meaning of the phrase ‘Free from the five faults’ and so on has already been written in some commentary books, it will not be repeated here.

In the phrase ‘In the dispensation’ (Sāsane), the dispensation of the ascetics refers to the Jhanas and higher knowledges (Abhiññā). While being one who was proficient in those Jhanas and Abhiññās, and while I was in such a state, Dīpaṅkara Buddha appeared in the world. The people cleared and cleaned (the path). By the synonymous terms ‘Añjasa, Vaṭuma, Ayana’, the path itself is meant. In the phrase ‘Do not step on him’, the word ‘naṃ’ is merely an expletive particle (nipāta) used to complete the verse. In the phrase ‘I shall clear (the path)’, ‘a’ and ‘haṃ’ are particles, or ‘ahaṃ’ is a single particle made with nasalization (niggahīta). ‘Of the offerings’ (Āhutīnaṃ) means of the gifts to be given. ‘Me’ means the Buddha spoke to me or about me.

Although the Bodhi tree was mentioned after passing through aeons, in order to include the Bodhi tree while praising the mother and others, he said ‘The Bodhi tree of that Blessed One’ and so on. ‘With happiness’ means with noble happiness. ‘Incomparable’ means being unlike other ascetics. I have obtained such happiness, which is superior even to the happiness of mundane Abhiññā, arising from the prophecy of Buddhahood. ‘Which’ refers to which omens. ‘Turns’ means turning clockwise. ‘They cry out’ means making sounds. ‘They came out’ means they departed. ‘Does not go upwards’ means not moving to the top. ‘Both’ refers to both words. ‘Firm and stable’ means eternally constant, the unchanging meaning itself. ‘Of pregnant women’ refers to women who are with child. ‘As far as the ten directions’ means in those directions. ‘In the Dhamma-element’ means ‘I shall investigate in the Dhamma-element’ or in all phenomena (dhammas).

Just as a pot full of water pours out that water without remainder. The use of the plural ‘these’ is because, although it is only the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), it has many various aspects. ‘Protects the (tail-hair) that is stuck’ is an addition to complete the sense, or the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. ‘In the four grounds’ means in the grounds of restraint such as the Pātimokkha. ‘One with a non-dual mind’ means having a mind that does not reach a state of duality such as sometimes being patient and sometimes impatient, or being patient with some and impatient with others. The path of truth (Saccassa vīthi) is the reality as it is, whether seen or unseen. ‘Determination’ (Adhiṭṭhāna) is the firm establishment in undertaking merit; it is called determination when there is immovability in the meritorious qualities already undertaken. Equanimity like the earth means not reaching a state of transformation (not reacting). ‘Other’ means another phenomenon. In the words ‘Sabhāva, Rasa, Lakkhaṇa’, ‘Bhāva’ means the unchanging reality, the state of existence. Because it exists along with that reality, it is called ‘Sabhāva’ (own-nature); one's own unchanging...
26:
The function (rasa) known as the task of maturing Bodhi-knowledge, and the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) known as the relinquishing of faultless objects and so on, is called ‘Sabhāva-rasa-lakkhaṇa’. It occurs through the power of my knowledge (ñāṇa) which contemplates in such a way. ‘Dhammatejena’ means by the power of knowledge. ‘Calatā’ is due to the state of trembling. ‘Sesī’ means sleeping or lying down. ‘Mā bhātha’ means ‘Do not be afraid’. ‘Sabbītiyo’ means ‘May all calamities avoid you’.

## The Commentary on the Story of Sumedha is finished.

‘Pavacchati’ means ‘gives’. ‘Yogena’ means by an expedient cause. ‘Samiṃsu’ means ‘they assembled’. ‘Appattamānasā’ means the monks who have not yet reached the fruit of Arahantship are to be reproached. ‘Rittā’ means being void of essence, disappeared. It is said that a type of tree called Sālakalyāṇī appears in a single day only during the time of a Buddha's arising or when a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) appears.

‘Liṅgasampatti’ means the state of being male. ‘Hetu’ means having a rebirth with three roots (tihetuka). ‘Guṇasampatti’ means the attainment of higher knowledges (Abhiññā) and meditative attainments (Samāpatti). ‘Adhikāra’ means performing services and offerings to the Buddhas. ‘Chandatā’ means being endowed with the desire to attain Buddhahood. ‘Sabbaṅgasampannā’ refers to those who have made a resolve (paṇidhāna) by combining the eight factors. ‘Pakkhikā’ are those who must travel by wheeled stools. ‘Paṇḍakā’ are those lacking both genders (eunuchs). Bodhisattas also lack both genders when they are born in the Brahma realm and during the beginning of an aeon; however, they are not included among the ‘Paṇḍakas’. To show this meaning, it is said ‘Pariyāpannā na bhavanti’ (They are not included). Or, they are not included in all the aforementioned defects. Or, those included among the Bodhisattas are contained within them. Or, because they have limited their Saṃsāra, Bodhisattas coming from Saṃsāra do not become hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka) or eunuchs (paṇḍaka).

Because they have pure objects of focus in all things, they do not resort to wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi). ‘Micchādiṭṭhi’ refers to the views of nihilism (natthika), non-causality (ahetuka), and the inefficacy of action (akiriya). ‘Bhavābhave’ means in small and large existences. ‘Bhojaputte’ refers to hunters. ‘Laganaṃ’ means attachment. ‘Aññathā’ means shrinking back (sloth/torpor). ‘Gāmaṇḍalā’ means village children. ‘Rūpaṃ’ means various transformations. This is the connection of the meaning of the Nidānakathā which proves that the Abhidhamma was spoken by the Buddha.

## The Commentary on the Nidānakathā is finished.
27:
## 1. Section on the Arising of Consciousness

## Commentary on the Terms of the Triad Matrix

Now, in order to compose the commentary as promised, he says: "Now I have reached the opportunity to speak..." and so forth. "Starting from here" (ito paṭṭhāya) means starting from the term "wholesome states" (kusaladhamma).

The "triad named by all its terms" (sabbapadehi laddhanāmo) refers to the triad that receives its name from the word "feeling" (vedanā), which is clearly present in all three terms. An objection may be raised: In the sentence "states associated with pleasant feeling" (sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā dhammā), there are four words. Following this method, there are twelve words in total for the remaining sentences, not three. If "by all terms" refers to the word "feeling" being a component of the three terms, it is inappropriate. This is because the word "feeling" (vedanāya) is a distinct term and is not a part of any other term, nor does it become the term "pleasant" (sukhāya) and so on. If so, how can the name derived from that word "feeling" be a "name derived from all terms"? The answer is: Because a collection of words (a sentence) that conveys a specific intended meaning is called a "term" (pada). It is called a term because the meaning is understood through it. Since the intended meaning is fully understood through this collection of words, "states associated with pleasant feeling," this collection of words is called a "term." The other collections of words should be understood in the same way. Therefore, it is appropriate to say "the triad named by all its terms" regarding the name derived from the word "feeling," which is a component of those three collections of words.

In the phrase "by way of the composed text (gantha) and by way of the meaning (attha)," the mutual connection should be understood as being by way of the text because of the connection with terms such as "root" (hetu) and "with roots" (sahetuka), and by way of the meaning because of the connection with meanings such as the meaning of root and the meaning of having roots. The "dyad of having roots" (sahetukaduka) and the "dyad of associated with roots" (hetusampayuttaduka) are connected to the "root dyad" (hetuduka) because they are connected with roots in the root dyad. The "dyad of root and having roots" (hetusahetukaduka) is connected to the root dyad and the dyad of having roots by way of two terms and one term. Similarly, the "dyad of root and associated with roots" (hetuhetusampayuttaduka) is connected to the root dyad and the dyad of associated with roots. The "dyad of not-root and having roots" (nahetusahetukaduka) is connected to the root dyad and the dyad of having roots by way of one term and two terms.

"Like a flower pericarp (kaṇṇikā)" means like a central point made of flowers. "Like a bouquet (ghaṭā)" means like a cluster of flowers in a bouquet and so on. Just as in a flower pericarp or a bouquet, the flowers are mutually connected by their stalks and so forth, the connection of these dyads is described in that manner. "By commonality of dyads" (dukasaamaññato) means because of being similar in the nature of a dyad with other dyads such as the root dyad. "Others" (aññehi) refers to the dyad of having an object (sārammaṇaduka) and so on. Those triads and dyads that have a remaining portion not included in them are called "with a remainder" (sappadesa). Those triads and dyads that have no such remaining portion are called "without a remainder" (nippadesa).
28:
"Is the venerable one well (kusala)?" To clarify the meaning of this question, it is asked, "Is the venerable one free from illness (anāmaya)?" Therefore, the word kusala has the meaning of health (freedom from illness). In the Bāhitika Sutta, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, Venerable Ānanda, while praising the bodily conduct (kāyasamācāra) and so forth of the Blessed One, said, "Great King, that bodily conduct which is blameless (anavajja) is wholesome (kusala)." Since the Blessed One no longer has karma that produces pleasant results, bodily conduct and so forth that are free from all blame are called wholesome. In the passage "in wholesome states" (kusalesu dhammesu), the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) are also called wholesome. Since those factors of enlightenment are associated with insight, the path, and the fruit, and are not exclusively for the purpose of pleasant results, the word kusala has the meaning of blamelessness (anavajja). The word "aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ" uses the genitive case in the sense of the locative because of its association with the word kusala. Alternatively, it means being skilled in matters such as the names, actions, and applications of the major and minor limbs. The word "naccagītassa" is also a genitive in the sense of the locative. Alternatively, it should be applied as being skilled in the specifics of dance and song. In the passage "Because of undertaking wholesome states, thus this merit increases," the karma that produces the result of merit is called "wholesome." "States arise" means they are merely natural phenomena (sabhāvamatta) because they are void of a being or soul (suññadhammatta). Similarly, in the passage "contemplating states in states" (dhammesu dhammānupassī), the word dhamma should be understood as having the meaning of voidness (suññata).

In the phrase "salayanti... viddhaṃsenti," the subsequent word explains the meaning of the preceding word. Alternatively, the three words such as calana (shaking), which clarify the meaning of the action salana (trembling), should be associated with the abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgapahāna) and so forth. Because they have not been abandoned by the path, unwholesome states that lie in the continuity of beings are said to "lie" (sayanti) in a contemptible manner (kucchitena ākārena) because of their association with impurities such as greed and because they are the cause of various kinds of suffering. Even for wholesome states dissociated from knowledge, knowledge acts as a decisive support condition (upanissayapaccaya); thus, all wholesome states are called kusala because they are to be proceeded with by the wisdom called kusa. Because they are included in both the arisen and unarisen portions, they cut (lunnanti) the group of defilements occurring in both parts by way of abandoning and non-arising, like the two right efforts (sammappadhāna).

Beings and so forth, which are the objects of consciousness that grasp at "beings" and so on, are not without intrinsic nature when investigated with wisdom. Rather, they are called "states" (dhamma) because they bear (dhārenti) their own nature (sabhāva). There is no such thing as a "state" separate from the nature being borne. In truth, there are no "material forms" (rūpa) separate from the nature of being deformed (ruppana) and so forth, nor are there "earth elements" (pathavī) separate from the nature of hardness (kakkhaḷa) and so forth. However, because it is impossible to make them understood in any other way, the natural states—whether known or unknown—are treated as if they were distinct through the power of names, [saying] "their own nature..."
29:
It has been stated, 'They bear their own nature.' To show the specific meaning regarding states with conditions, it is said, 'Or they are borne by conditions.' 'Are borne' (dhārīyanti) means they are upheld by the mind or are characterized.

The term 'unwholesome' (akusala) does not merely signify the negation of the wholesome, the absence of the wholesome, or something other than the wholesome; rather, it is a term signifying its opposite. To demonstrate this, it is said, 'Like an enemy (amitta) who is the opposite of a friend,' and so forth. That it signifies the opposite is also understood by the mention of the third group, the indeterminate (avyākata). For if the word 'unwholesome' merely signified the absence of the wholesome, it would not denote any specific state, and thus the third group would not be established by the word 'indeterminate' alone. It would then follow that there is only a dyad (duka) of wholesome and indeterminate states, not a triad (tika). In such a case, the word 'unwholesome' would have no meaning. If it were considered to have meaning, then just as there is the absence of the wholesome, there should also be the absence of the indeterminate, and it would have to be called 'non-indeterminate' (anavyākata). Therefore, if it were a term for mere absence, 'unwholesome' would not be a distinct group of states, and 'indeterminate' would not be the third group. Since the indeterminate is taught as the third group, it is understood that the unwholesome is also a distinct group.

Therefore, it does not signify mere absence. Also, because it shares the same grammatical footing with the word 'dhamma'—which has meanings such as bearing its own nature—the word 'unwholesome' does not signify the mere absence of the wholesome. Nor does it signify merely what is other than the wholesome, precisely because of the mention of the third group. If all states other than the wholesome were called 'unwholesome,' just as all states other than mental factors (cetasika) are called 'non-mental factors' (acetasika), then all states would be included within the two terms 'wholesome' and 'unwholesome.' Consequently, there would be no third group called 'indeterminate,' and it would have to be stated as a dyad: 'wholesome states, unwholesome states.' However, that third group was indeed stated. Therefore, the word 'unwholesome' does not signify merely what is other than the wholesome.

By the method of residue, and as seen in the usage of the prefix 'a-' for opposites in the world (e.g., 'amitta' for enemy) and in the Dispensation (e.g., 'alobha' for non-greed), it is established that here too the word 'unwholesome' signifies the opposite. This opposition is understood through their contrary natures and because they are states to be abandoned by the wholesome. It is not because they destroy the wholesome. Unwholesome states cannot abandon the wholesome. Rather, it is only the powerful wholesome states, through the fulfillment of practice, that abandon the unwholesome states—which always lie latent—by means of substitution (tadaṅga), suppression (vikkham-bhana), and eradication (samuccheda).
30:
'Indeterminate' (avyākata) refers to states that are undeclared. But why are these states called 'undeclared'? Are they not declared in the triads and dyads such as 'states associated with pleasant feeling,' and by terms such as 'eye-consciousness' and 'contact'? It is not that they are not declared; they are indeed declared. However, those declarations are not intended here in defining the meaning of 'indeterminate,' because they were not mentioned previously and thus do not follow the sequence.

The Buddha did not say 'indeterminate' after having taught 'states associated with pleasant feeling,' etc. Therefore, those terms do not follow here, and their being 'undeclared' is not due to being declared by those terms. However, the terms 'wholesome' and 'unwholesome' are taught in this triad and thus follow the sequence. Therefore, the state of being 'undeclared' is understood through the fact that they are not declared as wholesome or unwholesome. Thus it is said, 'The meaning is: states not declared as either wholesome or unwholesome.'

Alternatively, 'indeterminate' means those without result (avipāka). The meaning of being without result can be understood from the word 'indeterminate' itself. The Buddha's word does not need to be established by external proof (ñāpaka). The Buddha, being skilled in the dispositions (āsaya), underlying tendencies (anusaya), and temperaments (carita) of beings, taught the Dhamma for the understanding of those to be led (veneyya); they were able to penetrate the meaning immediately after his words.

However, later generations must understand everything—how the Buddha spoke those various words for the understanding of the audience present before him, and how they penetrated that meaning—by approaching and listening to teachers (ācariya). Therefore, without stating the reason, it was said, 'The meaning is: states not declared as either wholesome or unwholesome.'

If someone were to say, 'Because they are not declared as the result of the unwholesome, wholesome states become indeterminate; and because they are not declared as the result of the wholesome, unwholesome states also become indeterminate,' they should be refuted by saying, 'The Buddha's words are not established by external proof.' They should also be refuted because only that which is not declared by the words following the sequence is 'indeterminate.'

The word 'without result' (avipāka) was not taught previously, nor was the word 'wholesome' not taught. Therefore, the sequence of the word 'without result' and the 'undeclared' status of wholesome states cannot exist. Thus, wholesome states cannot be indeterminate. The fact that unwholesome states are not indeterminate should be understood by applying this same method.

Alternatively, the prefix 'vi-' signifies opposition, and 'ā-' signifies facing or manifesting. Therefore, wholesome and unwholesome states are called 'declared' (vyākata) because they are made to face mutual opposition by their own conditions, due to opposition in characteristics and the relationship of destroyer and destroyed.

Those that are not thus opposed are called 'indeterminate' (avyākata). Indeed, they are not contrary in characteristics like the wholesome and unwholesome. For the state of being without result (avipākatā) does not oppose the state of having a pleasant result (sukhavipākatā) or the state of having a painful result (dukkhavipākatā), in the way that having a painful result opposes having a pleasant result. Furthermore, these indeterminate states do not abandon any state, nor are they to be abandoned by any state. This is the author's own opinion in this context.
31:
In the term "Anavajjasukhavipākalakkhaṇā," because these wholesome states (kusala dhamma) have no censurable fault (avajja), they are called "anavajja." It means states that are free from a censurable nature and are faultless. By the word "anavajja," the non-censurable nature of those wholesome states is shown. It does not merely show the absence of what is censurable. There are also indeterminate states (abyākata) other than wholesome ones that are faultless. Therefore, seeing the fault that those indeterminate states might also be considered wholesome by the mere word "anavajja," the word "sukhavipāka" (having pleasant results) was spoken to remove that fault (to exclude the indeterminate). Alternatively, here "anavajja" means the opposite of fault. It does not mean faults that have been stilled or the mere absence of faults as mentioned in the Bāhitika Sutta. Therefore, by the word "anavajja," the nature of destroying faults is shown. To show the distinction of the wholesome within the "characteristic of having results" (savipākata-lakkhaṇa)—which is common to both wholesome and unwholesome states, unlike indeterminate states—the word "sukhavipāka" was spoken. This is because the distinction of the wholesome from the unwholesome and indeterminate is already established by the preceding word "anavajja."

Because those wholesome states have pleasant (desirable) results, they are called "sukhavipāka." By that word "sukhavipāka," although wholesome and unwholesome states share the common nature of being subject to ripening (vipākadhamma-bhāva), the nature of producing good results is shown. It does not merely show the existence of pleasant results for them. Because they are both blameless and have pleasant results, they are called "anavajjasukhavipāka." Since the wholesome states are to be marked by this mark, it is called "lakkhaṇa" (characteristic). Because they have the characteristic of being blameless and having pleasant results, they are called "anavajjasukhavipākalakkhaṇā." One might ask: "Are not those wholesome states themselves the blameless and pleasant-resulting states? How can they be their own characteristic?" This is appropriate because of the relationship between the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) and the thing to be characterized (lakkhitabba) through the nature of the known and unknown meanings. Wholesome states, which are unknown (not clear) through the sense of the word "kusala," are the things to be characterized (lakkhitabba). Those that are known (clear) through the sense of the words "anavajjasukhavipāka" are the characteristic (lakkhaṇa). Thus, this statement is appropriate. Alternatively, "lakkhaṇa" means the nature (sabhāva) that is to be marked. Because they are both the nature of being blameless and having pleasant results, and are the nature to be marked, they are called "anavajjasukhavipākalakkhaṇā." It means that the natures which are marked as being blameless and having pleasant results are called "wholesome" (kusala).

In another way, by the word "anavajja," the state of being blameless is stated. By the word "sukhavipāka," the state of having pleasant results is stated. Therefore, the blamelessness and the having of pleasant results are "anavajjasukhavipāka." That is the characteristic (nature) of these wholesome states. It means that the states marked by the nature of being blameless and having pleasant results, as well as the states possessing that nature, are called "wholesome." Therein, by the word "anavajja," the happiness at the moment of occurrence (pavatti-sukha) of the wholesome states is shown. By the word "sukhavipāka," the happiness in the ripening of results (vipāka-sukha) is shown. The former is the statement of the characteristic by way of its own nature of occurrence, while the latter is the statement of the characteristic by way of its ability to produce results in the future. Likewise, by the former word, the self-purity of the wholesome states...
32:
By the latter term 'sukhavipāka' (having happy results), he shows the state of having pure results. By the former term 'anavajja' (blameless), he excludes the wholesome from the nature of the unwholesome; by the latter term 'sukhavipāka', he excludes it from the nature of the indeterminate (avyākata). This is because the latter term 'sukhavipāka' illustrates the state of having a result. Alternatively, by the former term 'anavajja', because it shows the state of being the opposite of fault, it illustrates the function of destroying the unwholesome by way of its characteristic function (kicca-rasa). By the latter term 'sukhavipāka', it illustrates the state of having a desirable result by way of the property of attainment (sampatti-attha).

By the former term 'anavajja', by way of manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna) as the mode appearing in the yogi's knowledge, he shows the state of appearing as a pure dhamma. By the latter term 'sukhavipāka', by way of manifestation in the sense of a fruit, he shows the state of having the result of happiness. By the former term 'anavajja', he clearly explains wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) as the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of wholesome states. This is because those wholesome states arise as blameless dhammas due to that wise attention. By the latter term 'sukhavipāka', he shows that wholesome states are the proximate cause of other resultants. This is because those wholesome states are the cause of happy results.

In this context, within the term 'sukhavipāka', the word 'sukha' should be understood as a synonym for 'iṭṭha' (desirable). Wholesome states are those that have the four desirable mental aggregates as their result; they do not only have pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) as their result. Nibbāna, which is the calming of the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha), can never be a 'sukhavipāka'. This is because Nibbāna is not a resultant (vipāka). If, however, the word 'vipāka' is a synonym for 'phala' (fruit), then the state of 'sukhavipāka' should also be applied to desirable matter (iṭṭha-rūpa) which is a produced result (nissanda-phala).

In the phrase 'sāvajja-dukkhavipāka-lakkhaṇā' (having the characteristic of being faulty and having painful results), the meaning and application should be understood as far as possible according to the method already mentioned. The fitness to give a result has been stated as the characteristic of the wholesome and unwholesome. The indeterminate (avyākata) states, which are not described by that fitness to give a result, have the nature of not being fit to give a result. Therefore, it is said: 'avyākatā are those with the characteristic of being without result' (avipāka-lakkhaṇā). Just as the wholesome and unwholesome are described by their characteristics as 'sukhavipāka' and 'dukkhavipāka' because they are fit to give happy and painful results, so too these indeterminate states are described by their characteristic as 'avipāka' because they are not fit to give a result.

Therefore, regarding such cases as 'there was kamma, but there was no kamma-result; there will be no kamma-result; there is no kamma-result; there is kamma, but there is no kamma-result; there will be no kamma-result; there will be kamma, but there will be no kamma-result'—in such instances, it is impossible for the wholesome and unwholesome to lose their status as wholesome and unwholesome, or to reach the status of being indeterminate. For those wholesome and unwholesome states that have become 'ahosi-kamma' (lapsed kamma) are not unfit to give happy or painful results because they possess the nature of giving results; nor are they unfit to give results because of a lack of the nature of giving results.

Regarding 'kusalā ti vā dhammā ti vā' etc., there are two terms for wholesome dhammas, two terms for unwholesome dhammas, and two terms for indeterminate dhammas. By the phrase 'ekattha-nānatthāni' (same meaning or different meanings), he questions the identity or difference of meaning between each pair in relation to one another, not for all six at once. Knowing that the questioner (codaka) asks this wishing to point out a fault, the Teacher (the Commentator) says: 'Kiñcettha?' (What of it?).
33:
In this matter of having the same meaning or different meanings, some further criticism could be made; your objection is not yet complete, so speak first of what remains. If they have the same meaning, differing only in sound like the terms 'Inda' and 'Sakka', then the terms 'kusalā' and 'dhammā' would be the same; there would be no difference in meaning. Just as when one says 'Indo Sakko', it is like saying 'Indo Indo', so this expression 'kusalā dhammā' would be like saying 'kusalā kusalā'. Similarly, for the others, the likeness to saying 'akusalā akusalā' and 'abyākatā abyākatā' should be applied. If, however, they have different meanings, like the terms 'Inda' and 'Kuvera' which differ both in sound and in meaning, then the terms 'kusalā' and 'dhammā' would be different. In that case, by the six terms and four terms, six and four different meanings would be expressed, and thus the Wholesome Triad (Kusala-tika) etc. would become a Wholesome Six-fold group (Kusala-chakka), and the Root Dyad (Hetu-duka) etc. would become a Root Four-fold group (Hetu-catukka).

One might object: 'Is it not that, like three instances of the word Inda, the three instances of the word dhamma do not differ in form, and thus there is no difference in meaning, so they would not become a six-fold group? Therefore, should it not rather be said that the Triads and Dyads become Four-fold and Three-fold groups?' This should not be said. Just as there is no purpose in uttering three instances of the word 'Inda' which have the same meaning, there is no purpose in uttering three instances of the word 'dhamma' if they have the same meaning. Those words 'dhamma' spoken by the Buddha, though not differing in form like the words 'māsa', should appropriately have different meanings. Even so, one might object: 'Just as a single word 'māsa' of unchanging form can denote a period of time (month), a type of bean, and a weight of gold, so a single word 'dhamma' should be able to express different meanings. Therefore, just as time etc. are not different as meanings of the term 'māsa', so those wholesome states etc. are not different as meanings of the term 'dhamma', and thus they should only become Four-fold and Three-fold groups.' This is not possible. A single word cannot denote different meanings distinguished by class (jāti), quality (guṇa), or action (kiriya).

Indeed, a single word 'māsa' cannot denote time etc., which differ by class, without the use of 'sarūpekasesa' (the elision of identical forms). And in this context of the Triads and Dyads, if 'sarūpekasesa' had been employed, the second and third 'dhamma' words would not have been spoken; but they were spoken. Therefore, just as the words 'kusalā' etc. occur in reference to dhammas of the same class such as the wholesome, so the three and two 'dhamma' words—though similar in form like the words 'māsa'—occur in reference to meanings of different classes. Thus, the Triads and Dyads would indeed become six-fold and four-fold groups.

'Padānañca asambandho' means that there would be a lack of connection between the terms 'kusalā' and 'dhammā', and likewise for 'akusalā' and 'dhammā', and 'abyākatā' and 'dhammā'. Only the connection between each pair is desired, not a mutual connection between all six or all four. Why is this objection raised? Is it not that when there is a difference in meaning, the 'dhamma' words are spoken for the purpose of showing a different meaning...
34:
Is it not appropriate to say that there is no connection (between the dhamma words), just as there is no connection between the words kusala, akusala, and abyākata? This statement is true. However, having established that lack of connection, the previous objection was made: "In the triads and dyads, the state of being six or four would occur." It should be understood that this objection is raised here specifically to prove that very lack of connection.

Alternatively, the construction should be understood thus: If you do not desire the state of being six or four, there must be a connection of words according to the method already mentioned. Such a connection between two words with the same case ending (samānavibhatti) is appropriate only when they have the same meaning (ekattha). But since you assert a difference in meaning (nānattha), for you, the lack of connection (asambandha) between the words must necessarily follow; it cannot but occur. The word "ca" carries the sense of restriction (niyama).

"The preceding and following... become useless" means that this is the view of one who does not desire the state of being six or four, but desires a difference in meaning. To show that a connection must certainly be desired because otherwise a contradiction between preceding and following statements would occur, he said: "Yāpi cesā" and so on. For the question "Which states are wholesome?" (katame dhammā kusalā), by transposing the words, shows the identity of meaning (ekattha) of the words kusala and dhamma mentioned here, as "The states themselves are wholesome." According to your view, which asserts a difference in meaning, it would result in "States are not wholesome," thus contradicting that question. Although there is such a contradiction, that question was taught in that very way; therefore, a difference in meaning is not appropriate.

"Aparo nayo" (Another method) means that the identity of meaning of the pairs such as "wholesome states" (kusalā dhammā) is questioned through the identity and diversity of meaning of the three dhamma words. In the passage beginning with "tiṇṇam dhammānam ekattā," just as the meanings of "Inda" expressed by three "Inda" words are one by way of being Indra, and thus the meanings of the words Sakka, Purindada, and Sahassakkha—which are not other than that—are one; so too, because the meanings of the three dhamma words are one by way of being dhamma, the meanings of the words kusala, akusala, and abyākata—which are not other than that—would also result in being one. This is the meaning.

"Dhamma is called nature (bhāva)" means it is called dhamma because of the sense of "bearing its own nature" and so on. And that nature (bhāva) belongs only to ultimate reality (paramattha-sabhāva), not to what is not nature, namely concepts (paññatti); this is the intended meaning. Let it be nature; what follows from that? If the three dhamma words have different meanings, then among the three dhammas, any one dhamma would be nature (bhāva), and each of the kusala, akusala, or abyākata which is not other than that would alone be nature. The other two dhammas remaining from the dhamma that is nature would be non-nature (abhāva). Among the kusala and so on, which are not different from those, two would also be non-nature. Even that one dhamma taken as nature—since among the three identical-looking dhamma words there is no rule that "only this dhamma word has the sense of nature"—if another dhamma word were to have the sense of nature, then that first one would become non-nature. Then, the kusala and so on which are not other than that would also become non-nature, thus all kusala and so on would result in being non-nature. Just as if Indra were a non-human, there is no humanity for Sakka and others who are not different from him.
35:
Even so, it is not possible to state the non-existence (abhāva—i.e., being a mere concept rather than an ultimate reality) of other things while excluding the ultimate reality (paramattha-sabhāva) of one thing. Furthermore, among those three things, since there is no fixed rule that only one specific thing must be an ultimate reality, if the ultimate reality of all three is established, does it not also establish the ultimate reality of kusala (wholesome) and so on, which are not distinct from them? Such an objection might be raised.

That is not possible. This is because the variety of meanings (nānattha) of the three types of the word Dhamma is permitted. If all three things were solely ultimate realities, there would be no variety of meanings; and you, the objector, have already conceded that variety of meanings.

If it is further argued: "Even if the meanings of all three things are abhāva (not ultimate reality), would there not still be no variety of meanings?"—Let there be no variety of meanings; I say this is merely the fault of you, the objector, who acknowledges such variety. As for me, since I have permitted neither the variety of meanings nor the singularity of meaning, how could there be any contradiction on my part?

Alternatively, regarding the statement "Kusala and so on, which are not distinct from the things that have reached the state of abhāva, would also be abhāva," this was said without a fixed rule. When any two unspecified things reach the state of abhāva, it refers to the attainment of the state of abhāva by any unspecified two among kusala and so on, which are not distinct from them, by saying "because of the ultimate reality of one thing." The statement "the thing following kusala, which is different from those things, would also be abhāva" is intended to demonstrate the lack of a fixed rule, not to establish the abhāva of all things. The meaning here is: if the word Dhamma following akusala or abyākata is an ultimate reality, then the word Dhamma following kusala, which is different from them, would be abhāva.

In the phrase "All this is without cause (akāraṇa)," "cause" refers to reason (yutti). All the logical faults you raised—such as redundancy (punarutti), the sixfold and fourfold fallacies (chakka-catukka-āpatti), and the fallacy of non-connection and contradiction—are unreasonable (ayutti). This is because there is no such absolute singularity or variety of meanings.

This is due to the accomplishment of conventional usage (vohāra) according to the respective acceptance (anumatī) of the wise. Anumatī (acceptance/convention) occurs for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of a word that is not explicitly defined by distinguishing actions, qualities, etc., in things that are essentially indistinct due to the absence of the relationship between a qualifier (visesana) and the qualified (visesitabba). For example, the names "Sakka, Inda, and Purindada." In some places, it occurs in things that are absolutely distinct, such as "Bring the Dhava, Khadira, and Palāsa trees." In some places, it occurs in things that possess both distinction and non-distinction due to the relationship of qualifier and qualified, such as "blue lotus" (nīluppalaṃ) or "wise man" (paṇḍita-puriso). Through those respective acceptances, those respective conventional usages are accomplished. Therefore, here too, the words kusala and dhamma are permitted to occur with a shared meaning, involving both distinction and non-distinction, by distinguishing the specific meaning (visesattha) and the general meaning (sāmaññattha) through the relationship of qualifier and qualified.
36:
"Anumata" means that this conventional usage is accomplished according to the acceptance of various wise people and in accordance with that acceptance. Therefore, it is said, "All this is without cause" (akāraṇa).

The phrase "They show their own specific meaning to that word Dhamma" means that they demonstrate the nature of kusala and so on—such as being faultless and having pleasant results—which they themselves encompass and express, as the meaning of the word Dhamma through the power of showing that meaning. This is because the word Dhamma does not inherently possess the meaning of kusala and so on. The phrase "By this method alone" refers to methods such as "the word Dhamma is found in pariyatti (scriptures) and so on" and "they bear their own nature" (sabhāva). That method is consistent across all triads (tika) and dyads (duka). The specific method, such as "the word kusala is found in health and so on" or "it destroys what is contemptible," has been set aside by the statement "hereafter I shall speak only of the distinction." This is because distinctions such as "associated with pleasant feeling" do not arise by taking the specific meaning of kusala and so on.

In the passage "due to the abandoning of pleasure (sukha)," the faculty of pleasure (sukhindriya) is referred to as sukha. Since that sukhindriya is indeed pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā), it is said "it is found in pleasant feeling." This is not said because the word sukha is synonymous with the word vedanā as in the passage, "Monks, there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling..." (sukhā vedanā). This word sukha in the sense of sukhindriya occurs by taking the specific gratification of bodily pleasure and bodily support (anuggaha). It does not occur by taking general gratification, unlike the word sukha in passages such as "whatever feeling one feels, whether pleasant..." or "one who sees pleasure as suffering."

When a certain cause exists, the occurrence of the causes of pleasure is called the root of pleasure (sukha-mūla). When there is the arising of a Buddha and the state of dispassion (virāga) such as the transcendence of sensual desires, the causes of pleasure—such as merit (puñña) and tranquility (passaddhi)—arise. Therefore, that cause is called "pleasure which is the basis of pleasure" (sukhamūlaṃ sukhaṃ). Because it is the object of pleasure, it is said "form (rūpa) is pleasure."

The word "puñña" (merit) is a designation for pleasure and a designation for desirable results (iṭṭha-vipāka). This means that merit, which is the essence of puñña, brings about desirable results. Because they are the locations or spaces for desirable objects which are the conditions for pleasure, it is said "heavenly realms are pleasure, the Nandana grove is pleasure." "Diṭṭhadhamma" refers to the Dhamma in this very existence (attabhāva). "Sukhavihāra" refers to dwelling in the first jhāna and so on. They are called "abyāpajjha" (free from affliction) because they are free from the oppression of hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so on. Because it extinguishes all the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha) or because it is the cessation of that suffering, it is said "Nibbāna is pleasure." By the word ādi (and so on), it includes neutral feeling (adukkhamasukha) as in "the peaceful neutral feeling is spoken of as pleasure" and "I have [spoken of] two feelings..." and so on.
37:
“Ānanda, I have taught two types of feelings by way of method: pleasant feeling and painful feeling” (Saṃ. Ni. 4.267). The occurrence of the word ‘sukha’ is also included in contexts such as pleasant equanimity (sukha-upekkhā) and desired meanings.

‘Dukkha-vatthu’ means the location (okāsa) of suffering. Indeed, although that suffering arises due to its own causes, it arises based on birth (jāti) and so forth only when those things are manifest. ‘Dukkha-paccaya’ means the cause of suffering, the cause that generates suffering. ‘Dukkha-paccayaṭṭhāna’ occurs in the realm or location of the supporting (upatthambhaka) causes, such as undesirable visible forms, which are associates of the generative kamma (janaka-kamma) that produces suffering. For the word ‘cause’ (paccaya) applies both to the generative cause (janaka) and to the associate of the generative cause. By the word ‘ādi’ (and so forth), the occurrence in ‘suffering of formations’ (saṅkhāra-dukkha) and so forth should be understood, in the manner of “whatever is impermanent, that is suffering” (Saṃ. Ni. 3.15, 45-46, 76). It is called ‘sukhā’ because it makes the associated states and the physical body (karaja-kāya), which is the base of feeling, comfortable, and because it performs the act of favoring those that have obtained enjoyment. In the word ‘sukhā’, the feminine gender is used in consideration of the word ‘vedanā’, and the neuter gender is not used because it does not merely express the state of pleasure. Whether by nature or by intention, whatever object is desirable (iṭṭha), the experiencing of that object or the experiencing of the desirable aspect is called ‘iṭṭhānubhavana’.

‘Sama’ means not uneven, but equal. It should be connected as states that are fit to be associated as if they have reached a state of oneness, or associated together. ‘Ekuppāda’ means ‘having a common arising’ because the arising of these states is the same; it means states that have a simultaneous arising due to common causes. Since the simultaneous arising of materiality (rūpa) and mentality (nāma) might lead to their being considered associated (sampayutta), it is said ‘eka-nirodha’ (common cessation). By saying that only those states which have a common arising and a common cessation are associated, the mutual association of materiality and mentality is excluded. Even with this exclusion, since the inseparable materialities (avinibbhoga-rūpa) might be considered mutually associated, it is said ‘eka-vatthuka’ (having a common base). Only those states which have a common arising, common cessation, and common base are associated. Even so, among the inseparable materialities, one great essential element (mahābhūta) is the support condition (nissaya-paccaya) for the remaining great essentials and derived materialities (upādā-rūpa); thus, because of that one great essential, the remaining materialities could be considered ‘eka-vatthuka’. Or, from the perspective of one who imagines that a single base depends on the great essentials which are the support for the eye-base and so forth, those materialities might be considered associated. To exclude those, it is said ‘ekārammaṇa’ (having a common object). Those states which have a common arising... and a common object are associated. Alternatively, in reverse order, if ‘ekārammaṇa’ is said, the association of consciousnesses with different bases arising on a single object—such as the fivefold sensory consciousness and receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana) within a single cognitive process (vīthi), or in different processes, or in the continuities of others—might be assumed. Therefore, it is said ‘eka-vatthuka’. Those states which, having a common base, also have a common object, are associated. Even so, the association of receiving (sampaṭicchana), investigating (santīraṇa), and so forth might be assumed; therefore, it is said ‘eka-nirodha’. Those states which...
38:
Those states are associated (sampayutta) by having the same cessation, the same physical base, and the same object. In the investigation of whether states with various arisings also possess these three characteristics, or only those with the same arising, the word 'ekuppādā' (having the same arising) is stated to show that only those with the same arising possess these three characteristics.

Regarding 'vipakkabhāvama-pannānaṃ arūpadhammānaṃ' (of mental states that have reached the state of being ripened): Just as the fruits of rice seeds and the like are called 'ripened' (vipakka) when they arise similar to those seeds and acquire the designation 'resultant' (vipāka), whereas the roots, sprouts, leaves, stems, and stalks are not called 'ripened' nor do they acquire the designation 'resultant'; similarly, the results of wholesome and unwholesome [actions] acquire the designation 'resultant' (vipāka) because they have reached the state of being 'ripened' (vipakka), being similar to those [actions] by way of being mental states, having objects, and being bright (sukka) or dark (kaṇha), etc. This is stated to show that material states born of kamma do not acquire [the designation 'resultant'] because they are not similar to kamma. 'Jātijarāsabhāvā' refers to [beings] who have the nature of being born and aging. 'Vipākapakatikā' refers to [states] that have the nature of ripening (producing results).

The nature of ripening (vipaccanasabhāvatā) refers to the activity (byāpāra) [of kamma] to produce results within the continuity of the aggregates where ignorance, craving, and conceit have not yet been abandoned. Therefore, even if the results of wholesome states like direct knowledge (abhiññā) or unwholesome states to be abandoned by development (bhāvanā) are not produced, the fact of having the nature of ripening (vipākadhammatā) is established (evident). Here, in the term 'vipakkabhāva', the word 'bhāva' refers to 'sabhāva' (nature) itself. Taking that aforementioned 'vipakkasabhāva' and the 'vipaccanasabhāva' mentioned in the second term, it is said: 'by way of rejecting both natures'.

States that are taken (ādinnā) by that which is 'upeta' (approached/possessed) are called 'upādinnā'. If it is asked: What is that 'upeta'? By what is it approached? How is it approached? And what states are taken by it? — Although some supramundane states can be objects [of mundane states], to exclude those supramundane states, [it is said that] it is approached by craving (taṇhā) and view (diṭṭhi), which are the four types of clinging (upādāna) expressed by the word 'upaya' related to the word 'upeta'. These [craving and view] approach by way of making [them] an object, not by way of possession (samannāgama). Although all states of the three planes (tebhūmaka) are objects of clinging, those kammas of the three planes are like those who take [results], saying, 'These results are ours because they were produced by us.' Here, those kammas of the three planes are taken as 'upeta' by bringing them into a single state as kamma. The resultants (vipāka) and kamma-born matter (kaṭattārūpa) produced by those kammas are the 'appropriated' (upādinnā) states. To show all this, it is said: 'by way of making [them] an object,' and so on. This method of interpretation should be applied as appropriate, not necessarily in the order of the words.

What is said here is: If states taken by that which is approached (upeta) by craving and view through making [them] an object are called 'upādinnā', then all states of the three planes are objects of craving, etc., and the word 'upeta' is not established only in kamma; therefore, there is no reason to take only kamma. Therefore...
39:
...it would follow that all states of the three planes, which arise from causes such as ignorance and are results such as formations (saṅkhāra), would be 'upādinnā' (appropriated). This is because they too are taken as results by ignorance and so on. Furthermore, by the prefix 'upa-', only the state of being approached is highlighted, not the making of an object as a means of excluding possession (samannāgama). And by the word 'ādinnā', only the state of being taken is stated, not the specific quality of being born of kamma. Therefore, does it follow that all conditioned states are 'upādinnā'?

It does not follow. This is because the teaching proceeds according to the disposition (ajjhāsaya) of those to be enlightened. For the sake of enlightening those for whom this word 'upādinnā' was spoken, they understood the states of the various kinds mentioned by that very word. But now, for those who cannot understand by that much, the meaning should be understood by listening [to a teacher]. Thus, the clarification of the meaning was made as 'kammunā' (by kamma).

This other meaning should also be noted: The prefix 'upa-' indicates 'upeta' (approached). When this prefix 'upa-' is used in a compound, like the word 'ati-' in 'atimālā' etc., it expresses 'approaching' (upagamana) along with its means, just as 'ati-' expresses 'surpassing'. Approaching is the nearing of clinging (upādāna). Therefore, that which is approached is 'upeta'. What is that? It is kamma of the three planes, which does not exist if clinging is absent, and which is spoken of as 'with clinging as condition, existence (bhava) arises'. It is called 'upeta' because it is approached by the previously arisen clinging as a condition. Indeed, no one performs kamma without being approached by clinging or without desire. By that approached kamma, there is the taking (ādāna) of renewed existence (punabbhava). Because of kamma associated with taints (sāsava), beings take renewed existence; therefore, renewed existence is evident as that which is to be taken.

That 'resultant existence' (upapattibhava) is a collection of resultants and kamma-born matter of the three planes, and it is included in the word 'birth' (jāti) in the phrase 'with existence as condition, birth arises'. Therefore, by the word 'upādinnā', 'resultant existence' is meant. It has been explained in the Dhātukathā that 'resultant existence' consists of resultants and kamma-born matter of the three planes. Therefore, it is established that those very states are meant by 'taken (ādinnā) by the approached (upeta)'. Having stated the meaning of the word 'upādinnā' and setting it aside, in order to state the meaning of the word 'upādāniya' separately without depending on the word 'upādinnā', [the teacher] said: 'having approached the state of being an object,' and so on. For that very reason, without making a distinction, it is said: 'This is a designation for states that are the object-condition for clinging.' That 'upādāniya' is of two kinds: appropriated (upādinnā) and unappropriated (anupādinnā). Therefore, wishing to show that state with a distinction, [the teacher] said: 'those which are both appropriated and subject to clinging,' and so on.

'Saṃkilesa' (defilement) refers to the ten bases of defilement. 'Saṃkiliṭṭha' (defiled) refers to those states afflicted and tormented by them. Because those states are associated with defilement and are not different [from them] by way of simultaneous arising, etc., they have reached a state of unity, as it were. Like ghee and the like mixed with poison and the like...
40: Defilements are states that oppress, stain, and burn. Therefore, it is said: 'States associated with defilement are saṅkiliṭṭha (defiled).' 'Deserving of defilement' means they are worthy of receiving defilement by being its object. By the phrase 'due to not transcending the state of being an object,' it shows the inability to transcend defilement. The formation of the word saṅkilesika should be understood like the words vatthayugika and suṅkasālika. The remaining words 'they occur with initial thought' should be connected [with the verb honti]. Even if not explicitly stated, it is understood because the meaning of existence is clear. Taking the word 'mattā' as a term denoting measure (pamāṇa), the meaning is stated as 'sustained thought alone is the measure of these states.' Among initial and sustained thoughts that are inseparable in other [savitakka] consciousnesses, sustained thought alone is the measure in these states; beyond that, they do not reach association with initial thought—this is the meaning. Another meaning is: the word 'matta' has the sense of excluding a specific quality. States with initial and sustained thought are called savicāra because they occur with sustained thought distinguished by initial thought. But these [second group] states have only sustained thought, devoid of the distinction known as initial thought. Therefore, they are called 'vicāramatta,' meaning states having only sustained thought. Although the absence of initial thought (avitakka) is established by the term vicāramatta, the word 'avitakka' is used to indicate that there are other avitakka states that are not vicāramatta. Avitakka states include both those with vicāramatta and those that are avicāra (without sustained thought). Thus, there are states to be excluded and states to be included. If the word avitakka were not mentioned, the excluded and included states would not be shown, and it might be thought that all avitakka states are only vicāramatta. Since the relationship between the qualifier (visesana) and the qualified (visesitabba) can be as desired by the speaker, the sequence of words 'avitakka-vicāramatta' was made to show the qualification of the state by being vicāramatta along with the general state of being avitakka. Alternatively, savicāra states are of two types: those with initial thought (savitakka) and those without (avitakka). Among these, the first term (savitakka-savicāra) is spoken to exclude the avitakka states. Avicāra states are also of two types: those with initial thought and those without. Among these, the third term (avitakka-avicāra) is spoken to exclude the savitakka states. Regarding the avitakka-savicāra and savitakka-avicāra states excluded by both terms, either one or both should be shown. If both were shown and one said 'savitakka-savicāra,' it would result in the meaning of the first term. If one said 'avitakka-avicāra,' it would result in the meaning of the last term. If one said 'avitakka-savicāra savitakka-avicāra,' there would be either no difference in meaning, like internal (ajjhatta) and external (bahiddha), or the fault of confusion (saṅkara-dosa), or the contradiction (virodha) of the same state being both with and without initial thought, and with and without sustained thought.
41: Therefore, to clarify the other savitakka-avicāra states by showing one of the avitakka-vicāramatta states, among the two types that should be spoken, the Buddha spoke 'avitakka-vicāramatta,' showing the avitakka-savicāra states while excluding the savitakka-avicāra states. Or else, these states are vicāramatta (sustained thought only) because of the absence of initial thought; the word avitakka qualifies the vicāramatta states to show that it is not because of the absence of any other state besides sustained thought. 'He looks on' (upekkhati) means that although there is feeling, the neutral feeling (upekkhā-vedana) is indifferent to the modes of pleasure and pain. Alternatively, upekkhā is the appropriate seeing or experiencing that is not contrary to pleasure and pain. 'By way of showing the distinction' means by way of showing the difference. If states accompanied by joy (pīti) were the only states accompanied by happiness (sukha), then since it is established by the term 'pīti-sahagata,' the term 'sukha-sahagata' should not be spoken. Or if 'sukha-sahagata' were spoken, 'pīti-sahagata' should not be spoken. In that case, to complete the triad, the term 'dukkha-sahagata' (accompanied by pain) would have to be spoken. If so, the statement 'this is just the feeling triad' would follow. Therefore, the Teacher, having spoken 'pīti-sahagata' and then 'sukha-sahagata,' intends to show the happiness associated with the third jhāna and body-consciousness—which is separate from happiness accompanied by joy—by considering that there is also happiness dissociated from joy. Or else, this triad is spoken for the purpose of showing the difference between joy and happiness, which is difficult to distinguish. In the term 'pīti-sahagata,' a part of happiness is included, but not joy [itself as the main subject]. In the term 'sukha-sahagata,' joy is included, but not happiness [as the main subject]. Since states accompanied by happiness dissociated from joy are not included by the former term but are included by the latter, the distinction between joy and happiness is established and clear. 'Vision of Nibbāna' is said with reference to having Nibbāna as an object. Alternatively, 'vision' (dassana) refers to the Dhamma-eye which has not yet reached the state of development (bhāvanā) through repeated occurrence. The Dhamma-eye is superior to that gotrabhū (change-of-lineage) because it sees the Four Noble Truths by performing functions such as full understanding (pariññā). Therefore, in this context, gotrabhū does not attain the name 'vision.' 'By way of rejecting both' means by way of rejecting the states spoken in the first two terms, not by way of rejecting the abandoner (pahāyaka). For if it were by way of rejecting the abandoner, it would imply there is another abandoner besides vision and development that abandons by way of eradication (samuccheda), and thus the meaning would be 'states to be abandoned neither by vision nor by development' because they are abandoned by that [other] state. But there is no other abandoner by way of eradication besides vision and development. Defilements set aside by other [states like] calm and insight (samatha-vipassanā) can occur again. Nor are the states to be abandoned included by the third term...
42:
In fact, they are only states that are not to be abandoned. Therefore, by applying the term 'pahatabba' (to be abandoned) separately, it should be understood that 'neither to be abandoned by vision nor to be abandoned by cultivation' refers to states other than those to be abandoned by vision and cultivation.

By the phrase 'without taking the meaning in this way,' the teacher shows the unsuitability of such a view due to both the inappropriateness of the interpretation and the inappropriateness of the grammar. If only those states having causes not to be abandoned by vision and cultivation were taken, the rootless (ahetuka) states would not be included; thus, the intended meaning would be incomplete, resulting in the inappropriateness of the interpretation. Furthermore, while the word 'pahatabba' always requires a relation, the compounding of the word 'pahatabba'—which looks for a negation other than the abandoner (pahāyaka) as its correlate—with the word 'hetu' is not grammatically feasible; thus, the inappropriateness of the grammar should also be understood. 'The meaning should be taken in this way' means that without connecting the word 'pahatabba' with the negation, the compound is formed in the sense of another word (aññapadattha); then, by connecting the word 'atthi' (exists), which is the qualifier of those words, with the negation, the meaning should be understood as: 'For these states, there is no cause that is to be abandoned by vision or cultivation.' In this way, all the intended meanings are included.

Let there be no inappropriateness of interpretation, yet the grammar is still not suitable in this method. The compounding of the two words 'pahatabba' and 'hetu' is suitable only for those who strictly follow the sense of 'atthi' (existence), but not for those who look for a negation. Therefore, this grammatical analysis (viggaha) is made only to show the meaning that should be taken; as for the grammar, it should be applied as is appropriate.

It is appropriate if applied thus: 'The cause to be abandoned exists for these states, therefore they are called pahātabba-hetuka.' By what is it abandoned? It is abandoned by vision and by cultivation. By connecting this term 'pahātabba-hetuka' separately with the terms 'vision' (dassana) and 'cultivation' (bhāvanā), and then separately connecting the negation with those combined terms, it is said: 'Those states which are not states having causes to be abandoned by vision, and are also not states having causes to be abandoned by cultivation, are called neva dassanena na bhāvanāya pahātabba-hetukā.'

Like the phrase 'neva-vipāka-na-vipākadhamma-dhamma,' this is a designation of other states by negating the states included in the preceding two terms; it is not like the term 'ahetuka,' which expresses the mere absence of a cause. By doing so, the two negations become appropriate.

For those states, there is simply no cause that could be abandoned by vision or cultivation. In the previous interpretation, the fact of causes being abandoned by vision and cultivation was rejected. Rejection occurs only when there is a doubt about the possibility of being abandoned. Doubt about being abandoned would occur only if a cause existed. But for those rootless (ahetuka) states, there is no cause at all that could be abandoned by vision or cultivation; because of the absence of such a cause...
43:
Since there is no doubt about being abandoned, the rejection which has the sense of preventing that abandonment is not possible. Therefore, the meaning is that taking the rootless (ahetuka) states in the sense of 'for these states, there is no cause to be abandoned by vision or cultivation' would not occur. Or else, because the meaning 'otherwise, the rootless states would not be included' is clear, this is not something to be established by reasoning alone; rather, intending only the reason for the meaning to be taken, he said 'For those states, there is no cause at all,' and so on. For those states designated by the term 'neva-dassanena-na-bhāvanāya-pahātabba-hetuka,' such a cause that could be abandoned by vision or cultivation does not exist. Those states are of many kinds, being both with causes (sahetuka) and without causes (ahetuka); therefore, the meaning should be taken as: 'For these states, there exists no cause that is to be abandoned by vision or cultivation.'

'Having made that [Nirvana] the object'—this should be understood as referring to making it an object by way of accomplishing the four functions such as full understanding (pariññā), etc. Otherwise, change-of-lineage (gotrabhū), fruit (phala), and reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā), etc., would also become 'leading to diminution' (apacayagāmin). Alternatively, they are called 'leading to diminution' because they go towards Nirvana, which is the diminution [of defilements], by way of being a cause. Although Nirvana has the nature of not being produced, the relationship of cause and effect between the Path and Nirvana is appropriate because of their status as the attainment and the thing to be attained, or as the abandonment of the origin and the cessation of the origin. As it is said: 'Knowledge of the cessation of suffering is the Discrimination of Meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā); knowledge of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering is the Discrimination of Law (dhammapaṭisambhidā).' For 'attha' means the effect of a cause, and 'dhamma' means the cause. Between the preceding and succeeding terms, in the preceding term, states are mentioned together with their associated (sampayutta) states; in the succeeding term, they are mentioned alone. Just as in the preceding term, in the succeeding meaning also, all supramundane wholesome states of consciousness should be taken, headed by the Noble Path. In the second alternative interpretation, in the phrase 'ācayaṃ gāmino,' it should be noted that the nasal (niggahīta) has been elided. Or else, they are called 'ācaya' because they accumulate; the meaning should also be understood as 'having become accumulations, they proceed or occur.'

The seven types of Sekha (learners) are called 'sekha' because they have the habit of training; they are called 'sekha' because these [states] belong to them, namely, the states of the three lower paths and fruits which are not shared by others. The sentence 'they train by themselves' is an illustration of those states that have the habit of training. For those states that train are those that have the habit of training. As for the literal meaning, they are called 'sekha' because training is their habit. 'Not-sekha' (na sekha) refers to the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) where there might be a doubt about its being 'sekha'; in that case, the negation 'na' is used to exclude it.
44:
It should be understood that mundane states and Nibbāna cannot reach the state of 'asekkha' (beyond training). The trainings (sikkhā) known as virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā) are particularly liberated and pure from their opposing defilements and, because they do not become objects of the corruptions (upakkilesa), these states are rightly called 'sikkhā' and exist only in the four paths and four fruits. Therefore, just like the four lower paths and the three lower fruits, the states of the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) also arise within these trainings. One might doubt whether these states should be considered 'sekkha' (belonging to one in training), thinking that if an Arahant possessed of these trainings were like others in the state of a learner, these states would belong to a learner, or that they have the nature of practicing these trainings. To prevent such doubt, they are called 'asekkha', thereby negating the aforementioned state of being a learner (sekkha).

In truth, the trainings occurring in the Fruit of Arahantship have completed the task of training and no longer perform the function of practicing; they exist merely as the result of training. Therefore, they do not deserve the name 'sikkhā' (in the sense of active training), nor does the one possessed of them deserve the name 'sekkha'. The states of the highest fruit cannot be 'sekkha' through meanings such as 'arising in the training'. In the three lower fruits, however, the trainings still perform the function of training because they continue to serve as a strong sufficing condition (upanissaya) for the insight of the path of the Once-returner and so forth. Therefore, they deserve the name 'sikkhā', and the one possessed of them deserves the name 'sekkha'. The states in those lower fruits are indeed 'sekkha' according to the stated meanings.

Alternatively, by the word 'sekkha', the incomplete training is shown, and by the subsequent word 'asekkha', the completed training is shown. Thus, mundane states and Nibbāna cannot reach the state of 'asekkha'. In the sense that 'states which have reached growth are sekkha', if it is argued that among the sekkha states, some that have reached growth could become 'asekkha', and if it is asked whether the states of the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga)—being both grown and sekkha—thereby become 'asekkha', the answer is no. This is because the term 'asekkha' is used only for the Fruit of Arahantship which is similar to it. The Fruit of Arahantship has no distinction from the Path of Arahantship except for the performance of tasks like full understanding (pariññā) and its nature as a resultant (vipāka). Therefore, those very sekkha states can be said to have reached the state of the Fruit of Arahantship. Because resultant bliss (vipākasukha) is more peaceful and sublime than wholesome bliss (kusalasukha), those states are said to have reached growth and are called 'asekkha'.

They are called 'limited' (paritta) due to reasons such as the inability to suppress defilements. All three meanings of this term are suitable for wholesome states, but for resultants and functionals, only 'long continuity' (dīghasantānatā) is suitable. Alternatively, they are called 'limited' because they are delimited by coarse sense-desire (kāmatanhā) and the like, which create boundaries. States that cannot be delimited by those defilements but are delimited by subtle fine-material desire (rūpatanhā) and the like, and have reached greatness in extent, are called 'exalted' (mahaggata). States that cannot be delimited by any craving whatsoever are called 'immeasurable' (appamāṇa).
45:
The meaning of 'atappaka' is that even if supramundane states are contemplated with reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) all day long, they do not produce satiety; even if the states of the fruit are attained as an attainment (samāpatti), they do not produce satiety. Thus they are called 'atappaka'.

Those who engage in acts such as matricide (mātughāta) still do so desiring their own welfare and happiness. Therefore, they aspire to those acts, thinking, 'These acts of matricide and so forth will bring me welfare and happiness.' Furthermore, because of the firmness of the perversion of perceiving beauty and so forth in the five aggregates—which are actually unattractive (asubha), painful (dukkha), impermanent (anicca), and non-self (anatta)—the occurrence of heinous crimes (ānantariya kamma) and fixed wrong views (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) takes place. Thus, those states have an occurrence that is perverted, seeing beauty and so forth in what is unattractive and so forth. 'Wrong nature' (micchā-sabhāva) means having a false nature.

When many heinous crimes have been committed, the one among them that is powerful produces the result, while the others do not. Considering that it is not possible to state the nature of being 'fixed' (niyata) solely on the basis of inevitably producing a result, the text says 'when there is the giving of a result' (vipākadāne sati) and so forth. In that phrase, 'immediately after the breaking up of the aggregates' (khandhabhedānantara) means immediately after death (cuti). This is because the Buddha described death in the 'Explanation of Death' (Maraṇaniddesa) as the 'breaking up of the aggregates'.

By this statement, 'if there is the giving of a result, it is only immediately after death', it is said that the state of being 'fixed' (niyata) is stated only because of the certainty of the time of the result, not because of the certainty of the giving of the result itself. Therefore, other kammas to be experienced in the next life (upapajja-vedanīya) and kammas to be experienced in this life (diṭṭhadhamma-vedanīya), which have a fixed time for giving results, would also fall into the category of 'fixed'.

Therefore, just as wholesome and unwholesome states that have the nature of giving results are understood as having the nature of result (vipākadhamma) by their own essence even if they do not produce a result due to the deficiency of other conditions, so too, when one powerful heinous crime has given its result, the other heinous crimes that do not produce a result still possess a fixed nature and an 'immediate' (ānantariya) nature in their occurrence regarding the giving of results. Thus, the nature of being 'fixed' and 'immediate' should be understood by their own essence through the certainty of the timing of the result. It must be accepted that their occurrence is inevitably of a fixed and immediate nature, because in the absence of another powerful heinous crime, they certainly give their result immediately after death.

If this is so, an objection is raised: 'Do not other kammas to be experienced in the next life also possess an immediate and fixed nature, since they certainly give their result immediately after death when there is no other kamma to give the result?' This is not possible. Why? Because they do not have the nature of certainly giving a result in the immediate next existence, as their result can be prevented by a kamma of a different class, by the power of mental aspiration (cetopaṇidhi), or by some destructive kamma (upaghātaka kamma). Just as kammas such as the second jhāna are kammas of a different class that can prevent the result of kammas such as the first jhāna, there is no kamma of a different class that can prevent the result of the kammas called 'ānantariya', because all heinous crimes have Avīci as their result. Furthermore, just as the mental aspiration of a virtuous person who desires rebirth in a lower realm can prevent the result of a kamma that would cause rebirth in a higher realm, the ability to prevent the result of a heinous crime...
46:
Even for a person who does not wish to fall into Avīci Hell, there is no mental aspiration (cetopaṇidhi) that can prevent the result of an ānantariya kamma from causing that fall. Furthermore, there is no other kamma that can destroy an ānantariya kamma. Therefore, it is the nature of these ānantariya kammas alone to invariably produce their result in the immediately following existence.

Even when many ānantariya kammas are committed, they are determined as fixed (niyata) by their nature, because they are firmly certain to produce their result and there is no doubt regarding their non-failing nature. The result that occurs immediately after death (cuti) is called anantara. These kammas are by nature ānantariya because they are associated with that immediate result, they have the habit of producing that immediate result, and they have that immediate result as their purpose.

Among those ānantariya kammas of similar nature, once one kamma has given its result, the others do not produce a second or third rebirth (paṭisandhi), because the function of giving result, which they themselves should perform, has already been performed by that one kamma. This failure to produce a further rebirth is not due to the destruction of their inherent capability. Therefore, there is no regression from their status as fixed (niyata) or as ānantariya. This is because a state of similar nature does not destroy the capability of another state of similar nature. In fact, it should be understood that the other kammas also support the one kamma that gives the result. "Sammā sabhāvā" means they have a true nature.

Because the four functions of the path are fulfilled, "magga" (path) here refers only to the four Noble Paths (ariya magga). "Paccayaṭṭhena" means by way of being a path-condition (magga-paccaya). In the Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa as well, it is stated, "excluding the path-factors of one possessed of the Noble Path" (ariyamagga-samangissa maggangāni thapetvā), etc., to show that those states which receive the path-condition but do not themselves become path-conditions are path-caused (magga-hetuka). In that same Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa, the phrase "or associated with the path" (magga-sampayuttā vā), etc., is stated to show the method beginning with "non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion of one possessed of the Noble Path; these states are path-causes (magga-hetu)." The phrase "Right View itself" (sammādiṭṭhi sayaṃ), etc., is stated to show the method beginning with "Right View of one possessed of the Noble Path is both path and cause (maggañceva hetu ca)." There, three methods are taught in sequence by way of including states not yet included. Here, the third method is stated as the second method by way of the plurality of causes (hetu).

"Abhibhavitvā pavattanaṭṭhena" means that the conascent predominance (sahajātādhipati), occurring in the state of leadership by way of prior preparation, occurs by overcoming the conascent states and making them follow its own will. The object predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) also occurs by overcoming those states that take it as an object, making them follow it in the same way as a leader, by way of being an object, and not by way of being a presently existing state. Therefore, it should be understood that both types of predominance are included. This meaning of "the path is the predominant factor of these" (maggo adhipati etesaṃ) is also found in the Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa...
47:
This meaning of "maggādhipati" is stated by taking the method of meaning that comes by way of illustration in the Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa. However, since it is stated in the Paṭṭhāna (Paṭṭhāna 2.16.11), "Dependent on a maggādhipati state, a maggādhipati state arises through a condition other than the predominance condition; dependent on maggādhipati aggregates, there is maggādhipati predominance," it should be understood that this meaning of "the path is predominant, thus maggādhipati" (kammadhāraya compound) is also included in the Pali text by way of the elision of similar forms (sarūpekasesa) or by way of the meaning of similar words.

By the word "unrisen" (anuppannā), all states of having arisen (uppanna-bhāva) are excluded, not just the state of a thing currently arising. Therefore, it should be understood that past states that have ceased and disappeared are also not included by that word. If they were included, it would have been stated, "An unrisen state is a condition for an arisen state by way of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya)," etc., but it was not so stated.
