"Mind arises first among those states" (mano tesaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭhamaṃ uppajjati) means that although the mind arises together with associated states, it is as if it arises first because it encompasses the associated states and occurs as the chief. Therefore, it is said thus. The associated states are also called unwholesome states following that mind. Or, "mind as precursor" is said with reference to the mind that acts as the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya). The phrase "led by the mind" (cittena nīyati) is said with reference to consciousness associated with the volition called abhisaṅkhāra, or with reference to the mind associated with craving (taṇhā). The word "luminous" (pabhassara) is said with reference to its naturally pure nature. "Unguarded" (arakkhita) means that because it is not guarded by mindfulness from greed, hatred, and so on, it reaches a state of corruption through greed and so on, and is soaked by those very same things. In establishing the precursor nature of the mind, the mutual protection of the Suttas should be understood through the power of mutual support. Or, in this context, the protection of the Suttas should be understood through the power of the long-term occurrence of the Suttas known by the Elders who bear the Abhidhamma. The words beginning with "What kind of wisdom do you have?" (katara-paññaṃ tvaṃ) are not included in the Pāḷi (not recited in the Councils). It is said only in the ancient Commentaries that the Blessed One asked this. "But what is the purpose of wisdom?" (paññā pana kimatthiyā) is also a supporting Sutta. The answer to that question is: "It has the purpose of direct knowledge (abhiññā), full understanding (pariññā), and abandoning (pahāna)." The word "pleasant" (sāta) is said according to the nature of pleasant feeling (somanassa-vedanā). "Sweet" (madhura) is said by way of a metaphor, as being like a sweet taste. "Leading to rebirth" (ponobbhavikā) means having the nature of frequently creating a new existence. Because of greatly delighting in various objects, it is called "delight" (nandī). Lust that occurs as delight is called "delight-lust" (nandirāga). Craving that occurs together with the state of great delight and attachment is called "accompanied by delight and lust" (nandirāgasahagatā). Here, since there is no co-existence by way of association (sampayoga), the word sahagata (accompanied by) only illuminates the nature of craving as being great delight and attachment. The meaning of that term is also "occurring as great delight and attachment." "Support" (nissaya) should be understood in the sense of a basis. "Having material and immaterial objects" (rūpārūpārammaṇānaṃ) refers to (attainments) that have material objects such as the earth kasiṇa and immaterial objects such as the concept of space. "Conjoined" (saṃsaṭṭha) should be understood in the sense of mixing and reaching a state of unity, like milk and water. "Co-nascent" (sahajāta) means co-nascent by association (sampayutta-sahajāta), not merely co-nascent. "Even here" (idhāpi) means "in this term also, this very meaning is intended," as found in this Commentary.
69: The previously shown word "conjoined" (saṃsaṭṭha) is intended in the sense of co-nascent (sahajāta). "Immaterial with material" (arūpaṃ rūpena) refers to (co-existence) with the heart-base (hadayavatthu) at the moment of rebirth-linking. "Excellent exposition" (ukkaṭṭhaniddesa) is a superior indication made by encompassing everything without remainder. "Not being brought forward" (anābhaṭṭhatā) is the state of not being fit to be spoken (abhāsitabbatā), like the states of being seen or heard in the phrases "seen, heard," etc. By the statement of the prompted nature (sasaṅkhārika) of the second mind, which is similar in all aspects, the unprompted nature (asaṅkhārika) of this (first) mind can be known; therefore, the meaning that it is not taken (in the Pāḷi) because it is not fit to be spoken is appropriate. The intention is that because it was not spoken in the Pāḷi, it was not taken or included as something to be taught in that Pāḷi, not because that meaning does not exist. Or else, because it was not spoken in the Pāḷi, it was not taken in the Commentary, and that meaning was not stated. By not stating it here, while later stating the prompted nature of such a state, the unprompted nature is determined (and taught). In this context of "mind-consciousness" (manoviññāṇa), the door (dvāra) is called the base (vatthu); or, by the door, the heart-base (hadayavatthu) which is the companion of that door is meant. "By its own essence" (sarasabhāvena) means by way of its own function. Ignorance (avijjā) has the function of being a condition for volitional formations (saṅkhāra). Or, the nature that is known without being mixed with other states is called "own essence" (sarasabhāva), such as the nature of ignorance, the nature of volitional formations, and so on. There is also a reading "sarasasabhāvena," which has the same meaning. Or, it is shown as "by its own function" through "conditioned by ignorance" (avijjāpaccayā) and "by its own nature" through "volitional formations" (saṅkhārā). The state of "single-origination" (ekasamuṭṭhāna) and so on should be applied only to material states, because such terminology is abundant regarding those material states. The state of being past, etc., should be applied to both material and immaterial states. Or, the states of single-origination, double-origination, and not-from-anywhere-origination (nakutocisamuṭṭhāna) of mind, mental factors, and Nibbāna should be applied according to their nature. "Not having come into range" (anāpāthagatā) means not falling into the range of the eye and so on, due to the smallness of the base, like subtle dust particles; due to the briefness of the moment, like a drop of water falling on a hot iron ball; due to being too far; due to being too near; or due to being past or future. It is called "objective field" (visaya) because it does not occur in other objects, and "range" (gocara) because it resorts to that object. Because of deciding on that object, the mind is the resort (paṭisaraṇa). This meaning is evident; otherwise, the Pāḷi statement "it experiences their range and objective field" would be inappropriate since those (sights, etc.) would be mind-objects (dhammārammaṇa). Although objects like forms that have not come into range are taken as objects by divine eye, divine ear, and the knowledge of psychic powers in the manner stated, they are not found to be called "mind-objects" (dhammārammaṇa) anywhere. In other ways, they are seen in phrases such as "he sees a form with the divine eye."
70:
Mind-consciousness and the fivefold consciousness come into range (āpātha) at the five doors by being capable of being grasped. *Ghaṭṭetvā* means having reached the range (āpātha) in the sense of being directly in front. It is like hearing the voice of a reciter (sarabhāṇaka) who delivers the Pali text. The appearance of an object should be understood through the power of what has been previously seen (diṭṭha), etc.; or through the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) in a waking person following a healthy body due to digestion, suitable climate (utu), special food, and exertion, or a body afflicted by wind, etc., in a sick person; or through the power of strong dependencies (upanissaya) such as bodily pleasure, pain, climate, and food; or through the power of directing the mind, seeing related objects (similar or dissimilar), etc.; and in the case of a sleeping person, through the power of the disturbance of elements (dhātukkhobha), etc., in dreaming. Unseen and unheard objects, such as the form of a future Buddha which is a basis for inspiration, appear in the mind only through the connection of what has been seen or heard, known as similarity (taṃsadisatā). Similarity (taṃsadisatā) is not the only 'dual connection' (ubhaya-sambandha); rather, opposition, being a part of it, association, etc., should also be understood as dual connection. Faith (saddhā) is believing without investigation when hearing someone speak. Preference (ruci) is liking something after investigating it oneself. Reflection on modes (ākāra-parivitakka) is investigating the manner, thinking 'it will be like this or like that.' Acceptance of a view after reflection (diṭṭhi-nijjhānakkhanti) is the intellectual approval of a certain meaning by one who is investigating.

The sign of taking something as beautiful among elements such as red chalk (geruka), orpiment (haritāla), and collyrium (añjana) is called the sign of beauty (subha-nimitta). That object is a basis (vatthu) for greed (lobha) because it is a cause for taking it as beautiful and because it is attractive. *Niyamitavasena* means by the power of a determined mind. The same applies to the other two. *Ābhoga* means attention (ābhujita). Persons with much hatred are rough individuals; those with much non-hatred are smooth and gentle individuals. *Tadadhimuttatā* means the state of the mind being inclined towards rapture (pīti). For these reasons, it should be understood that rapture is inseparable from joy (somanassa), and thus this wholesome consciousness is 'associated with joy' (somanassa-sahagata).

Because it is a means of livelihood, a craft such as elephant-riding is called the sphere of arts (sippāyatana). Work such as farming and trade is called the sphere of occupations (kammāyatana). Knowledge such as the science of longevity (Ayurveda) is called the branch of knowledge (vijjāṭṭhāna). *Abyāpajja* refers to being in the fine-material realm (rūpa-bhava) which is free from the affliction of displeasure (domanassa). *Dhammapada* are groupings of Dhamma. *Pilavanti* means they appear or manifest to knowledge. *Yoga* arises from concentration (samādhi) which is the application of meditation (bhāvanā). *Vatthu-visada-kiriya* is the cleansing of internal and external bases. Not letting the faculties (indriya) such as faith exceed one another is the balancing of the faculties (indriya-samatta-paṭipādanatā). Reflecting on the Suttas which are the domain of profound knowledge, or which should be traversed with profound knowledge, is the reviewing of the range of profound knowledge (gambhīra-ñāṇa-cariya-paccavekkhaṇā).

*Vaṃsa* means lineage, *tantī* means continuity, and *paveṇī* means connection. All these terms refer to the continuity of ancestral conduct and behavior. Because it is morality of conduct, it is called 'consisting in morality' (sīlamaya). From the moment one speaks the words 'I will give' and directs the object [to the recipient], the effort of giving (dāna) is considered to have begun.
71:
When an offense (āpatti) occurs regarding the directing of a gift to oneself, etc., the giving (dāna) is already undertaken by that person. Since it is said that giving is undertaken from the time of thinking about an existing object, it means that wholesome merit consisting in giving (dānamaya-kusala) occurs regarding that existing object. It is not that merit does not occur for a person who is preparing a gift that is not yet present. However, since that merit is the preliminary stage (pubba-bhāga) of the dānamaya, it should be classified under that dānamaya; so it is said in the Commentary. 'By the power of family lineage, etc.' is merely an example. Morality of conduct (cāritta-sīla) should be understood by the power of the duties one has undertaken oneself, as well as by the power of the duties of virtuous people, villagers, and countrymen.

'With the object' (sa-vatthuka) means doing it together with an object such as a drum. 'An existing object' refers to the drum, etc. In activities like announcing the hearing of Dhamma, giving sound together with an object is simply the production of sound along with the vocal organs (ṭhāna-karaṇa) which are the bases of sound. Therefore, the intention of the person making such an announcement should be understood as the relinquishing of an existing object. The Buddha, the King of Dhamma, analyzed and showed the nature of visible objects, etc., here; and in another Sutta, he spoke of the nature of dānamaya, etc., saying, 'Monks, there are these three bases of meritorious action'; and in another place, in the Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa, he spoke of the nature of bodily action, etc., saying, 'Which states are wholesome? Three... bodily action originating from those states.' 'Unincluded states' (apariyāpanna) are those not included [in the sense spheres] because they do not exist in the ultimate sense or because they belong to other spheres (āyatana).

Rapture and joy arising from the cause of enjoyment is called 'the taste of enjoyment' (paribhoga-rasa). This 'taste of enjoyment' is called a 'taste-object' (rasārammaṇa) by way of similarity to taste, but not according to its actual nature. If taken according to its nature, rapture and joy are only mind-objects (dhammārammaṇa); thus it is said, 'Pleasant feeling is a mind-object.' Because only the object is fixed to the mind, it is taught by determining them as visible objects, etc., up to mind-objects. 'Because kamma is not fixed' means because kamma is not certain regarding the doors. Just as a mind with a single object like a visible object does not change to another object, it is not the case that kamma occurring in one door, like the body-door, does not occur in another door; it can occur. Therefore, because kamma has no fixed door, the door also has no fixed kamma. Thus, it is not taught here as fixed, unlike the objects. The meaning of the phrase 'because it does not arise without an object' should be understood as: 'Just as a single kamma in bodily action, etc., moves to another door besides that door, a mind with a single object like a visible object does not arise in another object without that object.' Just as one can call it 'bodily action' even when it arises in the speech-door, one cannot call a mind arising in a sound-object a 'visible object'.
72:
## Wholesome States of the Sense Sphere
## Explanation of the Door of Bodily Action

The statement beginning with "Imassa panatthassa" is said to demonstrate, through such phrases as "actions move in the doors," that the doors of action are not mutually exclusive. In the phrase "five consciousnesses," the reason for not mentioning the sixth consciousness (mind-consciousness) and its door (the mind-door) is that the door and the consciousnesses possessing that door do not occur simultaneously. Because the "body produced by four causes" (catusamuṭṭhānika-kāya) is spoken of in terms of stable matter, sound-matter (sadda-rūpa) and the matter of alteration (vikāra-rūpa) are not included.

Although the air element (vāyodhātu) produced by the first impulsion (javana) is unable to move material phenomena to another location at that very moment, it should be understood as being accompanied by the alteration known as intimation (viññatti). This is because, whether one wishes to go in any of the ten directions or wishes to move one's limbs, that air element supports and sustains the material phenomena facing that direction, thereby creating a specific mode of movement directed toward that quarter. This specific mode of movement, which occurs together with the intention, is called "intimation." In this way, it is appropriate that the mind-door advertence (manodvārāvajjana) also produces intimation by generating the desired matter of alteration. Therefore, it is said that thirty-two types of consciousness produce ordinary matter, postures, and intimation. The air element, arising many thousands of times, reaches a state where it can be said, "He has gone a league (yojana)," or "He has gone ten leagues."

Regarding the phrase "vāyodhātuya... paccayo bhavitunti," there is a specific mode of the great primary elements (mahābhūta) produced by the mind that is capable of being the cause for the air element's functions of supporting and moving. This is called intimation. Because those mind-born primary elements possess such a mode, the air element is able to support and move. By the phrase "na cittasamuṭṭhānā," it is shown that intimation does not exist in the ultimate sense (paramattha). This is because just as no matter can exist without a cause, there is no ultimate reality that is permanent, except for Nibbāna. The term "viññattitāya" means because of being the alteration called intimation. It should be understood that just as it is mind-produced, it is also intended as derived matter (upādā-rūpa) because it is an alteration of the great primary elements.

"Kāyika-karaṇaṃ" refers to the activity of the mind (the intention) occurring at the bodily door. By the statement beginning with "kāreti manyeti," it is shown that intimation is known by perceiving the action produced by the intimation, which is itself perceived according to the sequence of cognizing color (appearance). This is because in things like the swaying of trees, which are devoid of intimation, there is no such cognition as "this tree intends to perform this action." The function of eye-consciousness is merely the falling upon the visible object; it is not the cognizing of the alteration of movement that occurs together with intention. However, due to the rapid changing of the mind...
73:
Because of the rapid succession of the mind, unlearned persons, who cannot distinguish the interval between the eye-consciousness process and the mind-consciousness that cognizes the movement (alteration) immediately after, imagine that they see it with the eye (or eye-consciousness). Just as one cannot perceive the interval between the eye-consciousness process occurring by falling upon a blue object and the mind-consciousness process that follows as "blue," so too, when that material body—which supports and moves the physical frame and is called the specific alteration—is grasped by the mind-door consciousness that follows the eye-consciousness process without a perceivable interval, the cognition arises: "This person intends to do this; this is his intention."

This is like seeing the color of palm leaves and, through the mind-door process occurring immediately after without a perceivable interval, grasping the sign and mode of palm leaves being constantly associated with water, and thereby knowing "water." In this context, by the phrase "there will be water," it should be understood that the sign and mode of that water are known through the cognition of the water itself, which is to be known by the mind-consciousness following the process that cognizes the visible form due to the association with water. It should be understood that for both the process of grasping the bodily action and the process of grasping water, the grasping of a previously established association serves as a strong dependence (upanissaya). Alternatively, even if intimation is not directly taken as an object, it assists the process of grasping the intention—which occurs immediately after the process of grasping the color that is accompanied by the desired alteration—by way of the strong dependence of grasping a previously established association. This is because, in the absence of the alteration that occurs with the intention, the cognition of the intention would not occur. Thus, just as the sign and mode of palm leaves become clear through the process of knowing water immediately after the process of knowing color, so too intimation becomes clear through the process of knowing the intention immediately after the process of knowing color. Therefore, it is said that intimation is known through the cognition of the intention: "I think this person intends to do this and that."

The phrase "this person wishes to strike us" shows the clarity of intimation through the cognition of intention. This is because if that intimation were not clear, the cognition of intention could not occur. By the phrase "occurs only in the presence," etc., just as the nature of being visible to the eye is established for visible objects that have not come into range because they are not present, so too the nature of that intimation, which is an actual reality, is established in two ways: (1) it is called intimation because it makes [the intention] known, and (2) it is called intimation because it is itself known. Even when there is no desire to inform another, by the mere occurrence of moving forward, etc., that alteration of matter occurring with the mind makes the intention known and is itself known. Therefore, it should be understood that both types are indeed intimation. "Established in that door" means it is established by way of being clear in that door, because it is to be known through that bodily door and because it receives the name "bodily action" (kāyakamma) through that very door. It should be defined as "wholesome or unwholesome." Why? Because in the doctrine of other schools (paravādī), the nature of action (kamma) in functional consciousness (kiriya-citta), which does not produce results, is not recognized. However, in the doctrine of our own school (sakavādī), the nature of action in functional consciousness is recognized. Therefore, the eleven types of functional consciousness that produce intimation (mind-door advertence, the smile-producing consciousness, eight great functionals, and functional direct-knowledge) are also included to complete the triad (tika) and are thus defined.
74:
In the view of the opponents (Paravādī), the status of kamma in functional consciousness (kiriya-citta), which does not produce results, is not established; however, in the view of our own school (Sakavādī), it is established. Therefore, the triad (tika) should be completed and set forth by means of the eleven functional consciousnesses that produce intimation (viññatti).

In the verse "Actions occur in the doors," this is the meaning: If doors were to occur in other doors, then due to the confusion of doors, there would also be a confusion of actions. In that case, there would be no mutual distinction such as "bodily action" and "the action occurring in the body-door." The same logic applies to actions occurring in other actions. If, however, there were no occurrence of doors in other actions in the capacity of a door, nor the occurrence of actions in other doors, the distinction between actions and doors would be even better established. But it is not that actions do not occur in other doors; rather, actions that usually occur in their own doors and other actions also occur in other doors.

Since one door cannot occur in another door, actions are distinguished by means of those doors which are the causes and do not occur in other doors, even though the actions themselves occur in other doors. It is not only that actions are distinguished by doors, but doors are also distinguished by those actions. Thus, actions and doors are mutually distinguished by the appropriate reasoning for distinction, stated as "because of occurring for the most part and because of occurring frequently." Among those doors and actions, the status of actions as bodily action and so forth is distinguished by doors that do not occur in other doors, because actions depend on doors. It is not that doors cannot be distinguished by actions that occur in other doors (they can indeed be distinguished). This is because bodily action and so forth, which have been distinguished by doors such as the body-door that do not depend on actions, perform the distinction of the body-door of action and so forth.

Alternatively, even when occurring in other doors, actions occur only as they are always characterized by the body-door and so forth. This is because killing (pāṇātipāta) and so forth have such a nature. Even one who is commanded by means of gestures of the hand and so forth is understood through the nature of what is to be accomplished by the body and other doors. Therefore, even if another action occurs in its own door, the other door does not give its own name to it, nor does the action give its name to the door. In fact, only the respective door gives its name to the action, and the action, even when occurring in another door, gives its name only to its own door. Thus, the mutual distinction is established. The previous statement about the non-fixity of actions in doors was made only with reference to the occurrence of actions in other doors, not with reference to this distinction.

"Tattha" means "among those doors and actions." By the phrase "the place of arising of bodily action," only the intimation (viññatti) co-arising with that action is meant. Although that intimation does not assist that action by any condition (paccaya), it is spoken of as its place of arising because the intimation that distinguishes the action co-arises with that action, and because, according to the stated rule, an action with a different attribute does not arise in another attribute. By the phrase "because it is done by the body," it is called "action done by the body" by way of its own accomplishment, because it produces bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti) and through that bodily intimation accomplishes the cutting off of the life faculty (jīvitindriya) and so forth. In this context, the body (bodily intimation) is the cause.
75:
In the phrase "mutually distinguished," the body is distinguished by the action as "the body-door of action," not merely as "the body." Just as a needle is distinguished as "the means of needlework" through the act of sewing, and not merely as "a needle," so too should this body-door of action be understood. "Mutually distinguished" means "mutually specified." With the phrase "this being so," the objection is raised by taking only the words "Actions occur in the doors" and so forth, without accepting the fixed rule of distinction mentioned above. In that objection, "this being so" means that it would be inappropriate if there were the occurrence of actions in doors, and the obtaining of names and specification through mutual distinction.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Body-door of Action is Finished.

## Explanation of the Section on the Speech-door of Action

In the phrase "monks, endowed with four factors," the volitions (cetanā) arising in such a way should be understood in these words: abstinence from slander (apisuṇavācā) known as speaking well, abstinence from frivolous speech (asamphappalāpa) known as speaking the Dhamma, abstinence from harsh speech (apharusavācā) known as speaking endearingly, and abstinence from false speech (amusāvāda) known as speaking the truth. The phrase "together with sound" is stated because that modification known as intimation arises together with sound. Because it follows the mind, that intimation should be understood as not lasting as long as the sound (i.e., not for the full 17 thought-moments). According to the view of the Great Commentary (Mahā-aṭṭhakathā), which states "the sound produced by the diffusion of thought is not cognizable by the ear," it follows that sound produced by the mind can arise even without the striking of intimation (viññatti-ghaṭṭana) because it is known from the statement "that intimation which is by that speech" that there is no arising of intimation together with sound that is not cognizable by the ear.

In the phrase "the sound-base (saddāyatana) produced by the mind," the view of the Great Commentary is refuted with the intention that there is no sound produced by the mind that is not included. This is because in the sixfold summary of form and so forth, when it is said "cognizable by the ear" and in the phrase "seen, heard," the word "heard" includes every kind of sound. However, in the Great Commentary, the subtle sound produced by thought that causes the movement of the tongue, palate, etc., which arises only together with intimation, is referred to in the Sutta as "having heard with the divine ear, he points out." And in the Paṭṭhāna, referring to gross sound, it is said "it is a condition for ear-consciousness by way of object-condition." With this intention, the state of not being cognizable by the ear might have been stated. (However, since these two statements—that it is sound and that it is not cognizable by the ear—are contradictory, the rejection by the author of the Sangaha should be noted.)
76:
The statement that sound is not to be known by ear-consciousness (*asotaviññeyya*) should be understood as rejected because it is contradictory. Impact caused by intimation is called *viññatti-ghaṭṭanā*. Or, intimation itself is called impact (*ghaṭṭanā*). This is because the specific alteration of the primary elements (*bhūta-rūpa*) that arises by way of the mode of impact is called "impact" (*ghaṭṭanā*). Sound arises only simultaneously with mutual impact, not in a sequence of before and after. This phrase "*pathavī-dhātuyā*" is stated by considering that just as the function of motion is primary for the air element (*vāyo-dhātu*), the function of mutual impact is primary for the earth element (*pathavī-dhātu*). The fact that the alteration (*vikāra*) is the cause of that impact should also be understood in the same manner as already stated. This is because the great primaries (*mahābhūta*) possessing that alteration serve as conditions for one another. All other arrangements should be understood just as in the case of bodily intimation (*kāya-viññatti*).

The section beginning with "*tisamuṭṭhānikakāyaṃ*..." cannot be obtained in this discussion on the door of vocal action (*vacī-kamma-dvāra-kathā*). This is because motion (*cālana*) is not the impact (*ghaṭṭana*) of the grasped-at matter (*upādinna-rūpa*). Motion (*cālana*) is the succession of arising in different locations, while impact (*ghaṭṭana*) is the arising of material clusters (*rūpa-kalāpa*) in extreme proximity due to a specific condition. In saying that there is no function of support (*upatthambhana-kicca*), it means that although it arises from the first consciousness without support, it occurs by way of the mode of impact; thus, there is no use for support for the sake of impact, because the impact is powerful through the consciousness that has attained repetition (*āsevana*). Whether support exists or not should be accepted after careful investigation.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Door of Vocal Action is Finished.

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Door of Mental Action

This statement, "It should not be said that such-and-such volition is not kamma," is stated for the purpose of showing that the mind (*mano*) is the door for that volition. "He arranges (*kappeti*)" means it occurs as if arranging thus: "You, contact (*phassa*), perform the act of touching; you, feeling (*vedanā*), perform the act of experiencing." *Pakappana* is also that same arranging. "How does it make a heap?" is asked by way of the meaning of accumulation (*āyūhana*). Setting the states such as contact (*phassa*) and so on into their respective functions without letting them be scattered is called accumulation (*āyūhana*). Striving laboriously in that very function is called *cetayana*. Acting in such a way is called *abhisaṅkharaṇa*. Since supramundane kamma brings about the destruction of kamma, only the kamma belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmaka*) is taken here.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Door of Mental Action is Finished.
77:
## Explanation of the Discourse on Kamma

In the phrase 'Having willed, one performs kamma,' because one performs the kamma of decision after having willed with the preceding volition, the kamma preceded by volition is of the same nature as that volition; thus it means 'I, the Buddha, call volition kamma.' Alternatively, although they occur at the same time, it is proper to speak of the causal action as if it were in the past, and the resultant action as if it were in the future. And because, having willed with volition, one performs the action of movement (copana) through body and speech, and the action of covetousness (abhijjhā) etc. through the mind, it means 'I call the volition that performs that action kamma.'

'Or in the body' means in the body known as bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti). 'When it exists' means while it is present or not yet ceased. The volition that causes bodily intimation to arise is called bodily volition (kāyasañcetanā). Here also, there should be kamma that produces pleasure and pain; and since volition is said to produce pleasure and pain, its status as kamma is established.

'Sañcetanīya' means that which has the nature of volition (kamma). The Elder Samiddhi answered without distinguishing: 'Friend... performed with volition... one experiences pleasure with the mind.' But that question should be answered by distinguishing it as 'to be experienced as pleasure' (sukhavedanīya) etc.; therefore, it is not called a correctly answered question. The same method applies to the other two.

According to the Suttas, the body and speech, which are the bases for the action of movement (copana), and the mind-doors, which are the bases for the action of covetousness (abhijjhā) etc., are called 'doors.' Just as one performs cutting etc. with instruments like a knife, the volition by which one performs the action of movement, covetousness, etc., through those instruments such as the body, is called kamma. Thus, in the occurrence at the doors, the non-confusion of kamma and doors, and the definition of kamma and doors, are evident. This being so, verses such as 'If kamma is performed by the body...' are very appropriate.

Although the Supramundane Path (lokuttaramagga) is not intended in this discourse on mundane kamma, if it is included, it falls into the three kammas. 'Immorality by mind' (manena dussīlya) includes all unwholesome states except for bodily and vocal transgressions; or it takes wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. That statement is also said by way of the opposite of restraint (saṃvara), as in 'Restraint by mind is good,' not by way of the failure of virtue (sīlavipatti). This is because that failure of virtue in the mind-door does not exist. The inclusion of only the Path is because of its vast range. The factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) would fall only into mental action; it is not that the inclusion of those factors of enlightenment cannot be known by the inclusion of the Path.
78:
The coordination of doors (dvāra-saṃsandana) refers to the confluence and inclusion of actions in their respective doors even before they reach the status of a course of action (kamma-patha), and the non-destruction of the doors of kamma even when another kamma arises in another door. Because it is said in the passage beginning with, "Monks, there are three kinds of bodily volition (kāya-sañcetanā) that are unwholesome bodily action," that only the concluding volition (sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā) which has reached the status of a course of action is called 'kamma', it is stated that all preceding volitions do not constitute bodily action. The phrase "having commanded... for one who does not obtain" is said with reference to the fact that those commanded have not yet killed; it means that it is merely verbal misconduct (vacī-duccarita) because it has not reached the status of a course of action. By the power of the ill-will (byāpāda) that arises as "May these beings be killed," they are included in the side of volition because they receive the designation of bodily action. Alternatively, they are 'non-expressive' (abbohārika) because they lack the designation of mental action. The water element and others in the earth and buildings are examples here. 

'Kulumba' means a fetus or a clan. Because it was not permitted to be included in all three Councils (Saṅgīti), it is said, "to your Sutta." The ten kinds of psychic power (iddhi) should be taken from the Discussion on Iddhi (Iddhikathā) in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. 'Bhāvanāmaya' (produced by development) is said with reference to the power of determination (adhiṭṭhāniddhi). The comparison is consistent: the killing of others is like the breaking of a pot, and the destruction of psychic power is like the destruction of water. "Your question" refers to the meaning intended to be known, that one can kill others through psychic power produced by development. Atharvana power (āthabbaṇiddhi) is psychic power produced by science (vijjāmayiddhi). "At the seventh step" means at the seventh step from the circle or such area. 

'Neyyattha' is the meaning to be inferred through other words; 'nītattha' is the meaning to be understood directly by itself. The question "Does it arise from action or from non-action?" is asked with reference to the deliberate lying (sampajāna-musāvāda) intended by that person, and not to the teaching in the Uposathakkhandhaka. This is because that person speaks by assuming that the ignoble speech (anariya-vohāra) not taught in the Uposathakkhandhaka was actually taught. 'Vācāgira' means the sound called speech or the utterance of words. 

In the phrase "The gods Khanda and Siva are supreme," 'Khanda' refers to the Kumāra gods, and 'Siva' refers to the Mahessara gods. It should be understood that this is said to illustrate wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). This is because only views such as the nihilistic view (natthika-diṭṭhi) are kammas that reach the status of a course of action. Here, the statement that volition is 'non-expressive' (abbohārika) means that although it arises in the bodily door and verbal door, it does not receive the name of bodily action or verbal action because greed (abhijjhā) and so on are predominant. However, according to the teaching, "Monks, there are three kinds of mental volition (mano-sañcetanā) that are unwholesome mental action," that volition is mental action by its own nature, and not because it is an associate of greed and so on. Therefore, it is not said to be "an associate of greed and so on." However, in this context, when one thinks without moving the limbs of the body or the organs of speech, both the volition and the mental states associated with volition...
79:
...arise only in the mind-door (manodvāra). Therefore, the intention of the author is that the 'non-expressive' (abbohārika) nature of volition does not exist for any reason. 

According to the teaching beginning with, "Monks, there are three kinds of bodily volition (kāya-sañcetanā) that are wholesome bodily action," only those volitions characterized by abstinence from killing and so on, which are the opposites of killing (pāṇātipāta) and so on, constitute the abstinence from killing and so forth. Therefore, it is said they "belong to the side of volition," and not that they "belong to the side of abstinence (virati)." 'Rakkhati' (protects) means speaking without destroying. 'Bhindati' (breaks) means speaking by destroying. 

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Kamma is finished. 

'Cakkhu-viññāṇa-dvāra' (eye-consciousness door) means the door of eye-consciousness. Alternatively, it is the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) and also the door for those eye-door cognitive processes; thus it is called 'eye-consciousness door'. Alternatively, 'cakkhu viññāṇa-dvāra' is an uncompounded description. That eye-consciousness door is indeed the eye-sensitivity. This method applies to the remaining doors (ear-consciousness door, etc.) as well. In the verse beginning with "Restraint in the eye is good," the Buddha taught "restraint by the body (kāya-saṃvara)" by combining the restraint of the sensitive body (pasāda-kāya-saṃvara) and the restraint of the moving body (copana-kāya-saṃvara). In this commentary, that bodily restraint is divided into two, and the eight kinds of restraint (saṃvara) are explained, along with the eight kinds of non-restraint (asaṃvara) which are their opposites. Although the five kinds of restraint, such as the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), arise in all doors, they are only five in essence. Immorality (dussīlya) and so on, which are the opposites of those restraints, are called the five kinds of non-restraint. Among those five, immorality refers to the volition of killing and so on. Muddled mindfulness (muṭṭhassacca) refers to the unwholesome states that are the opposite of mindfulness. Some teachers call it negligence (pamāda). Irritation (paṭigha) occurring towards cold, heat, etc., is called intolerance (akkhanti). Sloth and torpor (thina-middha) is called laziness (kosajja). 

"Excluding the verbal door, it is called the pure bodily door"—this statement is made to prevent the impurity of the bodily door, because actions such as lying, which are marked by the verbal door, also clearly occur in the bodily door. In reality, that (lying, etc.) is not bodily action. It is only verbal action marked by the pure verbal door. Here, by the word 'non-restraint' (asaṃvara), the non-restraint marked by the pure bodily door is mentioned even if it arises in another door (the verbal door). All unwholesome acts occurring in that door that are not marked by another door should also be understood as included. By doing so, in the section on the coordination of the courses of action (kamma-patha-saṃsandana), the statement "Non-restraint arising by power of the door of non-restraint of the moving body is only unwholesome bodily action" becomes consistent with the statement "Unwholesome bodily action arises by power of the door of non-restraint of the moving body and by power of verbal non-restraint." This is because non-restraint...
80:
Non-restraint (asaṃvara), even if it arises in another door, is said to occur only in its own door; it is also said to arise by the power of its own door. Even if kamma arises in another door, it is said to arise by the power of that other door. In this way, there is no contradiction.

Alternatively, in this context, without distinguishing between purity (suddhi) and impurity (asuddhi), it means 'in this door of non-restraint of bodily movement' (copanakāya-asaṃvaradvāra). When this is the case, verbal or mental action (vacīkamma, manokamma) characterized by another door—namely the verbal or mental door—which has reached the state of a course of action (kammapatha), if it arises in the door of non-restraint of bodily movement, it is called 'non-restraint of bodily movement,' just like other unwholesome states arising in that door. Since bodily action (kāyakamma) arising in another door (the verbal door) by way of reaching the state of a course of action is not called as such (non-restraint of bodily movement), there might be a contradiction with the section on the comparison of courses of action (kammapatha-saṃsandana). I shall explain the lack of contradiction in that very section on the comparison of courses of action. The five types of restraint, such as restraint by virtue (sīlasaṃvara), will become clear in the Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa. Among those five, it should be understood that the virtue dependent on requisites (paccayasannissita-sīla) is included in restraint by knowledge (ñāṇasaṃvara), and the virtue of purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla) is included in restraint by energy (vīriyasaṃvara).

## Commentary on the Course of Unwholesome Action
Atipāta (killing) means the excessive causing to fall, even in the interval before the end of the lifespan, of a being who is prone to falling by its own nature of destruction. It means causing to fall quickly without allowing it to fall slowly. Alternatively, atipāta is causing to fall by overcoming with weapons and so on. The greatness of the fault (mahāsāvajjatā) is due to the greatness of the effort (payoga), the greatness of the object (vatthu), and so on. This is because of the strength of the intention (cetanā) arising from those causes. Even in the reversal of the aforementioned causes, the smallness or greatness of the fault should be understood by the strength or weakness of the intention arising from those respective causes. The use of power resulting from the fruition of kamma, such as the power of King Dāṭhakoṭika and others, is called iddhimaya payoga (effort accomplished by psychic power).

Gottarakkhitā refers to a woman protected by those of the same clan. Dhammarakkhitā refers to a woman protected by fellow practitioners (sahadhammika). Sasāmikā refers to a woman who has a husband (sārakkā). A woman for whose movement the king has imposed a penalty is called saparidaṇḍā. By the word 'atthabhañjaka' (destroyer of welfare), the act of lying that has reached the state of a course of action is meant. This is because this discussion is about the course of action. The statement 'unwillingness to give one's own property' and so on is mentioned because of its similarity to false speech (musāvāda). Only the speech of one who prioritizes deception with the desire to be humorous is called musāvāda. 'Suññabhāva' (state of emptiness) refers to being void because of the absence of joy and affection. Because the meaning is distorted, it does not reach the heart. 'Aggaṇhante' means if one does not believe, it does not reach the state of a course of action. It should be noted that any frivolous talk (samphappalāpa) is accomplished through two factors. It should be understood that the inclination towards oneself occurs only through the mind. 'Micchāpassati' means one sees incorrectly.
81:
'By way of parts' (koṭṭhāsato) means among the parts that are factors of the mind, such as contact as the fifth (phassapañcamaka), it refers to those parts. (An objection is raised:) Is it not the case that intention (cetanā) is not mentioned in the courses of action (as 'intention of killing' etc.), and therefore the status of the seven (killing, etc.) as courses of action in sequence is improper? No, the non-mention of intention is due to another reason. It is not that intention is not mentioned in the group of courses of action because it is not a course of action; rather, it is not mentioned because its status as a course of action is not constant, as it is a course of action only sometimes and not always. It should be understood that when it becomes a course of action, its inclusion in the group of courses of action is not prohibited. By the statement 'The five precepts have only limited objects (parittārammaṇa),' the commentator himself will resolve the contradiction regarding the status of taking what is not given (adinnādāna) etc., having beings as their object, by saying 'because they occur by taking as an object only the formations (saṅkhāra) designated as beings.' The view that 'there are no spontaneously arising beings (opapātika)' is said to have formations as its object because it has as its object the phenomena belonging to the three planes. The results of fruition (vipāka) and the results of natural consequence (nissanda) are, in order, the state of being in a miserable destination such as hell, and the badness of the physical appearance, and so on.

## The Commentary on the Course of Unwholesome Action is finished.

## Commentary on the Course of Wholesome Action

Regarding the statement 'abstinences from killing and so on,' it is said with the consideration that the intentions associated with those abstinences (virati) are called 'bodily and verbal actions,' and their status as courses of action is also proper. Therefore, it will be said later: 'In sequence, the seven intentions are also valid, and the abstinences are also valid.' 'Allasasamamsa' refers to the meat of a living rabbit. It is not known that he was one who had taken life. The life-faculty (jīvitindriya) and so on, which are the objects of immorality (dussīlya) etc., are the objects of those wholesome courses of action. To show how the wholesome courses of action having the life-faculty etc. as objects abandon immorality and so on, the passage beginning with 'Yatha pana' is stated. 'For one who abstains by way of non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) etc.' means for one who abandons covetousness. Indeed, there is no abstinence (virati) from mental misconduct, because that mental misconduct is abandoned by the very states of non-covetousness and so on.

## Commentary on the Comparison of Courses of Action

This is to show that there is no difference in meaning between non-restraints such as immorality (dussīlya) and misconducts that have reached the state of a course of action with the unwholesome courses of action; and similarly, between restraints such as virtue (susīlya) and good conducts that have reached the state of a course of action with the wholesome courses of action. Alternatively, some teachers say that the comparison of courses of action (kammapatha-saṃsandana) is the explanation of the non-contradiction of those non-restraints/misconducts and restraints/good conducts with the doors of contact (phassadvāra) and so on.
82:
Some teachers state (that showing the non-contradiction of non-restraint/misconduct and restraint/good conduct with sense-contact doors and so on is called the 'Correlation of the Courses of Action' [Kammapathasaṃsandana]). This statement should be scrutinized. This is because non-restraint and restraint arising in the five sense-contact doors, the five doors of non-restraint, and the five doors of restraint do not possess the status of a course of action (kammapatha). This is because killing (pāṇātipāta) and so on, as well as covetousness (abhijjhā) directed at others' property, ill-will (byāpāda) directed at beings, and the wrong view of non-causality (ahetukadiṭṭhi) and so on, do not arise in those doors.

It is well-known that the three types of bodily misconduct and so on are courses of action. What would be the benefit of showing that they are not different from the courses of action when this is already clear? Furthermore, the arising of misconduct and good conduct by way of sense-contact doors and so on has not been shown, nor has the non-contradiction of non-restraint and restraint with sense-contact doors been shown. Only the status of bodily action and so on of non-restraint and restraint arising purely by way of sense-contact doors and so on has been shown. If merely showing the status of bodily action and so on of such non-restraint and restraint were the 'Correlation of the Courses of Action,' then the correlation statement such as 'unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five sense-contact doors' would not exist. If it is argued that this also shows non-contradiction with the six sense-contact doors, then it would be improper to say 'Or else' (atha vā) to show it in another way.

If the word 'Or else' (atha vā) is used in the sense of conjunction (samuccaya), then those teachers who speak of things like immorality (dussīlya) that have reached the status of a course of action by the names of bodily action and so on should not speak of the arising of mental action by way of the six sense-contact doors. This is because that mental action does not arise by way of the eye-door and so on. If only those non-restraints and so on that have reached the status of a course of action are taken, then because there are no non-restraints other than misconduct, and because the status of those non-restraints as respective actions has already been stated, it would be improper to say, 'The non-restraint arising by way of the door of bodily non-restraint that causes movement is only unwholesome bodily action.' If that were said, there would be confusion (saṅkara). This is because verbal action and mental action also arise in the bodily door; likewise, other actions arise in the remaining doors.

Or else, if another action arising in a different door were also considered only an action of that door, then the statement 'the three types of bodily misconduct are only unwholesome bodily action' and the statement 'unwholesome bodily action arises either by way of the door of bodily non-restraint or by way of the door of verbal non-restraint' would be contradictory. Although misconduct occurs in other doors, an action arising in another door does not change into the name of that other action.

Therefore, because the status of bodily action and so on of misconduct that has reached the status of a course of action has been stated below (in the section on Correlation of Doors), and because the belonging of wholesome and unwholesome states arising in various doors to those respective doors has been established, the 'Correlation of the Courses of Action' [Kammapathasaṃsandana] consists of: showing the status of bodily action and so on for non-restraint and restraint—which do not reach the status of a course of action and are not called 'action' (kamma) because they are not volition (cetanā)—by classifying them as if they were courses of action; showing that the three types of bodily misconduct and so on, and the three types of bodily good conduct and so on, which have reached the status of a course of action, do not abandon their nature as bodily action and so on even when they occur in other doors; and showing the arising of those unwholesome and wholesome bodily actions and so on, whether they have reached the status of a course of action or not as previously explained, by way of sense-contact doors and so on.
83:
The manifestation of how unwholesome bodily actions and so on—whether they have reached the status of a course of action or not—and wholesome bodily actions and so on arise through the sense-contact doors and so on is called the 'Correlation of the Courses of Action' [Kammapathasaṃsandana]. Why? Because misconduct and so on that do not reach the status of a course of action are correlated here with those that are courses of action, and those that are courses of action are correlated with those that are not, by virtue of having the same name; and because actions that reach the status of a course of action do not abandon their general designation within the courses of action; and because both types are shown here as correlated within the doors by virtue of their arising.

In that section of the Correlation of the Courses of Action, because actions arising by way of the three action-doors (kammadvāra) are already known as actions, there is no need to state their status as such actions; and because their arising in the action-doors has already been stated; and because there is no scriptural statement explaining the arising of non-restraint and so on by way of the five consciousness-doors (viññāṇadvāra), the text avoids action-doors and consciousness-doors and states, 'arisen by way of the five sense-contact doors' and so on. This is because the Buddha taught the arising of non-restraint and so on by way of the five sense-contact doors through such passages as, 'Whatever [feeling] arises conditioned by eye-contact, whether pleasant...' and 'There is a wholesome aggregate of feeling conditioned by eye-contact.' There is no such statement as 'conditioned by eye-consciousness.' It has also been stated, 'The contact co-nascent with eye-consciousness is eye-contact.' By that statement, since non-restraint and restraint are not co-nascent with eye-contact and so on, it should be understood that only the non-restraint and restraint co-nascent with mind-contact (manosamphassa) are shown to arise by way of the eye-contact door and so on.

By the statement, 'When that non-restraint reaches movement (copana) in the bodily door, it becomes unwholesome bodily action,' and 'The non-restraint arising by way of the door of bodily non-restraint that causes movement is only unwholesome bodily action,' it should be understood that when verbal actions and so on, which have reached the status of a course of action and are of the nature of non-restraint, are about to assume the name of bodily action and so on, they are prevented by the exclusionary statement, 'The four types of verbal misconduct are only unwholesome verbal action.' By doing this, there is no contradiction with the first or second analysis of non-restraint shown previously. This is because bodily non-restraint that involves movement but is of the nature of verbal action and so on cannot become bodily action.

Unwholesome mental action arises by way of the six sense-contact doors; when that mental action reaches movement in the bodily and verbal doors, it becomes unwholesome bodily and verbal action. In this context, what is that unwholesome mental action? According to the method shown below, it refers to the three types of mental misconduct arising in the bodily and verbal doors and all unwholesome states that have not reached movement. If that is the case, since that mental action cannot possess the status of bodily or verbal action, the statement 'it becomes bodily or verbal action that has reached movement' is not...
84:
If it is asked, "Is it appropriate?" It is not that it is inappropriate; it is indeed appropriate. This is because the meaning is established that unwholesome action reaching movement (copana) in the body and speech occurs. If it is asked, "What kind of action is it when it occurs?" It should be answered that it is only mental action (manokamma). This is what is meant: unwholesome [action] reaching movement in the body-door and speech-door is mental action. Alternatively, without connecting the word 'taṃ' (that) with the word 'manokamma', it should be connected with the mere occurrence defined as what arises by way of the six sense-doors. If it is asked, "What is this taṃ?" Since it occurs in the discussion of kamma, it is understood as 'kamma'. Even though that kamma arises at the mind-contact door, it can be of all three types. To show these three divisions, [the teacher] said "kāyavacīdvāresu copanaṃ pattaṃ" (reaching movement in the body and speech doors), etc. There, because no restriction was made with the word 'eva' (only), the reaching of movement serves as a characteristic (upalakkhaṇa) that establishes the names 'bodily action' and 'vocal action'. However, it is not that all kamma reaching movement is only bodily or vocal action; nor is it the case that in the wholesome side, kamma not reaching movement is not bodily or vocal action—this meaning is established. 

Alternatively, 'taṃ' refers to mental action arising by way of the six sense-doors. This is said by taking the intention of the objector (codaka) that all kamma accomplished by the mind is mental action, and it does not refer to the mental action shown previously. To refute the objector's view that "Since it is accomplished by the mind, all should be mental action only, not bodily or vocal action," and to show the classification of the three kammas, [the teacher] began with "taṃ kāyavacīdvāresu copanaṃ pattaṃ", etc. Here, the absence of confusion [between kammas] should be understood in the same way as the previous method. Alternatively, connecting it with the general term 'kamma', it shows how the aforementioned divisions of kamma occur. The lack of confusion is as already stated. As for what the teachers of words (padakāra) say—"When greed (abhijjhā) etc. co-nascent with bodily and vocal action are on the side of volition, those mental actions become bodily and vocal actions"—that is not correct. Because greed etc. on the side of volition are not mental actions. If it is negligible (avvohārika), the state of being mental action is even less present. The teachers have said "avvohārikā vā". Therefore, mental action should not be called bodily or vocal action. Only greed etc. associated with volition performing the acts of greed etc. are mental action, not greed etc. associated with volition performing bodily and vocal acts like killing. Therefore, since those states are mental action, they should not be called bodily or vocal action. Thus, because actions are not fixed to doors, and doors are not fixed to actions, the binding of the mind by doors was not made. Now, even though the binding by doors is not made, according to the Pāḷi as it was handed down, showing the occurrence by way of those doors through which this consciousness arises and by way of the respective courses of action (kammapatha) in those doors...
85:
To clarify that meaning, [the teacher] said "Tattha kāmāvacaraṃ", etc. The statement that consciousness arises by way of the three doors of action is said by taking its occurrence as the door of mental action by its own nature. Alternatively, just as in the phrase "cittādhipateyya" (predominance of mind), it is called 'mind' by way of the associated states, so too should it be understood here. Regarding the mental sequence (manopabanda) devoid of the two types of movement (copana) [bodily and vocal], there is nothing further to be said about its being the door of mental action.

## The Explanation of the Comparison of the Courses of Action is finished.

## The Explanation of the Doors is finished.

"Ayaṃ yojanā" (This is the construction) means the benefit of the connection of this text "yaṃ yaṃ vā pana" with "rūpārammaṇaံ vā...pe... dhammarammaṇaံ vā". What is this connection (sambandha)? The purpose in the preceding and following words, by which the words are linked to one another, is called 'sambandha'. Here too, showing the state of having all objects etc. should be seen as the construction (yojanā), the purpose for stating "yaṃ yaṃ vā pana" immediately after "rūpārammaṇaံ vā...pe... dhammarammaṇaံ vā". In that commentary, having shown the fault that might arise with only the text "rūpārammaṇaံ vā...pe... dhammarammaṇaံ vā ārabbha", [the teacher] said "heṭṭhā" etc. to show the purpose of "yaṃ yaṃ vā pana" by way of removing that fault. In the second alternative interpretation, by the phrase "yaṃ yaṃ vā pana", even non-prominent objects like rūpa etc. are included. For the primary consciousness does not have the nature of being its own object. "Heṭṭhā vuttanayena" (by the method stated below/previously) means by the method of having all objects etc. Having said "what was taken below is indeed taken", [the teacher] said this to show the purpose of that statement: "rūpaṃ vā...pe... idaṃ vā idaṃ vā ārabbha". There, "idaṃ vā idaṃ vā" should be understood as being said with reference to the state of having all objects etc.

## The Discussion on the Summary of States (Dhammuddesavāra)

## The Explanation of the Group of Five Beginning with Contact (Phassapañcamaka)

"Ācariyānaṃ" (of the teachers) refers to the teacher Revata. However, this should not be regarded as the essence. For this was not begun to show the kāmāvacara nature etc. of contact and so on, but rather to show the nature of contact etc. at that time.

"Cittassa paṭhamābhinipātattā" (because of being the first impact of the mind): because all mental factors (cetasika) depend on the mind and are spoken of as the activity of the mind, contact is called "the first impact of the mind".
86:
In truth, the person for whom contact (phassa) has arisen, or the group of consciousness (citta) and mental factors (cetasika), being touched by the object, experiences it through the feeling (vedanā) born of that contact at the very moment that contact occurs. However, just as a lamp is the specific cause of light, contact is the specific cause of feeling and so on; therefore, it is called 'initial impact' (paṭhamābhinipāta), as if it occurs first. The wood placed crosswise on top of the rafters is called 'duck's wing' (pakkhapāsa). Just as two pieces of wood etc. adhere to each other in part, the common nature of contact with the material object is merely an impact without adhering; it is not the state of being the object itself. And the impact (saṅghaṭṭana) of contact is simply the state of the meeting of consciousness and the object.

Because it arises completely through the meeting of the base (vatthu) and the object (ārammaṇa), contact has the function of successful impact (saṅghaṭṭanasampatti-rasa). Like the meeting of two hands, contact, which is the meeting of consciousness and the object, is the cause for the occurrence of consciousness meeting the object; thus, in terms of its function, it has the function of impact (saṅghaṭṭana-rasa). That being the cause is indeed the impacting work of that contact.

Just as the impact of one palm against another is the result of material phenomena with an excess of the air element (vāyo-dhātu) which are the specific causes of that impact, so too the impact of consciousness on the object should be understood as a certain mental factor (phassa) which is the cause of that impact. By the words 'only in consciousness', the nature of the mental factor that produces feeling without mixing with the base and the object is shown; however, it does not reject the fact that there is a physical base (vatthu) as a support.

The attention (āvajjanā) that is the cause of that contact and is appropriate to it is called 'appropriate attention' (tajjāsamannāhāra). This means the turning of the faculty towards that object, the adverting's act of making it an object, and the preparation or conditioning of the object are the making of the object for consciousness.

The former teachers intended that (the function of experiencing) is obtained only in pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) because of its enjoyable nature. 'Worthiness' (vissavitā) means (experiencing) by way of being worthy. Since roots have many meanings, the root 'su' preceded by the prefix 'vi' has the meaning of 'worthy' (araha). Alternatively, 'vissava' means capability, power, or the ability to act according to one's will, which is called vissavitā. The statement that they experience only a portion of the flavor of the object is said because functions such as touching (phusana) are like experiencing only a portion. The nature of feeling (vedayita) alone is the primary experiencing. Alternatively, taking the object by way of touching etc. is experiencing a portion, while taking it by way of feeling is experiencing the whole according to one's desire.

Since such takings of the object are of this nature, one should not object that contact and so on also experience like a master by performing their own functions, as feeling does. By the words 'in this place', among the five types of feeling, the joyful feeling (somanassa-vedanā) intended in this consciousness is spoken of. Therefore, it should be understood that, excluding non-joyful feeling, the joyful feeling taken has the function of experiencing a desirable aspect (iṭṭhākārasambhogarasa), which is common to all (joyful feelings).
87:
Perception (saññā) has the function of recognizing again by means of a sign, and thus has the function of re-cognition (paccābhiññāṇa-rasa). The cause of recognizing again is called the cause of recognizing again (punasañjānana-paccaya); that sign itself is the sign; the making of that sign is the making of a sign (nimitta-karaṇa). Or, it means that the making of a sign, which is the cause of recognizing again, is the function of that perception. It should be understood as common to all perceptions that make a sign and recognize by a sign. It only follows the course of wisdom (ñāṇa); therefore, it means there is no wrong attention or perverted grasp. In this way, perception associated with concentration (samādhi) also does not perish quickly (it lasts long).

'Binds together' (abhisandahati) means it connects or causes to occur. The state of volition (cetanā) is the state of activity (byāpāra). 'Double effort' (diguṇussāha) is not said with reference to a double application of energy (vīriya), but it shows the greatness of its own function of activity. 'By way of the state of effort' (ussāhana-bhāva) means by way of the state of care (ādara-bhāva). For that volition is itself of the nature of care and causes the associated states to be careful.

Cognizing (vijānana) is the apprehension (upaladdhi) of the object. Connecting (sandahana) is the linking of the continuity of consciousness. 'Seen by the eye' means the object to be seen by the eye. Just as 'seen, heard, sensed, cognized' refers to the object seen etc., so should it be understood here. In 'by the eye' etc., it means by the eye-door... by the mind-door. Like a city gatekeeper, the function of consciousness is merely the manifesting of the object, merely reflecting, merely apprehending. However, functions such as penetrating the object and re-cognition are the functions of wisdom (paññā), perception (saññā), and so on. 'Shown previously' refers to the consciousness shown in the definition of the occasion (samayavavatthāna). It is not that it does not arise like a person developing (meditation), but to show that it does arise, it is said 'consciousness comes to be' (cittaṃ hoti). This would be appropriate if the word 'hoti' and the word 'uppajjati' (arises) had the same meaning. If they had the same meaning, it should not be said 'the consciousness that has arisen comes to be' in that place. For it is not proper to say that what has arisen arises. Since the state of having arisen of consciousness was already stated in the definition of the occasion, why show its arising again? It is not that the consciousness which made the definition of the occasion cannot be explained in detail, so why is a second summary (uddesa) needed to explain it in detail? Since the difference of consciousness from contact etc. is established by the detailed explanation (niddesa) itself, why say it again for that purpose? Because the first mention of consciousness has a different purpose, it is mentioned again later. The first mention was only for the purpose of defining the occasion, not for showing the states existing in the defined occasion. The other (later) mention was for showing the states existing in that occasion, not for the purpose of defining the occasion. A statement with one purpose does not speak of another purpose. And it is not that the Great Compassionate One, having spoken briefly, does not make the meaning clear.

## The Explanation of the Group of Five Starting with Contact is Finished.
88:
## Description of the Group of Jhana Factors
By the word 'vitakketi' (he thinks), it points to the mental state of applied thought (vitakka) itself as the agent, in order to eliminate any other agent such as a 'self' (atta). To prevent the sense of it being under one's control, it is expressed in the abstract form as 'vitakkanan' (the act of thinking). It has the characteristic of striking the object, as if one were striking an object repeatedly, saying 'color, color' or 'earth, earth.' Initial or direct striking is called 'āhanana.' Striking all around or repeatedly is called 'pariyāhanana.' Because applied thought is coarser than sustained thought (vicāra) in grasping the object, and because it precedes sustained thought, it is like the initial strike of a bell, which is coarser and precedes the resonance. Just as the strike of a bell occurs first, so applied thought has the nature of occurring first upon the object because it directs the mind towards the object.

'Vipphāravā' means particularly associated with movement. 'Anuppabandhena pavattiyan' means occurring in continuous succession in either access concentration (upacāra) or absorption concentration (appanā). In such continuous occurrence, applied thought occurs by entering the object steadily without wavering. 'Maṇဍala' refers to the circle of a threshing floor.

'Pīṇayati' means to please or to increase. 'Pharaṇarasā' has the function of pervading the body with refined material qualities. The state of an elated mind is called 'odagya.' Minor joy (khuddikā pīti) causes only a brief raising of the body hairs and, having broken up, does not arise again. Momentary joy (khaṇikā pīti) arises frequently. Pervading joy (pharaṇā pīti) is more refined than uplifting joy (ubbegā pīti) because of its steadiness and long-lasting nature. When it brings to maturity (takes the womb) as a cause for tranquility (passaddhi), [it fulfills it]. Only the joy associated with absorption is considered to fulfill absorption concentration; thus, that joy is set apart. The other two types of joy (minor and momentary) fulfill momentary concentration and access concentration.

'Samādhicittena' means with a mind accompanied by concentration. 'Avisāra' is the nature of non-scattering of itself. 'Avikkhepa' is the non-wavering of associated states. That state by which associated states remain unwavering is to be understood as 'avikkhepa.' 'Visesato' means for the most part. This is because there is also concentration devoid of pleasure (sukha). By showing the simile of a lamp, the [Teacher] shows the state of concentration as stabilizing the mental continuum.

## The Description of the Group of Jhana Factors is Finished.

## Description of the Group of Faculties
By the Pali 'saddahanti etāya' (they believe by means of this), the [Teacher] shows the assistance of faith (saddhā) by way of its lordship over the associated states occurring through the act of believing.
89:
When there is such assistance by way of lordship in the act of believing, the conventional expression 'the person believes' occurs. In objects worthy of faith, the unwholesome state that is the opposite of faith is called 'assaddhiya' (faithlessness); 'micchādhimokkha' (wrong conviction) is also called faithlessness. The decision/conviction regarding an object such as the Buddha, which is of the nature of clarity, is the characteristic of 'adhimokkha' (conviction); it should be understood that this is not the 'yevāpanaka' (miscellaneous) conviction. 'Exercising the meaning of lordship' means that it makes the associated states follow itself, as if saying, 'Without me, there is no conviction for you associated states; believe along with me.' The same applies to the remaining faculties.

'Pakkhandana' means entering into well. 'Paṅka' (mud) is mud that is harder (thicker) than 'kaddama' mud. 'Paṇaka' is the slimy impurity of water (water-scum/moss). 'Pīta' is water that has been drunk. The characteristic of 'okappana' is the characteristic of conviction, entering into [the object] in succession and deciding, 'This is exactly so.' The state of being non-turbid is 'akālusiya,' meaning the state of being clear (non-muddled). Objects such as the Buddha are called 'saddheyya' (worthy of faith). Associating with superior persons, hearing the Good Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma are the 'sotāpattiyanga' (factors of stream-entry). Faith should be understood as being like a hand in taking up wholesome states, like capital wealth in accomplishing all success, and like a seed in the plowing that produces the fruit of the Deathless.

'Vīrabhāva' means the state of a hero, the state by which one is called a hero (viriya/energy). Giving appropriate strength is 'paggaha' (upholding/exertion). 'The journey should be traveled,' 'the journey has been traveled,' 'the work should be done,' 'the work has been done,' 'a slight illness has arisen,' 'one has just recovered from illness,' 'while wandering for alms in a village or market-town, one does not get as much coarse or refined food as desired,' 'one gets [food],' etc.—these eight grounds together with appropriate reflection are called 'vīriyārambhavatthu' (grounds for arousing energy), or they are reflections based on those eight.

Establishing by approaching an object performed long ago, etc., or the non-relinquishing of the object is 'upaṭṭhāna' (appearing/presence). Placing the object steadily like a stone, not allowing it to float away like a gourd in water, making it remembered, and acting so it does not disappear is 'apilāpana' (non-floating/plunging). Because it acts to prevent floating, it is called 'apilāpeti.' 'Gati' refers to accomplishments by way of cause and by way of fruit. The phrase 'aparo nayo' (another method) is initiated for the purpose of showing the function (rasa), etc. The function that is the opposite of disappearing is 'asammoha' (non-confusion); it is not merely the absence of disappearing. The body and so forth, which are the objects of mindfulness, are called 'satipaṭṭhāna' (foundations of mindfulness), or prior instances of mindfulness are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for subsequent instances of mindfulness.

[By suppressing] the restless 'uddhacca' which tends to scatter. 'Paññāpeti' means it makes known in various ways. The phrase 'having a single light' is said in reference to the light of the defilements of insight (vipassanupakkilesa). It is called 'mano' (mind) because one cognizes by means of this state; having established this, [the Teacher] taught 'mano' as a cause in the passage, 'Dependent on the mind and mental objects...'
90:
Mind (mano) has been spoken of as a cause. It should be understood that all mind is the cause for the consciousness (viññāṇa) that immediately follows it. 'Vijānāti' (cognizes) means knowing by way of attaining a delimited object; it is not knowing by way of perceiving or penetrating as in the case of perception (saññā) and wisdom (paññā).

When it is said 'associated with joy and happiness' (pīti-somanassa-sampayogato), that state because of which the mind becomes 'sumana' (happy-minded) is called happiness (somanassa). Therefore, joy (pīti) also reaches the state of happiness. Thus, it should be applied as 'being associated with pleasant feeling even without the physical basis (kāya-vatthu).' When applied this way, happiness without joy is also included. Alternatively, somanassa characterized by joy should be understood as meaning somanassa with joy and somanassa without joy.

'Pavatta-santatādhipateyya' means being the predominant factor of the continuity known as occurrence. Because the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) protects during its own moment of presence, it is the cause for the arising of the states it protects in the immediate sequence; thus, the continuity lasts for a long time. That continuity, being distinguished by various specific karmas, proceeds uninterruptedly until death (cuti), or generally until Parinibbāna, and is endowed with the distinction of being alive. To describe the common characteristics of the material life-faculty and the mental life-faculty, it is said 'of the states not inseparable from itself.' It protects only during the moment of presence of the states to be protected. If the objects to be protected, such as a lotus, do not exist, what would the water protect? 'Tassa tassa' refers to the functions such as protecting. 'Sādhanato' means because of accomplishing. Such accomplishment is because it is the condition for the distinction of being alive.

## End of the Description of the Group of Faculties.

## Description of the Group of Path Factors.

'Sammā' (rightly) means by way of the non-perverted state of leading out (niyyānika). The state of being praised should also be understood in this same way.

## Description of the Group of Powers.

'Assaddhiye' means because of the cause of lack of faith. 'Ubhayapada-vasena' means by way of the two terms, such as the term 'faith' (saddhā) and the term 'power' (bala). This shame (hiri) is called 'internally-originated' (ajjhatta-samuṭṭhāna) because it has causes for arising such as one's own birth (jāti) which are internal to oneself. Listening respectfully when a teacher says something is called 'patissava.' Because it occurs together with that listening, it is called 'sappatissava.' It means a certain kind of respect that is 'patissava' or similar to it. Shame (hiri) that arises from reflecting on the greatness of one's birth and so forth also occurs by way of respect for that birth, etc.; therefore, it is said to have the 'characteristic of respectful listening' (sappatissava-lakkhaṇā). One fears blame and sees that blame as a danger; therefore, one is called 'one who fears blame and sees danger' (vajja-bhīruka-bhayadassāvī). Ottappa (moral dread) has such a nature. Hiri views evil unwholesome states like excrement. Ottappa views them like hot coals. 'Dāyajja' means inheritance.
