The internally-originated nature and so forth of Hiri and Ottappa are mentioned because they are evident in those respective contexts. However, it is not because those two states are ever separated from each other. This is because there is no shame (hiri) without fear (ottappa), nor is there fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) without shame (hiri).
91:
It means a certain kind of respect without specific distinction. Shame (hiri) that arises from reflecting on the greatness of one's birth and so forth is called 'sappatissava-lakkhaṇā' (having the characteristic of respectful listening) because it arises by way of respect and honor for that birth, etc. Because one fears blame and views that blame as a danger, one is called 'vajja-bhīruka-bhayadassāvī' (one who fears blame and sees danger). Ottappa (moral dread) has such a nature. Hiri views evil unwholesome states like excrement; Ottappa views them like hot coals. 'Dāyajja' (inheritance) refers to the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) and so forth. The internally-originated nature (ajjhatta-samuṭṭhāna) and so forth of Hiri and Ottappa are mentioned because they are evident in those respective contexts. However, these two states are never separated from each other. This is because there is no shame (hiri) without fear (ottappa), nor is there fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) without shame (hiri).

## Description of the Group of Roots.

'Agadha' (non-greed) means the absence of longing and the absence of desire. Because this non-greed has the intention or nature of non-attachment, it is called 'anallīnabhāva' (state of non-attachment); only by taking this meaning does it agree with the simile. 'Anukūla-mitta' (favorable friend) means a friend who is compliant in all matters. 'Vinaya-rasa' means having the function of removing. The statement that non-hatred (adosa) removes the stain of immorality is said with reference to the fact that immorality (dussīlya) originates from hatred and has hatred as its strong dependence. 'Abhāvana' refers to the non-occurrence of the development (bhāvanā) that accomplishes wisdom. That development means: developing states arisen in that absorption (appanā) in the sense of not overstepping each other; developing the faculties in the sense of having a single taste of liberation (vimutti-rasa); developing in the sense of conveying the energy (vīriya) that reaches those states; and developing in the sense of frequent cultivation. Alternatively, unwholesome states which are the opposite of non-delusion (amoha) are called 'abhāvana.' Taking qualities in one who has no qualities is 'adhika-ggahaṇa' (excessive taking). Taking by destroying even existing qualities is 'ūna-ggahaṇa' (deficient taking). Taking the four perversions (vipallāsa) is 'viparīta-ggahaṇa' (perverted taking).

'Yāthāva-sabhāva' (true nature) means knowing the nature of qualities and faults as 'this much is his quality, this much is his fault,' and because reflection can arise such as 'a state subject to aging will age; where can it be obtained in this state that it should not age?' Because of non-greed (alobha), householders do not have disputes over fields, property, and so forth. Because of non-delusion (amoha), monastics do not have disputes over wrong views. In truth, householders who are bound by attachment to sensual pleasures (kāma-rāga) dispute with householders; monastics who are bound by attachment to views (diṭṭhi-rāga) dispute with monastics. Friendship occurs by the power of lust (rāga), and opposition occurs by the power of hatred (dosa). Because of those specific friendships and oppositions, there are approaches and departures. Alternatively, there are compliance and opposition toward objects such as visible forms. The state of not being neutral (amajjhatta-bhāva), known as aversion and attraction, occurs because of delusion (moha). When there is the occurrence of aversion (paṭigha) in the face of the change of happiness or the encounter with suffering, the discernment of feeling (vedanā-pariggaha) cannot be accomplished; therefore, only by the power of non-hatred (adosa) can the mindfulness of feeling (vedanā-satipaṭṭhāna) be accomplished. 'Dibba-vihāra' (divine abiding) refers to the four jhānas. 'Ariya-vihāra' (noble abiding) is the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). One who does not investigate or reflect due to delusion (moha), even regarding neutral beings and formations...
92:
One who is not deluded should be understood as not having excessive attachment to all beings and formations that should be treated with equanimity. Because hatred is the near enemy of seeing suffering, seeing suffering is possible through non-hatred, which is the opposite of that hatred.

## Explanation of the Group of Courses of Action

It should be noted that one does not cause distress or destruction to the happiness and so on of oneself or others. They are taken by the power of the courses of action (kammapatha) because of being a course of action and because of having the same nature as those courses of action.

## Explanation of the Pairs starting with Tranquility

Distress (daratha) means intense oppression (sārambha). This name 'distress' is either a name for the defilements such as restlessness (uddhacca) which have suffering and displeasure as their cause, or it is a name for the four mental aggregates. Defilements dominated by restlessness are called 'defilements beginning with restlessness'; or, starting with restlessness, it includes all defilements. Just as pure gold is suitable for use in various ornaments, so too these wieldiness of body (kāyakammaññatā) and wieldiness of mind (cittakammaññatā) are suitable for use in beneficial actions.

Knowing evenly or knowing all around in various ways is called clear comprehension (sampajañña). The wisdom that discerns whether an action is beneficial or not in activities such as going for the purpose of worshipping a pagoda is called clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña). Even when there is a purpose, the wisdom that discerns suitable or unsuitable objects and so on is called clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña). The wisdom that does not abandon the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) while going to the alms-resort village and so on is called clear comprehension of the resort (gocara-sampajañña). The investigation of activities such as going by way of elements (dhātu) and so on is called clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña). To all practitioners (yogis) who are devoted to all meditation developments (kammaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā), these two states are always helpful because they remove obstacles and increase meditation. Therefore, it was said: 'Two states are of great help: mindfulness (sati) and clear comprehension (sampajañña).'

They are called 'yoked together' (yuganaddha) because they occur evenly through mutual causation, like noble horses harnessed to a yoke. In the Sutta, 'Furthermore, friends, a monk develops tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) yoked together,' the 'yoked-together' nature of these states is taught. The absence of sluggishness and restlessness in all wholesome states is due to these two, energy (vīriya) and concentration (samādhi), being evenly joined. Therefore, it is said, 'for the purpose of joining energy and concentration.' This means the manner of joining.

## Explanation of the 'Or-Whatever-Other' Factors

'By the absence of form' (rūpābhāvena) means because of the absence of transformation (ruppana). The meaning of the word 'states' (dhammā) is those things that are found by their own nature. 'The preliminary stage of loving-kindness' (mettā-pubbabhāga) refers to loving-kindness occurring in the stage before reaching absorption (appanā).
93:
Loving-kindness occurring in the stage before reaching absorption is called the preliminary stage (pubbabhāga). It means that in this first great wholesome consciousness, there is preparatory loving-kindness (parikamma-mettā). 'By way of abstinence' (virati-vasena) means fulfillment not by way of vocal activity (speech), but rather fulfillment by being associated with abstinence (virati). 'Unfailing factors' (apaṇṇakaṅgāni) refers to mental factors that do not fail. Deciding upon an object in one way or another, whether wrongly or rightly, is called determination (adhimokkha). This is because one who cannot decide cannot engage in immoral acts like killing or in meritorious acts like giving. Faith (saddhā), however, is the determination characterized by clarity/confidence in objects worthy of devotion. This is the distinction between determination and faith.

The opposite behavior of being unable to decide, like a child moving here and there, thinking 'Shall I do it or not?', is called non-wavering (asaṃsappana). 'From the preceding mind' (purima-manato) means from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Because it produces a mind called cognitive process impulsion (vīthi-javana) which is unlike the life-continuum, it shows the attention that brings about cognitive process impulsion (vīthijavana-paṭipādaka-manasikāra) by way of the commonality of attention. 'In those states' (tesu dhammesu) means in the associated mental states of consciousness and mental factors. Although one does not take those mental states as objects, when those mental states occur evenly, one observes them with neutrality; thus it is called equanimity (tatramajjhattatā). Because it is the cause for occurring without sluggishness and without restlessness, it has the function of preventing deficiency and excess. 'Of the objects of bodily misconduct and so on' (kāyaduccaritādi-vatthūnaṃ) refers to living beings and so on. 'Non-crushing' (amaddanā) is simply the state of being the opposite of crushing or violating.

States that are free from differentiation by way of the function of various groups are called undifferentiated (avibhattika). 'Herein' (ettha) means that even when these differentiated states are analyzed in the second section and so on, there is nothing new. 'The term is fulfilled' (padaṃ pūritaṃ) means that terms such as 'jhāna' are fulfilled by way of the five factors and so on. This is because the five factors are the meaning of the term 'jhāna,' and if even one of those factors is missing, the term 'jhāna' is deficient in meaning. A collection of words (sentence), a group of states, or a particular word is called 'pada'. Since it would be called 'diminished' if not spoken, it is said to be 'fulfilled' (pūritaṃ). When teaching again what has already been taught, thinking there is no connection like many repetitions of the word 'purisa' (man), it is called 'a discourse without connection' (ananusandhikā kathā). When teaching again what has already been taught at intervals, because the states are not taught in sequence, it is called 'out of order' (uppaṭipāṭiyā).

The group of five starting with contact (phassapañcamaka-rāsi) is taught by way of being common to all arisings of consciousness and by way of including the four mental aggregates and their causes. Among the groups such as the jhāna-group already mentioned, because they cannot perform even a single function of those groups, states like desire (chanda) are taught by way of 'or-whatever-other' (yevāpanaka). Just as the nature of factors of jhāna and so on was taught for states like feeling (vedanā) which were already mentioned, the specific names such as gentleness (sovacassatā) and good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā) have not yet been taught. Therefore, to include those specific names, some states like desire are set aside, and those states along with those specific names are taught as 'or-whatever-other' (yevāpana). Or, alternatively, after teaching the states with remainders according to the inclinations of those to be led (veneyya), it is said 'or-whatever-other'.

## The Explanation of the 'Or-Whatever-Other' Factors is finished.
## The Explanation of the Section on the Summary of States is finished.

## Kāmāvacara Kusala
## Commentary on the Section on Definitions

'By way of contacting' (phusanakavasena) means: whether the object is ultimately present or not, it refers to the contact that arises by way of the mind's thorough falling upon the object when it comes into range. Just as in passages like 'cittaṃ mano' (Dhs. 6, 17), a specific function is shown; as in 'mānasaṃ' etc., a specific term is shown despite having the same meaning as 'mind'; as in 'paṇḍaraṃ' etc., a specific quality of the mind's purity is shown; as in 'cetasikaṃ sātaṃ' etc. (Dhs. 2, 18), a specific dependence on the mind is shown; as in 'cittassa ṭhiti' etc. (Dhs. 15, 24), the specific absence of any other state but the mind's duration is shown; as in 'alubbhanā' etc. (Dhs. 32), the specific mode of non-attachment of a state other than non-greed is shown; and as in 'alubbhitattaṃ' etc. (Dhs. 32), the specific manifestation of the mode of a state other than non-greed is shown—without regarding such specific distinctions, a term that points merely to the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) is called a 'natural term' (sabhāvapada). Indeed, the act of touching or the mode of touching by the mind that touches an object is called 'phusanā'. 'Samphusanā' refers to the contact that is the meeting with the object, not the contact that is acquisition. The state of the mind that has met with the object is 'samphusitattaṃ'. That state because of which the mind is said to be 'contacted' (samphusita) is the 'state' (bhāva) of that mind. This should be understood in the same way for other definitions of states (bhāvaniddesa).

Showing another synonym or alternative phrasing is called 'aparadīpanā'. Or, clarifying the preceding meaning with another synonym is 'aparadīpanā'. Although specific types of wisdom such as 'paṇḍiccaṃ' (erudition) and 'kosallaṃ' (skill) may be obtained at different times, they can also be obtained in a single consciousness. To show that in one specific quality, other qualities also follow, such a classification is a classification by way of meaning (atthato vibhatti), because the detailed classification is made due to the difference in meaning. Alternatively, just as in the definitions of intrinsic nature, mode, and state (sabhāva, ākāra, bhāva niddesa) like 'kodho, kujjhanā, kujjhitattaṃ' (Dhs. 1066), only the meaning of the mode of being angry is stated, it is not so here. In this definition of wisdom, however, the meaning is stated as distinct by way of the modes of being a wise person (paṇḍita) and so on. Therefore, reaching such a detailed classification occurs by the power of the meaning. In the term 'samphusitattaṃ' as well, it is not that only the meaning of the mode of 'contact' (phassa) is stated; rather, because the mode of contact as meeting with the object is stated, it is said to be a classification by way of meaning.

In the summary (uddesa) 'doso byāpādo' (hatred, ill-will), hatred is pointed out as distinct due to the difference in name. In the definition (niddesa) as well, it is explained in detail because of that very difference in name. The statement 'it is a single aggregate' is made with reference to the fact that it should be spoken of by the single term 'aggregate' (khandha). By the term 'cetanā' (volition), the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is shown, as volition is the leader of it. 'Asaddhammā' refers to the states of the ignoble (asataṃ), or bad states (asanto dhammā), or states that are not the true Dhamma (na saddhammā). Thus, although it is unified under the name 'asaddhamma', it reaches distinction through the difference of rejecting the regard for the true Dhamma (saddhammagarutā), characterized by the regard for anger (kodhagarutā) and so on.
95:
It is taught as 'four'. Although the 'disregard for the true Dhamma' (asaddhammagarutā) is unified as the state of disregarding the true Dhamma, it reaches distinction through the difference of rejection characterized by anger (kodha) and so on. Or, the opposite is rejected by that [opposite state], or it rejects [the opposite] itself; thus it is called 'rejection' (paṭikkkhepa). In this way, due to the difference in the rejection of the regard for the true Dhamma, such as the regard for anger and so on, the types of disregard for the true Dhamma (asaddhammagarutā) or the bad states (asaddhammā) reach distinction. The distinction of terms like 'non-greed' (alobha) from terms like 'contact' (phassa) should be understood by the rejection characterized by greed (lobha) and so on, or by being the opposite of greed and so on. The mutual distinction between non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion (alobha, adosa, amoha) should be applied through the difference in rejection as already stated. The clarification of the meaning of a preceding word by a subsequent word is called 'padatthuti' (exaltation of the word's meaning). By that subsequent word, the preceding word is shown to be of great meaning and is also embellished. Even when there is no specific difference in meaning, repeating the word by way of embellishment or by way of respect is called 'reinforcement' (daḷhīkamma).

'Tajjā' means the meaning that is appropriate to that result. It is not that only the pleasant happiness (sāta sukha) currently being defined is prioritized; rather, because the previously defined objects are also prioritized, it is stated as 'tehi vā' (or by them) and so on. Or, it is called 'tajjā' because it arises for the sake of contact as its cause. Because it causes the person possessed of it, or the associated states (sampayutta dhammā), to enjoy themselves, the letter 'da' is changed to 'ta' to form 'sāta' (pleasant). Because it experiences suffering well, or because it digs out (khanti) suffering, it is called 'sukha' (happiness).

'Pāsa' (snare) refers to the snare of lust (rāga). Because it is unobstructed, it moves in the atmosphere. If even the unwholesome is called 'paṇḍara' (radiant), what need is there to mention the wholesome? This is the intended meaning. For that wholesome state emerges from the radiant life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and is itself radiant. Alternatively, all mind is radiant by nature; however, due to adventitious defilements (upakkilesa) and purifications (vodāna), there is the defilement of the faulty unwholesome mind and the superior purity of the faultless wholesome mind. Because there is no designation of 'aggregate' (khandha) in stones etc. which have the dimensions of a log, the designation of aggregate occurring in a log without regarding any sign is stated as 'by way of the meaning of mere designation'. By the word 'taṃ' (that), only the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) should be meant; because it is what is to be defined, the state of being 'tajjā' (appropriate) is not possible for it. Even if it is said to be 'tajjā' because it is born from those objects, the state of being 'born of contact' (samphassaja) should not be stated. For that contact is neither the object nor the specific cause. It is taught that 'the meeting of the three is contact', and thus only consciousness is the specific cause of contact. Therefore, consciousness, being the specific cause, does not receive the designation 'tajjā-manoviññāṇadhātu-samphassajā' (born of contact with the appropriate mind-consciousness element) by way of being born of contact; nor is it easily understood when that very consciousness is spoken of as both the cause and the result of that contact. Or rather, what is the use of seeking this cause? These states are of that nature just as the Blessed One has taught; one should not seek a cause in states of such a nature.
96:
This means it is well-known in the world by the power of such reflection. Thinking in various ways that 'it should be thus and thus' is called initial application (vitakka) because it draws the object just as one draws water from a well. Wandering around [the object] is called sustained application (vicāra).

In the term 'delight' (attamanatā), the word 'self' (atta) does not refer to the mind. For the mind does not have a mind [of its own]. Having said that the state of a person who has a delighted mind (attamana) is 'delight' (attamanatā), the phrase 'of the mind' is used again to negate the view of a 'person'.

Why is [one-pointedness (ekaggatā)] called 'stability' (avaṭṭhiti) even when it is not strong? Because in performing [an act] such as taking life with a one-pointed mind, there is just enough immersion and stability to complete that action. Disordered or various types of gathering, or scattering, is called 'dissipation' (visāhāra). Alternatively, 'gathering' (saṃharaṇa) means the collection of associated states, and the absence of such collection is 'dissipation' (visāhāra).

'By another method' means in another cause. The occurrence of two or many words in a single meaning is the state of 'co-referentiality' (samānādhikaraṇa). Striving means also arriving [at an offense]. Upward exertion is called 'effort' (uyyāma). 'Burden' (dhura) is the wholesome [deed] undertaken to be accomplished, or a promised responsibility (paṭiññā).

'The three' refers to the Three Jewels, starting with the Buddha. The presence and illumination of the object in the mind occurs only because of mindfulness; therefore, this is the characteristic of mindfulness (sati).

Ground that is free from stones, gravel, sand, etc., is called 'subtle' because of its smoothness.

This [life faculty (jīvitindriya)] occurs by the power of the continuity of beings such as humans produced by a single kamma. Even in wholesome and unwholesome states, the life faculty, while causing the associated states to occur by way of the faculty-condition (indriya-paccaya), is the cause for the non-interruption of those states.

In the phrase 'that which is loathed' (yaṃ hirīyati), the nature [of loathing] expressed by the word 'hirīyati' is denoted by the word 'yaṃ'. Therefore, this 'yaṃ' should be understood as a neuter abstract noun (bhāva-napuṃsaka). In the word 'by that which should be loathed' (hirīyitabbena), the instrumental case is appropriate in the sense of 'cause' (hetu).
97:
In the word 'non-greed' (alubbhana), it should be understood that 'alubbhana' itself is 'alubbhana' by way of the description of the state (bhāva-niddesa). 'Non-ill-will' (abyāpajja) is also appropriately interpreted as the state of not being oppressed by anger, which is of the nature of suffering known as mental distress (domanassa).

42-43. Because it is the opposite of sloth and torpor (thina-middha), etc., the ability to cause [the mind] to turn repeatedly and quickly in wholesome states and in the attention to impermanence, etc., is called 'lightness of transformation' (lahu-pariṇāmatā). For beings possessed of the hindrance of ignorance and the fetter of craving, the occurrence of unwholesome states is their natural state; therefore, there is no benefit of 'lightness of transformation' in those unwholesome states. Since the nature of those unwholesome states is only 'heaviness' (garutā), 'lightness' (lahutā) should be understood in the wholesome states which are of the opposite nature. That lightness, when it occurs, becomes the cause for the quick emergence from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

44-45. Unlike states associated with delusion, the non-resistance and non-obstruction in performing wholesome deeds by states that have unimpaired lightness is called 'malleability' (mudutā). Because of such non-resistance, the malleability of mental states is also called 'softness' (maddavatā), etc., due to its similarity to the form of [physical] malleability.

46-47. A mind that is wet with the moisture of craving and is excessively soft is 'unwieldy' (akammañña) for work, like molten gold. A mind that is excessively stiff due to conceit (māna), etc., is also unwieldy for work, like gold that has not been heated. That mind which is endowed with appropriate malleability is 'wieldy' (kammañña) for work, like gold that is appropriately soft. The mode of being wieldy for work of such a soft mind is called 'wieldiness' (kammaññatā). Therefore, 'wieldiness' should be understood as a specific mode of 'malleability'.

50-51. The unwholesome state itself that occurs in the mode of shrinking back is 'shrinking back' (paccosakkana). The twenty-one kinds of 'wrong livelihood' (anesanā) are: practicing medicine, acting as a messenger, acting as a servant, lancing boils, applying ointment, giving emetics, giving purgatives, preparing nasal oil, preparing eye-oil, giving bamboo, giving leaves, giving flowers, giving fruits, giving bath-powder, giving tooth-sticks, giving water for washing the face, giving face-powder, giving clay, using flattery (cāṭukakamman), speaking words that are mostly false with little truth like green-gram soup (muggasūpiya), and acting as a menial servant such as fondling children (pāribhaṭya). The twenty-second, 'running errands on foot' (jaṅghapesaniya), is similar to acting as a messenger, so it is said to be twenty-one. The six 'unsuitable resorts' (agocara) are: the resort of prostitutes, widows, old maids, eunuchs, taverns, and the resort of bhikkhunīs. The reason for saying 'in brief' is that because they have not yet been shown by way of their specific forms, it is said, 'Therein, what is desire (chanda)?' and so forth.
98:
It means that the exposition (niddesa) beginning with "yo chando chandikatā" has been summarized and presented as the exposition "yevāpana" (whatever other [states]).

## The explanation of the Exposition Section (Niddesavāra) is finished.

## Explanation of the Classification Section (Koṭṭhāsavāra)

58-120. In the Exposition Section, although the questions and so forth are numerous individually, they are brought into a single state as questions etc., and it is stated that there are four divisions. Taking them by summarizing as "four", "two", and so forth, or by grouping them together, is called saṅgaha (grouping). The phrase "excluding the yevāpanaka states" is said with reference to the states that ought to be grouped together. Those states (such as contact, feeling, etc.), because they are individually specified and extensively pointed out, remain scattered and thus ought to be grouped together. As for the yevāpanaka states, because they are included by the summary "whatever other" (yevāpana), they do not remain scattered in that way. However, because those yevāpanaka states are included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), in the exposition of that aggregate, it is stated only as "yevāpana" to prevent the misconception that they are not aggregates. Therefore, the yevāpanaka states should not be excluded. "Paccayasaṅkhātena" means in the sense of what is called the condition of nutriment (āhāra-paccaya). Alternatively, between the two types "root" (hetu) and "condition" (paccaya), the cause that produces is called "root", and the cause that supports is called "condition". Among such specific causes, they are nutriments in the sense of what is called the supporting condition. Just as physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra) supports the material body by bringing the octad of pure matter (ojāṭṭhamaka-rūpa), so too these (mental nutriments: contact, volition, consciousness) support the mental body by bringing forth resultant states such as feeling. In saying "they also become so," it is said with reference to common conditions such as the co-nascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya). "Aññathā ca" means that because they also assist by another mode of supporting (upatthambhana) different from modes like co-nascence, they are called "nutriments". Therefore, for states such as the six roots and four predominants, which are devoid of the function of bringing forth results, the status of being a nutriment cannot be applied. The statement "it brings the three feelings" and so forth is said according to the possibility. It is not said by the power of contact and so forth in this first great wholesome consciousness alone. In the phrase "the three existences," it specifically brings the rebirth-linking consciousness which is the cause of existences such as the sense-sphere existence. Generally, however, it brings the five aggregates of clinging which are the objects of grasping.

Closely contemplating and knowing the object is called "upanijjhāyana". "Hetvaṭṭhena" is in the sense of a means (upāya), not in the sense of the primary roots (the six roots). The eightfold path factors practiced prior to the supramundane path, occurring at various moments, are called "the path as it has come" (yathāgata-magga) when they arise together only at the supramundane moment. Even before the moment of insight, because bodily actions and so forth are very pure, the "noble eightfold path, which is the strong dependence for the noble path, [goes] to the fulfillment of development..."
99:
By the figurative method (*pariyāya*) taught as "The Noble Eightfold Path goes to the fulfillment of development" (MN 3.431), the fact that the insight path (*vipassanā-magga*) preceding the supramundane path has eight factors is shown by the word *yathāgata*. It is not shown because of the simultaneous presence of the eight factors in a single moment; thus, it should be understood that this teaching is also a figurative teaching (*pariyāya-desanā*). Meaning that cognizing itself is the diversity of the mind, it is said, "The aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*) is a single state because of the sense of the mind's diversity."

Although the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and so on are included in passages such as "Four aggregates arise," the statement "There is one aggregate of feeling" and so on is made for the purpose of showing that in this summary section (*saṅgaha-vāra*), the numerous aggregates of feeling and so on are not taught by way of the classification of types (*jāti-niddesa*). Regarding the faculties (*indriya*), when the classification of type for the single mind-faculty (*manindriya*) is rejected, the rejection of that classification of type for the other faculties, nutriment (*āhāra*), and so on is also accomplished; thus, it should be noted that it is done only for the sake of the preceding mind-faculty.

## The Explanation of the Section on Groupings is Finished.

## Explanation of the Section on Emptiness

121-145. Here, "*ettha*" refers to this aforementioned occasion, or to these states. "*Bhāva*" refers to a being, or any indefinite thing.

## Explanation of the Second Consciousness, etc.

"*Sappayogena*" means being together with an effort (*payoga*) that encourages a sluggish mind. "*Saupāyena*" means being together with a means (*upāya*) such as reflecting on the disadvantages and advantages of performing or not performing wholesome deeds, encouragement by others, and so on.

156-159. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, by the statement permitted regarding development (*bhāvanā*) that is not yet very concentrated, the state of being without distinction even among the "or-whatever" (*yevāpanaka*) states is shown.

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Bases of Meritorious Action, etc.

Reverence itself is the base of meritorious action associated with reverence (*apaciti-sahagata*), just like the phrase "associated with delight and lust" (*nandirāga-sahagatā*). Or, states associated with volition, or bodily and vocal actions, are called reverence (*apaciti*); the volition together with those states is called "associated with reverence." "*Hita-pharaṇena*" means either by pervading with loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward the speaker, or by a mind desiring welfare that occurs as "In this way, welfare will come to me."
100:
Knowledge of the ownership of kamma (kamma-ssakatā-ñāṇa) is called the straightening of views (diṭṭhijukamma). The characteristic of certainty (niyama-lakkhaṇa) is the mark of constant determination in the state of having great fruit. By virtue of moral conduct (cāritta-sīla), they are included in the base of meritorious action consisting in virtue (sīlamaya-puññakiriyavatthu). Just like one who gives away a blameless object, one who greatly rejoices also rejoices because of another's success; therefore, rejoicing in others' merit (abbhanumodanā) is included in the base of meritorious action consisting in giving (dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu). The phrase "bhāventopi" (even while developing) refers to incomplete development (bhāvanā). This is because completed development is absorption (appanā). "Having made eight portions" means showing one first consciousness occurring in one moment for one being, and without showing other such consciousnesses, all of them are made into one by way of similarity; likewise, the remaining consciousnesses are treated, thus meaning the making of eight types.

## The Explanation of Wholesome Consciousness of the Sense Sphere is Finished.

## Wholesome Consciousness of the Fine-Material Sphere

## The Explanation of the First Jhāna according to the Fourfold Method

By eliding the subsequent word "bhava" (existence), "rūpa-bhava" (fine-material existence) is taught as "rūpa". Although jhāna is not the Path (magga), the use of the word "magga" is said to be for the purpose of excluding the path-nature of other states; it is objected that this does not show the path-nature of all wholesome jhānas. In that objection, because the occasion (samaya) is defined by the development of the Path, the wholesomeness of states such as contact (phassa) occurring during the development of non-path jhāna would not be shown; therefore, the path-nature of all jhānas should be shown. It should be understood that the word "magga" is used to show that "there is no other path than this," which is the opposite of states occurring in other planes, and which has the nature of producing rebirth in the fine-material plane when other conditions are present, being similar to the nature of resultant states (vipāka-dhamma) in all respects by way of the nature of resultant states. "Kusalaṃ dānaṃ" (wholesome giving) refers to non-greed (alobha). Alternatively, volition (cetanā) is called giving; excluding that volition, the other two are said to be states associated with volition. "Vaṭṭanti" means that because it is the Path, it is appropriate to call it "Path" by including it under the term jhāna. "Okappanā" means conviction. Why is the meaning "produces, increases" given, abandoning the meaning found in other Suttas? Because in other places, a word without a prefix (upasagga) is found with only this meaning; to clarify this meaning, Suttas such as "Puna caparaṃ Udāyi" are cited. Since other jhānas of certain noble ones (ariyas) accomplished through the Noble Path also have the nature of development (bhāvanā), the definition of the occasion by the person producing those jhānas is also accomplished.
101:
They escape (from sense pleasures) by means of this jhāna, or they escape in this jhāna; therefore, it is called "nissaraṇa" (escape/means of escape). What states escape? They are sense pleasures (kāma). The escape from those sense pleasures means abandonment (pahāna). In this case, the genitive case in the word "kāmānaṃ" is appropriate in the sense of the agent. In the phrase "vatthukāmehipi", the word "pi" has the sense of inclusion (samuccaya) of another appropriate meaning, because it can also take the meaning "only by being secluded from the objects of sense pleasure (vatthu-kāma)"; it is not for the inclusion of the defilement of sense pleasure (kilesa-kāma). Why? Because in this context, seclusion from the defilements of sense pleasure has already been stated by the second phrase ("vivicca akusalehi dhammehi"). Although the defilements of sense pleasure are taken by the word "akusala", all unwholesome states are included. However, because seclusion from the defilements of sense pleasure in every way is intended, it is said, "because seclusion from the defilements of sense pleasure is stated by the second phrase." Due to the desire to obtain the strands of sense pleasure, impure efforts (payoga) such as killing living beings can occur; by seclusion from those sense pleasures, the purity of effort is made clear. By cleansing the defilement of craving (taṇhā), the disposition (āsaya) is purified.

"And of others" (aññesampi ca) refers to views, conceit, etc., and contact, etc. The hindrances (nīvaraṇa) which are the opposites of the jhāna factors to be mentioned above are taught in order to show that those jhāna factors have an opposing nature that abandons their respective hindrances. By the words on seclusion from ill-will (byāpāda), the abandonment of anger (dosa) which has as its object the various grounds for resentment (āghāta-vatthu) such as "he has done me harm," is stated. By the words on seclusion from sloth and torpor (thīna-middha), etc., which are dominated by delusion (moha), the seclusion by suppression (vikkham-bhana-viveka) of delusion is stated, which has as its object the various aspects such as the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca), the past (pubbanta), etc., by way of covering. This jhāna removes sensual lust (kāma-rāga), ill-will (byāpāda), and sloth and torpor (thīna-middha), etc., which stand together with those states on a single object. Although all wholesome states have an opposing nature to all unwholesome states and thus abandon all unwholesome states by that opposing nature, because it specifically has the nature of removing sensual lust, etc., it is said that the seclusion by suppression of the hindrances and unwholesome roots, etc., is stated without distinction because of that nature.

In the first jhāna concentration which has reached steadiness due to the specific function of initial application (vitakka) in directing onto the object, and in the second jhāna concentration, etc., which are devoid of initial application but are steady like that first jhāna due to being far from the opposing hindrances, there is the commentarial term "appanā" (absorption). Therefore, the association of initial application with absorption is stated. Otherwise, if initial application itself were absorption, its association with absorption would not be possible. By showing the possession of initial application and sustained application (vicāra) by a person endowed with jhāna, it is taught that jhāna itself is accompanied by initial and sustained application; therefore, this meaning should be understood in the same way in the Jhāna-vibhaṅga Pali.

In the phrase "vivekajaṃ pītisukhanti", in the first sense, "vivekaja" refers to jhāna. Because the suffix "a" with the meaning of "existence" is added after the word "pītisukha", it means "in that jhāna, there is rapture and pleasure." In the second sense, rapture and pleasure themselves are called "vivekaja" because they are born of seclusion (viveka). In forming the compound in the sense of another word as "vivekajaṃ pītisukhanti", the nominative case ending is not elided. If it were elided, the reading would be "vivekajapītisukhanti". This is a peculiarity. "Gaṇanānupubbata" means by way of numerical order. Alternatively, it means that the word "paṭhamaṃ" (first) is a term intended merely for numerical order.
102:
Alternatively, if there is the reading "vivekajapītisukhaṃ," this is the distinction. It is called numerical order either because it follows the numerical sequence or because the word "paṭhamaṃ" (first) simply denotes numerical order. By abandoning the perversions (vipallāsa) such as permanence and so on, the path penetrates the characteristics of impermanence and so forth without delusion; thus, it is called meditation on characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna). Nibbāna, which is not subject to disappearance, has the true characteristic (tathalakkhaṇa) because of its non-perverted nature and because it does not become otherwise.

## Explanation of the Second Jhāna

161-2. By the phrase "with the subsiding of initial and sustained thought," it is shown that the second jhāna is attained through the transcending of those initial and sustained thoughts which cause the coarseness of the first jhāna, and not through the transcending of contact (phassa) and so on, which are not coarse by nature. In this same way, it should be understood in phrases such as "with the fading away of joy" (pītiyā ca virāgā). Therefore, the words expressing the transcending of initial thought, sustained thought, joy, and happiness indicate the attainment of the second jhāna and so on by transcending the increasingly coarse factors of jhāna. The phrase expressing the transcending of initial and sustained thought, which is a part of those words, is said to indicate that meaning. Alternatively, just as the phrase expressing the subsiding of initial and sustained thought indicates the attainment of the second jhāna through their transcending, the phrases such as "fading away of joy" (pīti-virāga) indicate the attainment of the third jhāna and so on through the transcending of joy and so forth. Thus, it is said that this phrase indicates that meaning.

The meaning is that just as a cloth is called blue because of its association with the color blue. When that internal tranquility (sampasādana) is shown, since the occurrence of the word "sampasādana" in jhāna due to its association with that tranquility is already shown by the identical grammatical case (samānādhikaraṇa) in the expression "the jhāna which is internal tranquility," there is no contradiction. If it is asked, "How is it regarding the unification of mind (ekodibhāva)?" when unification (ekodi) is shown, the fact that jhāna increases unification is already stated by the identical grammatical case in the expression "the jhāna which is the unification of mind." If it is argued that one should not extract the term "ekodibhāva" to explain "ekodi" in detail, it is appropriate to say that the word "ekodibhāva" occurring in concentration (samādhi) occurs in jhāna just like the word "sampasādana."

"Appitā" means they have reached destruction. Since the absence of initial and sustained thought is already indicated by the phrase expressing the subsiding of initial and sustained thought—by indicating the means of attaining the second jhāna and so on, by indicating the cause which is the internal tranquility and unification of mind, and by indicating the cause of the absence of initial and sustained thought—why is the phrase "without initial thought, without sustained thought" (avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ) stated again? It is not redundant, because it has not been fully indicated. The phrase expressing the subsiding of initial and sustained thought does not imply the non-occurrence of initial and sustained thought. Indeed, the abandoning of craving for initial and sustained thought...
103:
The subsiding of these initial and sustained thoughts is the abandoning of craving for them. Just as the occurrence of formations (saṅkhāra) exists in the paths that abandon craving for formations and in the fruits where craving has been abandoned, so too in this second jhāna, even though craving for initial and sustained thought has been removed by the abandoning through suppression (vikkhambhanapahāna), the association with initial and sustained thought might not be prohibited by the preceding phrase "with the subsiding of initial and sustained thought." Therefore, in order to prohibit the association with those initial and sustained thoughts and to show that the transcending of the desire to advert (to them) and so on is indeed the subsiding of those initial and sustained thoughts, He said: "without initial thought, without sustained thought."

## Explanation of the Third Jhāna

Pure nature refers to the state of being free from defilements of an Arahant whose defilements are exhausted. "Upekkhānimitta" (the sign of equanimity) here refers to energy (vīriya) that stands in the middle, without falling into the two extremes of sluggishness and restlessness. That very preceding energy is called "upekkhānimitta" because it serves as the cause for the succeeding energy of a similar kind, which should be maintained by taking the aspect of equanimity. For the sake of attaining the first jhāna, from the abandoning of the hindrances... up to the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the knowledge in the equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā), which is the wisdom that stands well while rightly contemplating the perception of the sphere of nothingness, arises thus by the power of the eight attainments.

For the sake of attaining the path of stream-entry, the knowledge that rightly contemplates arising (rebirth), occurrence, the sign, accumulation (kamma-striving), rebirth-linking, destination, manifestation, reappearance, birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; likewise for the sake of attaining the fruit of stream-entry... the path of Arahantship, the fruit of Arahantship, the attainment of the void abiding (suññatavihāra), and the attainment of the signless abiding (animittavihāra), the knowledge in the equanimity towards formations, which is the wisdom that rightly contemplates arising, occurrence, accumulation, rebirth-linking, and so on, arises thus in ten ways by the power of insight (vipassanā).

"Whatever exists, whatever has come to be" refers to the group of the five aggregates. One abandons those five aggregates through the knowledge of desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatāñāṇa). Just as a person who has seen a snake with three coils gains equanimity in investigating the characteristics of the snake, so too, one who has seen the three characteristics gains equanimity in investigating the characteristics of formations. "Anābhogarasa" means having a function that is the opposite of craving, which tends to incline even towards that sublime happiness of the third jhāna. It is said that one who is possessed of jhāna experiences mental happiness through the mental body (nāmakāya) and bodily happiness by producing refined matter (paṇītarūpa) which is the cause of bodily happiness. "Phuṭattā" and "byāpitattā" mean due to being pervaded and suffused. For example, just as happiness arises for one whose body is pervaded by water when touched by tangible objects such as wind that are not too disagreeable, so too, happiness arises for one whose body is pervaded by these refined matters.
104:
## Explanation of the Fourth Jhāna
'Avibhūtapaccupaṭṭhānā' means having an unmanifest appearance like pleasure and pain. It has the nature of appearing before the yogi's knowledge through an unmanifest appearance that can only be inferred by those [pleasure and pain], like the track of a deer passing over a flat rock.

## The Explanation of the Fourfold Method is finished.

## Explanation of the Fivefold Method
'Yassā pana dhammadhātuyā' refers to Omniscience (Sabbaññutañāṇa). Through that omniscience, [the Buddha] knows the diversity of the characteristics of phenomena and determines the teaching accordingly. In this fivefold method (pañcakanaya), the second jhāna is classified within the portion of the second jhāna of the fourfold method (catukkanaya) and is analyzed as: "At whatever time... one develops the path, and enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is without initial application (avitakka), with sustained application only (vicāramatta), born of concentration (samādhija), and accompanied by rapture and happiness (pītisukha)." Why? Because it has a result similar to the second jhāna in the realm of beings with one body but diverse perceptions (ekattakāya-nānattasaññī), and because it arises from the concentration of the first jhāna. Only the first jhāna is secluded from sensual desires and unwholesome states; since these sensual desires and unwholesome states no longer exist in this second jhāna, it cannot be said to be "secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states," nor can it be called "born of seclusion" (vivekaja). In the Suttanta teachings, the second and third jhānas of the fivefold method belong to the second jhāna [of the fourfold method] because of the subsiding of initial application and sustained application, and because of being without initial application and sustained application.

## Explanation of the Four Modes of Practice
176-180. 'Upacāra' (access) of each respective jhāna refers to the stable sense-sphere concentration (kāmāvacara-samādhi) resulting from the subsiding of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), attachment (nikanti), and so on. 'Tadanudhammatā' means having a nature that conforms to that jhāna; this nature is called attachment (nikanti) to that jhāna, or wrong mindfulness (micchā-sati) which is the aggregates associated with that attachment. It can also be called the mindfulness that guards each respective jhāna where attachment has not yet faded; with this intention, the alternative is stated as "either by mindfulness or by attachment." The modes of practice (paṭipadā) also occur by way of arrival (āgamana); this statement is made with reference to the arrival at the second jhāna, etc., from the first jhāna, etc. The word 'api' indicates non-exclusivity (anekantika). Because of this non-exclusivity, in the Pali text, for each jhāna, the four modes of practice and four objects are combined separately sixteen times. Otherwise, nine jhānas would have to be combined with each mode of practice.
105:
## Explanation of the Tetrad of Objects
*Appaguṇa* refers to a state that has not yet been mastered through the five masteries (*vasitā*).

## Explanation of the Mixed Tetrad of Objects and Progress
"Below" (*heṭṭhā*) refers to the Pure Ninefold Method (*suddhikanavaka*), the Tetrad of Progress (*paṭipadācatukka*), and the Tetrad of Objects (*ārammaṇacatukka*) which occur before the sixteenfold method. By the phrase "those who produce jhāna," it refers to trainees (*sekha*) who have performed previous meritorious deeds (*adhikāra*) and possess jhānas produced solely by the Path (*magga*). Their jhānas should be understood as included in the Pure Ninefold Method because they are connected with the Path. This is because they cannot be called those who produce jhāna (deliberately through effort).

## Explanation of the Discussion on Kasiṇa
By the statement regarding being the basis for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is also shown to be the basis for the formless attainments (*āruppasamāpatti*). "Quick vision" (*khippadassana*) means having swift direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) and the ability to investigate quickly.

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Bases of Mastery
By the word "another" (*aññampi*), it is shown that it occurs not only as a *kasiṇa* base but also as a base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*). Although the bases of mastery are *kasiṇa* bases, they attain the state of a base of mastery distinct from the state of a *kasiṇa* base due to the distinctiveness of the meditation sign (*bhāvanānimitta*) that masters the *kasiṇa* sign.

Therein, it is called "master" (*abhibhū*) because it masters the object; this is either the preliminary work (*parikamma*) or knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Because it has this mastery-attaining preliminary work or knowledge as its base (*āyatana*), it is the jhāna called "base of mastery" (*abhibhāyatana*). Or, because it has the mastered object as its base, it is the jhāna called "base of mastery." Because it masters the object, it is "master" (*abhibhū*); and because it is the ground for the yogi's special happiness and is the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and mental-object base (*dhammāyatana*), it is "base" (*āyatana*). Thus, the jhāna together with its associated states is called the base of mastery.

Since it is connected with the Path, the advertence (*ābhoga*) of one who has emerged from the attainment at that time should be understood as occurring by taking the mode of mastery that occurred at the moment of jhāna through the power of preliminary meditation. In the Sutta texts, however, these four bases of mastery appear as: "Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms, limited, beautiful or ugly. ... Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms, immeasurable, beautiful or ugly. Not perceiving forms internally, one sees..." and so on.
106:
In the Sutta Commentaries (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.173, Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2. 249-250, A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 3.8.65), it is said: "Even though there is advertence by way of color, these bases of mastery are taught only by way of limited objects and immeasurable objects." This is because the state of being a limited object or an immeasurable object is the cause of mastery, whether there is advertence to color or not. In those Sutta texts, all limited objects, whether devoid of or accompanied by advertence to color, are taught as "beautiful or ugly"; likewise, immeasurable objects should be understood in the same way. There is this figurative method (*pariyāya*): having mastered limited objects, if they are sometimes adverted to by way of color, one masters beautiful or ugly forms. But in this Abhidhamma text, because it is a literal teaching (*nippariyāyadesanā*) and not figurative, objects devoid of advertence to color and objects accompanied by advertence to color are taught separately. This is because there is a distinction in the mode of mastery in both cases.

In those Sutta texts, because of the figurative teaching, there is also a figurative sense of mastery for the deliverances (*vimokkha*); thus, the pair of bases of mastery beginning with "perceiving forms internally" is taught. In the third and fourth bases of mastery, the second deliverance is included, and in the bases of mastery of color, the third deliverance is included, because of the occurrence of mastery. But in this Abhidhamma text, because it is a literal teaching, the bases of mastery are taught excluding the deliverances in order to show them without confusion. All jhānas involving the function of deliverance are taught in the teaching on deliverances. This distinction is understood because the two bases of mastery starting with "perceiving forms internally" are not mentioned among the (Abhidhamma) bases of mastery, and because phrases like "possessing form, one sees forms" are common to all functions of deliverance.

The phrase "because internal forms cannot be mastered" is the reason given for why it is never said in any text "one sees internal forms," but everywhere it is said "one sees external forms." By that explanation, whatever statement has another cause is taught for that reason. It shows that there is no need to seek another reason for the teaching in this Abhidhamma text of "not perceiving forms internally," which is due to the elegance of the teaching (*desanāvilāsa*). The inability to master internal forms is because they are not as distinct as external forms. The elegance of the teaching should be understood by the aforementioned distinction. If it is asked, "Since it is already established by the words 'beautiful or ugly,' should the bases of mastery such as blue (*nīla*) not be mentioned?" No, because for yogis who have performed previous deeds (*adhikāra*) regarding blue and so on, the very state of being blue etc. is the cause of mastery. For those yogis, the limitedness or immeasurability of pure or impure color is not the cause of mastery; rather, it should be understood that the very state of being blue etc. is the cause of mastery.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Bases of Mastery is finished.
107:
## Explanation of the Talk on Liberations
"Rūpī" (possessing form) means that this yogi is endowed with such form (such as hair, etc.) included within his own continuity; that form is a distinguished form because it is the cause of that jhāna. If one is called "Rūpī" because of being endowed with that distinguished form, it should be understood that only that object-sign of the kasina-form included within one's own continuity accomplishes the state of being "Rūpī" in the ultimate sense, just like jhāna. In the Abhidhamma, the teaching on kasinas proceeds by way of the jhānas themselves being kasinas; in the Suttas, however, it is by way of the objects (being kasinas). Therefore, it is said, "by way of the Abhidhamma."

## Conclusion of the Explanation of the Talk on Liberations.

## Explanation of the Talk on Divine Abidings
Delusion (moha), which is the opposite of knowledge and is devoid of joy (somanassa) and grief (domanassa), is indeed "aññāṇupekkhā" (equanimity of ignorance). One is called "anodhijina" because the limits of defilements have not yet been conquered by the limits of the Path. One is called "avipākajina" because the resultants (vipāka) that will occur from the seventh existence onwards have not yet been conquered. "By way of being faultless" means by way of being without anger (dosa). Since there is no counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) even in a single being, there is no grasping of a limit; and the grasping of a being that occurs by way of conventional truth (sammuti-sacca) is not the grasping of a delimited form, etc. Therefore, it should be understood that because of reaching absorption (appanā), and because of grasping the concept of a being without misapprehending it through craving or views, the divine abidings (Brahmavihāras) such as loving-kindness (mettā) which have a single being as their object are said to have an immeasurable object (appamāṇagocara).

## Conclusion of the Explanation of the Talk on Divine Abidings.

## Explanation of the Talk on Foulness
It is called "uddhumātaka" (bloated) because it swells up after death. A dark/blue corpse mixed with white and red, or a dark corpse that has transformed from its previous color, is called "vinīlaka" (livid). "Saṅghāṭa" refers to the well-connected state of the limbs. Weakness of the object means the inability to establish the mind by way of opposing (the hindrances). In the seeing of benefits in oneself and the subsiding of the disease of hindrances (nīvaraṇa), the similes of the flower-scavenger, vomiting, and purging should be applied respectively. Due to the commonality of contemplating loathsomeness, the jhāna that takes loathsomeness as an object through hair, etc., and the jhāna of the colors of the cemetery are included. This is because that jhāna also arises only by way of contemplating loathsomeness; or, the nine types of corpses in the cemetery are called "sivathikāvaṇṇa."

## Conclusion of the Explanation of the Talk on Foulness.

## Conclusion of the Explanation of the Talk on Wholesome Form-Sphere.
108:
## Explanation of the Talk on Formless-Sphere Wholesome
'Sabbākārena' (in every way) means in every way, such as seeing the potential for taking up a staff due to the cause of having a body, and by way of seeing the danger in all forms, in the signs of kasina-forms, and in the jhānas that take them as objects; or alternatively, by way of abandoning attachment to forms and not wishing to advert to them. 'Virāgā' (through dispassion) occurs because of revulsion (jigucchanā). By the teaching of 'āneñjābhisankhāra' (imperturbable formation), etc., the state of being imperturbable (āneñja) is stated; and by such passages as 'Cunda, these are the peaceful liberations (santa-vimokkha) in the Noble Discipline,' the state of peaceful liberation is stated.

Because the perceptions of resistance (paṭighasaññā) have been well-abandoned through the power of formless meditation, which is the opposite of seeing the danger in form, one does not emerge from a formless attainment even by a loud sound. However, because they are not so well-abandoned, emergence from all form-sphere attainments may occur. The first jhāna, however, cannot endure even a slight sound; therefore, it is said that sound is a thorn (kaṇṭaka) to one who has entered that attainment.

In the period when formless meditation is absent, the surmounting (samatikkama) and disappearance (atthaṅgama) of form-perceptions and resistance-perceptions that are liable to arise after death are stated by bringing about the nature of non-arising as long as one's own formless resultant (vipāka) continues. Among the perceptions of diversity (nānattasaññā), some do not arise in that formless existence because there is no place for them, not because they are prevented by formless meditation. Some perceptions of diversity do arise because they are not prevented. Therefore, the non-attention, non-adverting, and non-reviewing of those perceptions is called 'amanasikāra'. Alternatively, it refers to the mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana) that leads to the impulsion (javana) process not producing or introducing those perceptions of diversity in the intervals of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) stream. By this, the stability of concentration is shown through the surmounting of forms which are the causes for attending to diversity. Because there is no surmounting of form in form-sphere attainments, 'non-attention to perceptions of diversity' is not mentioned alone. What is the benefit? It means that one cannot see the benefit of a perception produced in space which is devoid of all objects of enjoyment. The statement regarding the surmounting of form-perceptions, etc., is merely a manifestation of the result, not the primary purpose.

'Aññattha' (elsewhere) refers to the Suttas. For in those Suttas, even in the removal of a limited kasina, immeasurable radiation (anantapharaṇa) is stated because one takes only the seclusion from form without grasping a limit. In this Abhidhamma, however, although immeasurable radiation exists, 'Infinite is space' is not said in order to show that there is both limited (paritta) and infinite (ananta) according to the removed kasina. The meaning here is intended only to distinguish the jhāna by the occasion (samaya), not by the practice (paṭipatti); thus it is not so stated.
109:
The first formless consciousness is called 'infinite' because it should be adverted to as 'infinite' only by way of its own mode of pervasion. The space-concept, which is the basis for the removal of the kasina, is called ugghāṭima.

'Akiñcana' (nothingness) refers to the teaching of complete non-existence (vibhāvana) in every aspect, without taking even a single mode of consciousness.

'Yā yā' refers to the perception with remaining formations. To show that practice, [the text] shows the non-occurrence of mastery in advertence, etc., which incline towards that third formless jhāna, by saying 'I will advert,' and so on. It does not show the occurrence of advertence-development for the sake of transcending that third formless jhāna. 'Nāsaññā' means that the state of perception of this perception also exists. Comprehension occurring by way of grasping groups is called kalāpasammasana. Insight occurring by way of grasping individual states such as contact (phassa), etc., is called anupadadhamma-vipassanā.

The third formless jhāna occurs due to the transcendence of the consciousness occurring in the space-concept. Because of transcending that consciousness, there is the elimination (vibhāvana) of that very consciousness. In eliminating the second formless consciousness, only that second formless consciousness would be transcended, not its object. It is also not logical to see a fault in the object and then eliminate and transcend the subjective jhāna (ārammaṇika) which is without an object. In the Pali text, it is also taught: 'Having attained the base of infinite consciousness mindfully, and having emerged from it, one makes that very consciousness non-existent.' It is not taught as 'one eliminates that very base of infinite consciousness' or 'one eliminates that very thing.' However, in this Pali passage, 'Having reached the base of infinite consciousness as "infinite consciousness,"' both the consciousness as the object and the base of infinite consciousness as the subject (ārammaṇika) are taught. Among those two, when the word 'that' (taṃ) is connected with either one or with that jhāna which is primarily indicated from which one has emerged, the word 'consciousness' (viññāṇa) is used to exclude the base of infinite consciousness. Therefore, the elimination and transcendence of only the first formless consciousness is mentioned. 'Tannissitaṃ' means 'one who is dependent on that.' Just as standing in a secluded place outside a pavilion, without depending on and being separated from the person clinging to the pavilion, so is the standing of the third formless jhāna in the absence of the first formless consciousness clinging to space, when that consciousness has departed.

## The Explanation of the Wholesome States of the Formless Sphere is finished.
110:
## Explanation of the Wholesome of the Three Planes

These words, 'the five methods of predominance of desire' (chandādhipateyye pañca nayā), are spoken with reference to the preceding methods' inclination towards that final method of predominance of desire. However, this distinction does not follow the Pali text. Indeed, in the Pali text, the methods such as predominance of energy, etc., are not taught only after teaching the pure methods (suddhika-naya), etc. In the Great Book (Paṭṭhāna), the triad of the inferior (hīna-tika) is analyzed through seven great cycles (mahā-vāra) which are diversified by methods such as the analytical order (anuloma), etc. In that triad of the inferior, these twenty mundane great methods are considered as a portion of the medium states (majjhima-dhamma), and thus it is said, 'they are analyzed in that Great Book.' It is not said because those methods appear in that Great Book in the same order as presented in this commentary.

Having thus shown the place of analysis for these methods, now, at the end of this discussion on the wholesome of the three planes, the passage beginning with 'But in this place' (imasmim pana thāne) is stated for the purpose of showing the eighteen doors of action (kamma-dvāra). Alternatively, the Blessed One, showing the inclusion within the medium group (majjhima-rāsi) by turning away from the inferior and superior, made the analysis of these methods of the wholesome of the three planes in the triad of the inferior. The connection of the passage beginning with 'But in this place' is just as stated. In the medium group of the triad of the inferior, those states which occur with results and are performed by way of giving (dāna), etc., depending on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), should be understood as 'inferior' (hīna). Those states which are performed by way of giving, etc., depending on the departure from the round (vivaṭṭa/Nibbāna), should be understood as 'superior' (paṇīta). States without result (avipāka) should be understood as 'medium' (majjhima). Because they are without result, excluding the medium group among those states, there are eighteen doors of action: nine doors of action which are solely dependent on the round, and nine which are the strong dependence for Nibbāna. These states are 'actions' (kamma), and because they are the causes for their respective results, they are also 'doors' (dvāra); thus they are called 'doors of action' (kamma-dvāra). Alternatively, the consciousnesses in those respective states are called 'doors of action.' Or, the doors of body, etc., which are those respective doors, are meant. Among the eighteen types of nobles (khattiya), the nine types such as the three 'inferior-inferior' types who are incapable [of realizing the truth], and the nine types such as the three 'superior-superior' types who are capable, should be understood according to their actions. Similarly, Brahmins, etc., and deities should be applied. The forty-eight lineages (gotta-caraṇa) are the divisions of those very nobles, etc. 'A wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen... predominance of consciousness'—the state of predominance of consciousness thus taught is the word 'consciousness' (citta) which determines the occasion (samaya) within the collection of consciousness and mental factors. Therefore, it is said, 'it is spoken by way of the associated states (sampayutta-dhamma).'

## The Explanation of the Wholesome of the Three Planes is finished.
111:
## Explanation of Supramundane Wholesome

By the words "lokaṃ tarati" (he crosses the world), the Path (Magga), which is the practice for transcending the world, is taught. By the words "uttarati" (he ascends/crosses out), the Fruition (Phala), which stands in the benefit of reaching the end of the world, is taught. By the words beginning with "samatikkamma" (having transcended), Nibbāna is taught. Indeed, "samatikkamma" means having escaped. "Abhibhuyya" (having overcome) means being dissociated (from defilements). These three meanings should be applied to each of the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna. Alternatively, since the Supramundane Wholesome is being shown here, they should be applied to the Path only. The term "ekacittakkhaṇika" (occurring in a single mind-moment) is taught with reference to the fact that a single Path does not occur twice. It develops through wisdom that accomplishes the non-transgression of associated states, and so on. Although it should be called "niyyānīya" because it "leads out" (niyyāti), the vowel 'ī' is shortened and the letter 'y' is changed to 'k' to form the word "niyyānika". It is called "niyyāna" because one escapes by it; "niyyāna" itself is "niyyānika", similar to the word "venayika". In this context, although it should be called "neyyānika", it is spoken without changing the vowel 'i' to 'e'.

The collection of consciousness and mental factors is called "Fruition" (Phala); that Fruition is the support (nissaya) for its own constituent associated states. Alternatively, the knowledge associated with fruition is called Phala, or the Path factors such as Right View are called Phala. "Lokuttarabhāva" means the state of having transcended the world. By that term, Fruition and Nibbāna are included. Among them, the Fruition that occurs is called "Bhūmi" (Ground/Plane). Just as the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) etc., produced by Kamma, are called "Bhūmi" because they are the support for the person endowed with them, so too the Fruition produced by the Path is called "Bhūmi" because it is the support to be attained from time to time by the Noble Disciple (ariyasāvaka). Because it is such a ground of support, the Noble Ones remain in it for a long time. In the phrase "samucchedavivekavasena" (by way of seclusion through eradication), one should understand the absolute eradication of unwholesome states leading to the lower realms, and the eradication of the remaining unwholesome states like lightning dispelling darkness. Mundane Jhāna cannot be accomplished without a practice (paṭipadā) for a worldling or for a Noble One who has not made a prior resolution (adhikāra). However, for a Noble One who has made a prior resolution, it is accomplished through the Path itself, just as results (vipāka) are accomplished through wholesome (kusala). Since such mundane Jhāna accomplished by the Path is not similar to the Noble Path and is not its result, the Path-practice cannot be said to be the practice for that Jhāna. Therefore, the teaching was not made by emphasizing the practice there, but a "Pure Teaching" (suddhika-desanā) was also made to include the aforementioned Jhāna attained through the Path.

In this Supramundane teaching, however, "dukkha-paṭipadā" (painful practice) etc. are taught to show emphasis because no supramundane jhāna is accomplished without practice. "Yo koci vāro" (whichever turn/method) refers to any one of the turns in removing defilements, such as once, twice, three times, four times, or many times. The turns of removing defilements once or twice are only "sukha-paṭipadā" (pleasant practice); beyond twice, there is no more pleasant practice.
112:
The teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) define the turn of removing defilements three times as "dukkha-paṭipadā" (painful practice). Once it is defined as such, there is no need to mention that the turns of four times or more are also painful practice. "Rūpārūpa-pariggaha" (comprehension of the material and the immaterial) means defining and taking them by their characteristics, etc. "Nāmarūpa-vavatthāna" (definition of mentality and materiality) means determining that this collection of states is merely mentality and materiality, and there is no other being, etc., apart from them.

If it is argued that the slowness of the Path's arising for one who has comprehended materiality and immateriality might be due to the difficult accomplishment of knowledges like the definition of mentality and materiality, and thus painful practice should not be stated merely because of the difficulty of comprehending materiality and immateriality—that argument is not valid. This is because even if knowledges like the definition of mentality and materiality are easily accomplished due to the weakness of opposing defilements, the slowness of the Path's arising can occur because the faculties (indriya) associated with the easily accomplished insight (vipassanā) are dull.

"Having comprehended materiality and immateriality" also means comprehending without difficulty. If comprehended with difficulty, there is no need to mention it. The same applies to the remaining knowledges. "They favor this turn" means that when the defilements of insight (vipassanupakkilesa) arise during the practice of contemplation on rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā) at the end of comprehension by groups (kalāpasammasana), they favor the difficult turn of removing them three times as painful practice. This is because this removal is the end of the practice. Even if it is not difficult in this turn, if it was difficult in the preceding stages like the comprehension of materiality and immateriality, it should be understood as painful practice according to the method already mentioned. Otherwise, "this turn" refers to the difficulty of all knowledges like the comprehension of materiality and immateriality by way of the turn of removing [defilements] three times. For one who finds no difficulty in any knowledge, it should be known as pleasant practice (sukha-paṭipadā).

False speech etc. are harsh and dry because they involve deceiving others, etc., and cannot win people over. Right Speech (sammā-vācā) is the opposite, having the nature of winning people over. Because Right Speech is smooth and pleasant, it wins over associated states and the group of people who listen to the good words based on Right Speech. It causes the performance of bodily actions that ought to be done. It has the nature of exertion and effort. Therefore, the abstinence (virati) called Right Action (sammā-kammanta) is also said to have the nature of "samuṭṭhāna" (origination/causing to arise). Alternatively, "samuṭṭhāna" means uplifting associated states, like lifting a load with bodily action. "Vodāna" (purification) means the purity of a living being or associated states. Or it means the purity of livelihood for the sake of the continuation of the life faculty (jīvitindriya).

"Maggasannissita" (dependent on the Path) means that because it has the nature of the ultimate Path, it is a state dependent on the whole as a part of the Path. "Patiṭṭhāna" (establishing) is by way of defilements; "āyūhana" (striving/accumulating) is by way of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra). Or "patiṭṭhāna" is by way of craving (taṇhā); "āyūhana" is by way of views (diṭṭhi). "Bodhi" (enlightenment) should be connected as meaning the harmony of these states (dhamma-sāmaggī). It is like the factors of an army or the parts of a chariot.
113:
By this word (such as 'senanga'), he shows the state of 'avijjamāna-paññatti' (concept of the non-existent) of the designation 'Bodhi' which is to be taken as a person. The word 'aṅga' also exists in the sense of 'cause'; therefore, they are called 'Bojjhaṅga' (Factors of Enlightenment) because they lead to the realization of the Four Noble Truths. They are called 'Bodhi' because they understand; those very states called 'Bodhi' are the 'aṅga' (factors/causes). Thus, [Venerable Sāriputta] said: 'They are Bojjhaṅgas because they understand accordingly (anubujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā).' By the prefixes (anu, paṭi, saṃ) which illustrate such specific meanings as 'they understand well, correctly, without perversion, directly by realization, and in accordance with the causes such as insight (vipassanā) and the Four Noble Truths to be known,' he said 'anubujjhanti' and so on. Indeed, the word 'Bodhi' generally encompasses the act of understanding (bujjhāna) associated with all specific meanings such as 'accordance' (anurūpa).

'Tiṇṇam' refers to the meaning of 'the three' such as greed (rāga) and so on. What is meant by 'does' (karoti) is the performing of subsequent misconducts (duccarita). The constant indulgence in requisites produced by killing (pāṇātipāta) and so on is called 'constant indulgence' (dhuva-paṭisevana). 'Sakiccako' means having one's own separate task. By the words 'na hoti' (is not), he rejects the state of having a different meaning (from right speech and right action). The three grounds of deception (kuhana-vatthu) produced by evil desire are: indulgence in requisites, talk related to them, and the display of postures.

Insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā) is the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) together with conformity (anuloma). That insight is called 'Suññata' (Void) because it views [formations] as empty of self. It is called 'Appaṇihita' (Desireless) because it views them as suffering (dukkha) and thus dries up the craving that longs [for them]. That insight, standing in the position of the practice that leads to [the Path] (āgamana-paṭipadā) for the sake of attaining the Path at the occasion of the Path's arising, gives the name 'Suññata' or 'Appaṇihita' [to the Path]. When the name is obtained through the 'arrival' (āgamana) of insight, the name is also established by its own quality (saguṇa) and by its object (ārammaṇa). However, when a name is obtained through own quality and object, the name cannot be established through 'arrival' in all Paths. Because it is the complete cause for the establishment of the name, and because all three names can be associated with all Paths through own quality and object, but the name can be specifically determined through 'arrival', it is said in the non-figurative teaching (Abhidhamma) that the name is obtained in this Path only through 'arrival' and not through the others (own quality and object).

'Animitta-vipassanā' refers to the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). 'In the sign-objects' (nimitta-dhammesu) refers to the contemplation in the aggregates (khandhas) which are possessed of substance through the power of compactness (ghana) such as mass (samūha) and so on, and which are delimited by their own functions. The contemplation of impermanence is called 'Animitta-vimokkha' (Signless Deliverance) [in the Paṭisambhidāmagga]. How can the comparison of the illustration be possible in this example? Just as there is no absence of the title 'predominant' (adhipati) called 'Path' for the desire (chanda) and consciousness (citta) [that are not predominant], there is no absence of the name 'Animitta' for the 'Animitta-vimokkha' which is excessive in the faculty of faith (saddhindriya). It is not proper to say that 'Animitta-vimokkha' cannot give the name 'Animitta' [to the Path], just as states that are not Path-predominants cannot give the name 'Path-predominant' [to the Path], because there is no state of not being 'Animitta' for 'Animitta-vimokkha'.
114:
This is because of the absence of the name 'Animitta' for 'Animitta-vimokkha'. It is appropriate to call it 'Path-predominant' (maggādhipati) in the sense that 'the Path is the predominant of these states'.
