Among those Path-predominant states, it is correct that there is no state of Path-predominance in those states associated with desire (chanda) and consciousness (citta). However, here, the meaning of 'maggānimitta' as 'the Path is the signless (animitta) of this [deliverance]' is not possible. Therefore, it is not that the signless nature of the Path is inappropriate because of that deliverance which is not the Path; or rather, what similarity is intended here?

It is simply the absence of the name 'Path' for what is not a Path-factor. For example, although desire and consciousness have the state of predominance, they do not receive the name 'Path' as in 'Path-predominant'; and because they are not Path-factors, they do not receive a name in the Path through them. Similarly, although faith (saddhā) exists as the 'arrival' (āgamana) of the Path, it does not receive the name 'Path' as 'Animitta'; and because that faith is not a Path-factor, it does not receive a name in the Path through it. In this way, it has been shown that in 'Animitta-vipassanā', the signless state (animitta) does not exist in the ultimate sense.

If it is asked, 'Is it not that here the Jhana is spoken of by the names Suññata etc., and not the Path?', the answer is no. Jhana possesses the names Suññata etc. because of its association with the Path. It is said that according to the Suttanta method, it also receives the name in this Abhidhamma through its own quality and object. Therefore, it was rejected by the statement 'but they do not receive [the name]'. For what reason? The intention is that in Abhidhamma, the name is obtained only through the 'opposite' (paccanīka) without considering its own nature (sarasa). Obtaining a name through own quality and object has 'own nature' as the primary factor. If the name were obtained through own nature alone, the determination of the state of Suññata etc. for all Paths would not be possible. Therefore, although there are two ways of obtaining a name in Abhidhamma, only the name obtained through the 'opposite' (paccanīka) which performs the determination is taken. Thus, it is said that the Suññata-path and Appaṇihita-path do not receive the name through their own quality and object.

Alternatively, 'they do not receive [the name]' means they do not receive it through own quality and object which do not regard other opposites. For what reason? Because in Abhidhamma, the name is obtained through own nature (sarasa) together with the opposite (paccanīka). In Abhidhamma, own nature alone, without regarding the determining opposite, does not serve as the cause for a name, because it would lead to the fallacy of non-determination. Therefore, the Paths that conform to insight which is the opposite of adherence to self (attābhinivesa) and longing (paṇidhi) receive the name through their own nature together with the opposite, even though other own natures exist.

However, the insight of the Animitta-path is not the opposite of the 'sign' (nimitta), because it itself takes the sign of formations (saṅkhāra-nimitta) as an object and cannot prevent the grasping of the sign. Therefore, the Path conforming to that insight is also not the opposite of the sign. If it were the opposite, it would also be the opposite of the insight occurring in the sign. Therefore, although own nature (sarasa) exists, because there is no determining opposite (paccanīka), the 'own nature' that gives the name 'Animitta' is not taken in Abhidhamma. The Path conforming to the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) should be understood as being included only in the 'Pure Practice' (suddhikapaṭipadā) method. For that very reason, that method was taught. Thus...
115:
"The path of one emerging by way of impermanence is the signless path"—this statement, which will be mentioned later, should be understood as being presented by the Teachers of the Commentaries in the following manner to illustrate the signless path (animitta-magga).

In the question "Emergence... what is its object?", the inquiry is made with the following thought: if the insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhāna-gāminī vipassanā) of one emerging from formations (saṅkhāra) such as impermanence has the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) as its object, then emergence from formations would not be possible; and if it has formations as its object, then the penetration of the characteristic would not be possible. Because it is meant that through the knowledge occurring in formations as "impermanent" etc., the characteristics are also penetrated by taking the formations which have those aspects, it is said: "having the characteristic as object" (lakkhaṇārammaṇā). To show that insight which has formations as its object is called "having the characteristic as object" in the sense already mentioned, he said "What is called characteristic" (lakkhaṇaṃ nāma) etc. Indeed, impermanence (aniccata), suffering (dukkhatā), and non-self (anattatā), if taken separately from the five aggregates, have the nature of a concept (paññatti) and do not exist in the ultimate sense (paramattha). Because they do not exist [separately], they are states that cannot be described by way of being "limited" (paritta) etc. Therefore, since the characteristic to be taken separately does not exist in the ultimate sense, while noting formations by way of their nature as "impermanent, suffering, non-self," one is said to be noting the characteristics. Thus he said: "He who notes the three characteristics: impermanence, suffering, non-self." And because only formations are seen as impermanent etc., those formations become something to be abandoned, like a corpse tied to one's neck.

## Lokuttarakusala (Supramundane Wholesome)
## Pakiṇṇakakathāvaṇṇanā (Description of the Miscellaneous Discussion)

In that passage, "therein" (tatra) means in the supramundane jhāna. With the half-verse "And internally" (ajjhattañca), he briefly points out the fivefold basis of insight which should be closely attended to and from which one should emerge. In "seven, eight" etc. factors, it should be understood that the word ādi is elided in "sattaṭṭhaṅgāni". "Sign" (nimitta) refers to those occurrences of signs from which emergence happens; he points them out using only the word "sign". Only the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa) determines the specific factors of the Noble Path (ariya-magga), such as the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). Why? Because for the knowledge of equanimity towards formations arising from this or that basis jhāna (pādakajjhāna) such as the second, etc., there is the development of detachment (virāga) and the lack of desire to attain those factors that have been transcended from the basis jhāna, and because such [detachment] does not exist in other [knowledges]. In the views of those [other] teachers as well... it should be understood that "only insight determines [the factors]." Why? Because only by the rule of insight, even in the view of the first Elder, the paths that have no basis jhāna and the paths that have the first jhāna as basis are only of the first jhāna level; and others are of their respective jhāna levels due to the rules of basis jhāna and insight. Thus, in the remaining views also, the rule of insight should be applied as appropriate.
116:
"Miscellaneous formations" (pakiṇṇaka-saṅkhāra) means formations other than the basis jhāna. By saying this, he shows that when the formations of the basis jhāna are contemplated, there is no need to even say [that it is a path of the first jhāna]. "Therein also" (tatrāpi) means in the view of the second Elder as well. The state of having this or that jhāna [in the path] occurs due to the rules of insight into this or that contemplated formation. For in that [second Elder's view] also, insight—by way of the development of detachment (virāga) or non-detachment (avirāga) towards those respective jhāna factors—becomes associated with joy (somanassa) or associated with equanimity (upekkhā), and thus determines the jhāna factors etc. of the path. Thus the rule of insight should be understood in the manner already stated.

"That" (taṃ) means the occurrence similar to that respective jhāna. This meaning should be illustrated by the Nandakovāda Sutta, which shows that without the supports (upanissaya) of basis jhāna and contemplated jhāna, it cannot be accomplished by mere inclination (ajjhāsaya); and that without support, the fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-phala) etc. cannot be accomplished by mere thought (saṅkappa). For in that sutta, the Blessed One, speaking of the state of fulfilled intention even for a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), [shows that] for whichever [path] there is the support, for that path alone the inclination is the determinant, not for any other. Thus the state of fulfilled intention occurs through that [path]. Beyond that, even if the intention exists, it is not accomplished—this is the meaning illustrated. Similarly here, in this view of personal inclination (puggalajjhāsaya-vāda), for whichever path associated with the second jhāna etc. there is the aforementioned support, for that path alone the inclination is the determinant, not for another, because even if that [inclination] exists, it is not accomplished [without support]. However, in this view, when the support of basis jhāna and contemplated jhāna exists, the inclination certainly arises, just as the respective intention arises when the support for the respective fruit exists. Therefore, it is said "inclination determines," because in the absence of that [support], [the path] does not occur.

"When there is no basis jhāna" is said with reference to the mundane jhānas which serve as bases, excluding the path of the fourth jhāna. And since the attainment of absorption (appanā) cannot occur without the five factors in the absence of the support of transcending the gross factors, he said: "it is a path associated with joy." By the phrase "path associated with equanimity," he shows that although the state of the fourth jhāna is similar [to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception], for the path capable of uprooting the underlying tendencies (anusaya), there is no remaining of formations. The meaning is that those views do not conflict, because the state of the fifth jhāna and the state of the first jhāna etc. are possible by the power of inclination. And inclination is purposeful; otherwise, if the determination were accomplished only by the basis jhāna and contemplated jhāna, saying that inclination is the determinant would be useless. But here in the Aṭṭhasālinī, in the matter of determination, the author of the commentary, extracting only the certain meaning called insight, says: "In the views of those [other] teachers as well... only insight determines." He thus shows the meaning that in all three of these views, only insight is the determinant. It is true; those respective views reach completion only when accompanied by insight. It has already been shown that the matter of attaining the path cannot be accomplished by the mere existence of basis jhāna without insight.

"Trembles" (paveḍhati) means it is unable to be the cause for change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). If it is said that the impulsion (javana) falls at the fifth thought-moment, then there is a question to be raised: "Why do change-of-lineage and the subsequent path occur at the moment the impulsion falls?" [This is possible] because there is no falling of a different, new kind of impulsion. In the commentary, wishing to show the question regarding the statement "At that time the impulsion is said to fall," he said "If at the fifth thought-moment" etc. Since sense-sphere impulsions normally occur seven times, they increase in order from the first impulsion, reach their peak at the fourth, and gradually decrease from the fifth onwards; therefore it is said "At that time the impulsion falls." Even though it is said to fall at the moment of the fifth impulsion, if it is asked why change-of-lineage and the path occur at that moment...
117:
The author of the Saṅgaha Commentary showed that only Vipassanā (insight) determines these three views. This means that those various views can only achieve their purpose when associated with Vipassanā, and not without it. "Trembles" means it is unable to be a condition for gotrabhū (change-of-lineage). If it is said that the javana (impulsion) falls at the fifth thought-moment, how then can gotrabhū and the Path immediately following it arise at the moment the javana falls? This is because there is no nature of falling for a new kind of javana. If that original javana itself were occurring many times, it could be said to fall; however, gotrabhū is a new javana that arises with Nibbāna as its object, which is different from the object of formations (saṅkhāra). Similarly, the Path is also a new javana by way of a different plane (the supramundane plane). 

One might ask: Is it not because the seventh javana cetanā (volition) is powerful that it becomes upapajjavedanīya-kamma (kamma to be experienced in the next life) and ānantariya-kamma (kamma with immediate result)? The intention in this objection is: because the final javana cetanā is well-prepared as the immediate condition (anantara-paccaya) for the resultant continuity (vipāka-santāna) of rebirth, that seventh javana cetanā becomes upapajjavedanīya and ānantariya; it is not merely because it is powerful like a javana cetanā that does not fall. 

Furthermore, "conformity (anuloma) should follow that gotrabhū" means that if gotrabhū has formations as its object, then that gotrabhū is also just conformity; thus, like the preceding conformity, that gotrabhū would follow another conformity, and the Path would not arise, nor would the emergence (vuṭṭhāna) which is the Path occur. This is because it does not obtain the condition standing in the place of adverting (āvajjana) which has an object similar to itself. 

Because they have not yet been abandoned, the defilements (kilesa) latent in the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā) are called "attained to the ground" (bhūmiladdhā) because they have obtained that ground of the five aggregates of clinging. They are also called "the bridge of the round" (vaṭṭasetu) because they bind one to the round of existence (vaṭṭa). The absolute eradication of those defilements is called the "shattering of the mass of greed" (lobhakkhandhādi-padālana), etc. That Path arises. 

"One existence" (eka bhava) is said because an Anāgāmī (Non-returner), even if reborn many times in that same Fine-material or Immaterial sphere, does not return to the lower sense sphere; thus it is taken as one existence. "Of this meaning" refers to the meaning of the Path emerging from the aforementioned upādinnaka-pavatta. The destruction of the cause of the abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa (kamma-formative consciousness) which gives results in the woeful states and in the happy states above the seventh existence should be understood as the cessation of abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa through the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa). 

"In two existences" means in the two existences that would arise in the sense sphere for a Sakadāgāmī (Once-returner) who has not yet developed the Path of Non-returning. By the word "trembles" (calati), only the nature of trembling is shown, not the absence of non-trembling. Therefore, after showing non-trembling, he said "Tathāgatassa hi", etc., to show trembling again. Or rather, it is said "trembles" to refute the view of those who, seeing all four paths in some noble person as having the same practice (paṭipadā), assume that by nature they do not tremble. Since it is not said to establish only trembling, showing both is appropriate. ...
118:
Some might see all four paths as having the same practice and assume they are inherently unmoving (acalana); to prevent such an assumption, it is said "trembles" (calati). It is not said for the purpose of defining only trembling. Therefore, showing both (trembling and non-trembling) is appropriate. Alternatively, although for some the four paths have the same practice, the practices accomplished through the faculties of defilement have the nature of trembling due to the power of those faculties. Therefore, it is only said "trembles", and not "does not tremble".

## The Explanation of the Miscellaneous Discussion on Supramundane Wholesome is finished.

## The Explanation of the Twenty Great Methods of the First Path

A person who previously had the inclination (ajjhāsaya), "I shall develop the Path," develops the Path. Thus, in all cases, the specific development is to be understood through the specific inclination.

In "predominance of desire" (chandādhipati), etc., among the states occurring in a single thought-moment, how does desire (chanda) reach the state of predominance over its co-nascent states, and how do energy (viriya), etc., become predominant? It is by the power of strong dependence (upanissaya). For if a wholesome state is accomplished for one who has desire, and the wholesome state is accomplished for one who proceeds with the thought "I shall accomplish it," then the desire co-nascent with that wholesome state, being distinguished by that prior strong dependence, brings the co-nascent states under its own influence. When that desire proceeds, those co-nascent states proceed; when it recedes, they recede; they have power corresponding to the power of that desire, just as the king's men follow the king's will. The same applies to energy and the others. As for the remaining states, although in some cases they may occur as described, they do not have the state of predominance because they lack that nature (of bringing co-nascent states under their influence).

## Explanation of the Second Path

By making the letter "ā" short, it is called "aññindriya". The letter "ā" has the meaning of defining the four noble truths.

## Explanation of the Third and Fourth Paths

The intention is that the path factors are not fulfilled because Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi) has no function (of killing/abandoning). For it is called "Path" (magga) because it goes while killing [the respective defilements]; however, for this Right View, there is no state to be killed. Of conceit (māna)...
119:
The occurrence of conceit as "I am" is a standing in the place of wrong view because it is similar to wrong view. The phrase "like the time of the occurrence of light" is said with reference to the long duration of light. This is because an analogy can be made based on a partial similarity in the intended sense. "Khāre vā" means in the alkaline ash of wood, etc. "Sammadditvā" means by moistening (softening). "Chanda" is craving (taṇhā). "Anusaya" refers to the latent tendencies of craving and conceit. In this Sutta, just as the absolute eradication of a scent that has not yet been removed is shown, the Elder Khemaka, by showing the absolute eradication of conceit, etc., which have not yet been removed, shows the meaning "one abandons other defilements"; therefore, this Pali passage is cited as evidence. It should be understood that it is not cited because the analogy was stated in the manner already mentioned in the Commentary. When the mind occurs continuously, the blameworthy and blameless mental factors (cetasikas) that cause the defilement and purification of that mind arise; since they become like parts or members of that mind, it is said "by the power of the parts of the mind" (cittaṅga-vasena).

## The Explanation of Supramundane Wholesome States is finished.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Wholesome States is finished.

## Unwholesome Section (Akusala-pada)

## Chapter on the Summary of States (Dhammuddesa-vāra)

## Explanation of the First Consciousness

Following the method stated in the Wholesome section, it should be understood accordingly; thus it is said "by the method already stated." "Gantabbābhāvato" means because there is no meaning to be known (realized). "Diṭṭhiyā gatamattaṃ" means the mere occurrence or the mere grasping of wrong view. Unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) is taken separately because it is the proximate cause for the arising of the unwholesome, and because it is a certain cause. "Sati-saṃvara" (restraint by mindfulness) here should be understood as the non-negligent endurance of a person touched by cold, etc. "Pahāna-saṃvara" (restraint by abandonment) is restraint by effort (vīriya-saṃvara).

"Assāda-dassana" is the view of gratification (assāda-diṭṭhi) which sees things as enjoyable. Delusion (moha) produces the result of improper practice through its manifestation as a result. Or, it has the mode of grasping as the opposite of right practice. Although all greed (lobha) is called covetousness (abhijjhā), in order to show the characteristics, etc., of covetousness that is endowed with a special potency beyond ordinary greed, which reaches the path of action (kammapatha) and arises in this unwholesome context, the phrase "Sā parasampattīnaṃ" etc., is said. Great delight (abhirati) is the intense enjoyment through craving that is preceded by the inclination towards oneself.
120:
"Anupaparikkha" is delusion (moha). By the power of delusion or by the power of wrong view, wrong conviction (micchā-adhimokkha) accompanied by craving arises, which draws the mind towards an object that is not worthy of conviction. "Asatiya-citta" means occurring in a mind that is devoid of protection due to lack of shame (ahiri-ka), etc. By the phrase "being devoid of mindfulness and being the opposite of mindfulness," it is shown that the unwholesome aggregates themselves, which are devoid of mindfulness and are the opposite of mindfulness, are called wrong mindfulness (micchā-sati).

Those unwholesome aggregates should be understood as being associated with sharp perception (saññā) when remembering deeds done long ago, etc., or at the time of nursing a grudge (upanāha), etc. The state of distress (sadaratha), etc., is stated generally as being associated with defilements without distinction. This is because some unwholesome mental factors like sloth and torpor (thina-middha), which are the absolute opposites of lightness (lahutā), etc., are absent in this unwholesome context. "Avūpasama" (un-calmness) refers to the clear absence of settling down. "Anavaṭṭhāna-rasa" (the function of unsteadiness) means the task of wavering. In the phrase "cetaso avūpasame," the locative case (sattami vibhatti) is used in the sense of the purpose to be accomplished. Alternatively, the object which is the cause of un-calmness is called "avūpasama."

## The Explanation of the Chapter on the Summary of States is finished.

## Explanation of the Chapter on Exposition (Niddesa-vāra)

Unwaveringness (akampana) in co-nascent states (sahajata-dhamma) should not be understood as unwaveringness due to being the opposite of laziness (kosajja). Rather, it is the firmness by way of being energetic in performing various evil deeds that is understood as unwaveringness in those co-nascent states.

"Diṭṭhiyā virūpaṃ phanditaṃ" (the distorted agitation of view) refers to the wrong view itself that occurs in various ways such as eternalism (sassata), etc. "Taranti" means they float as if at a landing place. "Vipariyesato" means by way of the perversion of the object.

Because it is the basis for the grasping of the non-existent such as a natural self (pakati-atta) by way of concealing the true nature, and for the perversion of perception (saññā-vipallāsa), etc., which is the uneven grasping of the impermanent as permanent, etc., it is said "one knows the non-existent and the uneven."

## Explanation of the Second Consciousness

By the sentence "Kiñcāpi ... uppajjati," the lack of distinction from the preceding first unwholesome consciousness is shown. "Thina" (sloth) is the state of being shrunken and combined by way of being dejected and lacking energy.

## Explanation of the Third Consciousness

Here, it should be understood that the five "apaṇṇaka" factors (unfailing factors) along with conceit (māna) are the factors of the mind that are unerring and worthy of arising. Since conceit is not a constant associate...
121:
Regarding the term "Niyatayevāpanakā"—to explain: In the Paṭṭhāna, it is stated, "Dependent on a fetter, a fetter arises by way of root-condition." Here, sensual lust (kāmarāga) occurs four times, aversion (paṭigha) three times, and these three states—conceit (māna), doubt (vicikicchā), and lust for existence (bhavarāga)—occur once each. Thus, the connection (yojanā) of fetters with fetters is shown in ten ways. In these ten connections, by saying "Dependent on the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of conceit and the fetter of ignorance arise," "Dependent on the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of ignorance arises," "Dependent on the fetter of conceit, the fetter of lust for existence and the fetter of ignorance arise," and "Dependent on the fetter of lust for existence, the fetter of ignorance arises," the non-fixed (aniyata) nature of conceit is revealed. The same is shown in the Kilesa-duka (Dyad of Defilements). In this commentary, it will also be said, "The connection of fetters is tenfold; likewise, the connection of defilements is tenfold." Uplifting (sampaggaha) has the function of only by way of arrogance/exaltation, not like energy (vīriya) which has the function of strenuous effort in accomplishing various tasks. Even inferiority conceit (omāna), which is taking oneself as low, should be understood as uplifting (sampaggaha).

## Description of the Fourth Consciousness
Those who, being distracted for the sake of avoiding danger, generate effort are called "those with effort for the sake of avoidance"; (this consciousness arises) in their mental continuum.

## Description of the Ninth Consciousness
It has the function of spreading (visappana) by way of the arising of unpleasant forms (aniṭṭharūpa) throughout the body, and by way of its own mode of occurrence. Hatred (dosa) should be understood as being like putrid urine mixed with poison, because it is unpleasant in the things it is associated with and in its results. In the words concerning the function (rasa) expressed through such negations as "it has the function of discontent (anabhirati)," it should be understood that the respective opposite function is to be taken. Being in a bitter mode is called harshness (kaṭukañcukatā). Regarding one's own accomplishments such as dwellings and so on, it should be understood as servitude (dāsabya) because of dependence on others. Just as in servitude, a slave is dependent on others, so too when there is remorse (kukkucca), the one possessed of that remorse is dependent on others. For he is unable to proceed according to his own nature in wholesome states. Alternatively, because of being dependent on the subsequent grieving over unwholesome deeds done and wholesome deeds not done, one is possessed of remorse by way of both; therefore, that remorse is like servitude.

"Opposite mode" means the mode of an opposing person or the mode of an opposing mind; therefore, it is the cause of an opposing person or mind. By that word, the meanings of opposition (virujjhana) and contradiction (virodha) are shown. The word "speech" (vacana) in the context of "well-uttered speech" should be understood as a mere example. For even if all tasks are performed with this hatred (or even by a person free from hatred), they are not well-performed. Some teachers explain the word "ropa" as having only the meaning of "speech" (vacana). The statement "that speech is incomplete" is said with reference to the fact that hatred does not have the nature to produce such complete speech, or that completeness of speech might occur due to some other reason.

It is shown by the Pali "vigatā cikicchā" (devoid of cure). It is said so because it is difficult to cure with the medicine of wisdom. It does not mean that doubt (vicikicchā) cannot be cured in every way; that is the meaning shown. Because of the absence of decision, or because it is merely the cause for the mind not being well-established, it is called "mere existence." Because it is unable to go towards (decide on) a single mode, it retreats from the object.
122:
Viruddhākāra refers to the mode of an opposing person or an opposing mind, which is the nature of opposition. By this expression, the state of opposition (virodha) is shown. The word 'vacanaṃ' (speech) should be regarded as a mere illustration. For every action performed with this [anger] is not well-established or well-produced [as it would be by one without anger]. Some teachers explain the word 'ropa' as having the meaning of 'vacana' (speech). That this statement is not to be taken as authoritative means that because anger does not inherently have the nature of producing such [perfect] speech, the perfection of speech might occur due to some other cause (such as self-control or habit of good speech).

## Commentary on the Eleventh Consciousness
'Vigatā cikicchā' is said because it is difficult to cure with the medicine of wisdom; it does not mean that doubt (vicikicchā) is entirely incurable in every way.

Because of the lack of decision and because the mind is merely a cause for occurrence without being well-established, it is called 'mere occurrence and persistence.'

Because it is unable to go towards a single mode [of understanding], it recedes from its object.

## Commentary on the Twelfth Consciousness
Restlessness (uddhacca) wavers while remaining only in the mode it has grasped; thus, the fluctuation occurs in a single object. Doubt (vicikicchā), however, even if it arises in a single object such as a visible form, looks for another mode to be grasped, thinking "Is it thus? Is it this?" and then "Is it not thus? Is it something else?" Therefore, the wavering occurs across various objects.

With the phrase "It should be understood in this order," having shown the miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka) points mentioned regarding these two types of delusion-rooted consciousness, he says "In all [twelve] as well" to show them in all twelve unwholesome consciousnesses. Just as in the wholesome [triad], the object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) is not extracted but only the conascent-predominance (sahajātādhipati) is, so here too only the conascent-predominance should be extracted. It is not mentioned because object-predominance is not obtainable. However, that object-predominance is obtainable in the eight types of consciousness rooted in greed. "In the rest as well" means there is no other conascent-predominance to be extracted besides the predominance of investigation (vīmaṃsādhipati). Regarding object-predominance, there is nothing to be said. "Any state" (kañci dhammaṃ) refers to one conascent factor among [the predominances like] desire (chanda), etc. In the sections like the dependent-origination cycle (paṭiccavāra) of the Wholesome Triad, it should be understood that it is prohibited in the Paṭṭhāna Pali because not even a single question is raised as "not by root-condition, but by predominance-condition." If it were not prohibited but accepted, it would certainly be stated by the power of the question "Unwholesome... condition."

"By vision..." (dassanena...) is because there is no state to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (because it cannot draw forth rebirth-linking). Alternatively, it is because it is not included among the states to be abandoned by vision. By this text "because of the absence of being abandoned by vision," he shows that it is not included among states to be abandoned by vision because it does not draw forth rebirth-linking. By its non-inclusion in those states, he establishes the non-drawing of rebirth-linking. To establish the non-inclusion because of the non-drawing [of rebirth], he says "For in those," etc. Rebirth-linking results would only be given in these woeful states (apāya). If there were the giving of rebirth-linking in the woeful states, it would be a state to be abandoned by vision. This is because all unwholesome states leading to the woeful states are states to be abandoned by vision. Desiring to point out a flaw by citing the Commentary's statement "Rebirth-linking would only be given in this realm," he says "And if it were so... because of the nature of being abandoned by vision." It should be understood up to "this is the intention: it does not come [in the analysis of states to be abandoned by vision]" that if restlessness were to give rebirth-linking in the woeful states, it would be a state to be abandoned by vision.
123:
It should be understood that it is prohibited in the Paṭṭhāna because the question is not raised. If it were otherwise, i.e., not prohibited, it would be stated as 'one' by the power of the question: 'Dependent on an unwholesome state, an unwholesome state arises, not by root-condition but by predominance-condition.'

'Dassanena pahātabbābhāvato' means either because of the absence of the state to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry, or because of non-inclusion among the states to be abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry. By this statement of the absence of being abandoned by vision, in showing the meaning that it is not included among the states to be abandoned by vision because it cannot draw forth rebirth-linking, he establishes the non-drawing of rebirth-linking by its non-inclusion in those states. To establish the non-inclusion because of the non-drawing of rebirth-linking, he says 'For in those,' etc. Rebirth-linking results would only be given in these woeful states. If rebirth-linking were given in the woeful states, it would be a state to be abandoned by vision because all unwholesome states leading to the woeful states are states to be abandoned by vision. In reality, this consciousness associated with restlessness is not a state to be abandoned by vision; therefore, the intention is that it does not appear in the Dassanena-pahātabba-vibhaṅga.

How is it known that 'it is not included among states to be abandoned by vision because it does not draw forth rebirth-linking'? It is known because only for states to be abandoned by vision has the nature of being a multi-momentary kamma-condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya) been taught. Unwholesome states are of two kinds: those to be abandoned by vision and those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā). Among those two, the nature of being a multi-momentary kamma-condition is not stated for volitions (cetanā) to be abandoned by cultivation; it is stated only for the others [those to be abandoned by vision]. In the passage 'A state to be abandoned by cultivation is not a condition by way of kamma-condition for a state to be abandoned by vision nor for a state to be abandoned by cultivation,' only conascent kamma (sahajāta-kamma) is analyzed, not multi-momentary kamma. Similarly, in the negative (paccanīka) section, it is taught only this much: 'A state to be abandoned by cultivation is not a condition by way of object-condition... [pe]... conascent-condition... [pe]... decisive-support-condition... [pe]... is a condition by way of post-nascent-condition for a state to be abandoned by vision nor for a state to be abandoned by cultivation'; it is not stated that 'it is a condition by way of kamma-condition.' However, in the case of states to be abandoned by vision, the way it conditions by kamma-condition is taught.

Since volition associated with restlessness is included only among states to be abandoned by cultivation, it is said that it cannot be a multi-momentary kamma-condition. If it were, the nature of being a multi-momentary kamma-condition for volition to be abandoned by cultivation would also have been taught; but it is not taught. Therefore, if the nature of being a multi-momentary kamma-condition existed in volition associated with restlessness, it should have been taught among states to be abandoned by vision; it is not taught because that nature of being a multi-momentary kamma-condition is absent. The intention here is that it is not included among those states to be abandoned by vision because it cannot draw forth rebirth-linking. By not mentioning the multi-momentary kamma-condition, the fact that states to be abandoned by cultivation produce results during the course of existence (pavatti) is also excluded. This is because one is unable to prevent the nature of being a multi-momentary kamma-condition for restlessness which produces results during the course of existence.
124:
It has been stated: "A state associated with pleasant feeling is a condition for a state associated with painful feeling by way of asynchronous kamma condition (nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya)," and so forth (in the Paṭṭhāna). If states to be abandoned by cultivation (such as restlessness, etc.) do not produce results, why are they called states that have the nature of producing results (vipākadhamma)? It is because, like direct-knowledge consciousness (abhiññā-citta) and others, they have a nature worthy of producing results. The statement in the Vibhaṅga: "At whatever time an unwholesome consciousness arises, accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness... the knowledge of these states is the analytical knowledge of dhammas (dhamma-paṭisambhidā), and the knowledge of their results is the analytical knowledge of meanings (attha-paṭisambhidā)," is also intended to mean that they are worthy of producing results. However, this point should be carefully investigated. For there is room for discussion here. This is because the word 'result' (vipāka) does not express the 'worthiness of producing results' in the same way that the word 'nature of producing results' (vipākadhamma) does.

## Conclusion of the Explanation of the Unwholesome Section.

## The Indeterminate Section

## Explanation of Rootless Wholesome Resultants

Among those states, the terms "resultant indeterminate" (vipākābyākata) and so forth are connected with the passage: "To show by analysis, which states are indeterminate?" and so forth. The term "tassāpi" is also connected with the passage: "Desiring to show the arising... it is stated," and so forth. "Upacitattā" (because of being accumulated) means because it has been increased (prepared) to the point of being capable of producing its own result by obstructing the result of another kamma. Since causes such as the form-object (rūpārammaṇa) are common to other consciousnesses, the names "eye-consciousness" (cakkhuviññāṇa) and "ear-consciousness" (sotaviññāṇa) are derived from the specific physical base (vatthu). This is also because the sharpness or dullness of the consciousnesses is due to the sharpness or dullness of the bases like the eye, which act as special conditions.

It is called "cognition of forms dependent on the eye" (cakkhusannissitarūpavijānana) because it is both dependent on the eye and is the cognition of forms. Eye-consciousness has such a characteristic. Among those words, by the phrase "dependent on the eye," other consciousnesses that have the form-object are excluded. By the phrase "cognition of forms," states such as contact (phassa) that are dependent on the eye are excluded. By the words "eye" and "form," cognition is made clear by way of the base (nissaya) and the object (ārammaṇa). Since the function of this eye-consciousness is the grasping of an object that is merely a form, it is said to have "the function of taking only the form as object" (rūpamattārammaṇarasa). The phrase "by way of jhāna factors" (jhānaṅgavasena) is used because equanimity, pleasure, pain, and one-pointedness, which exist in consciousnesses other than the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, are included in the jhāna factors; and in these (two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness) also, those states similar to them...
125:
The term "jhāna factors" is used figuratively. Indeed, without the jhāna condition (jhāna-paccaya), there is no state of being a jhāna factor. For it is stated in the Paṭṭhāna: "Jhāna factors are a condition for states associated with jhāna... and for matter by way of jhāna condition." The state of being a jhāna condition for the feeling and one-pointedness associated with these two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness is also rejected. As it is said: "Dependent on an indeterminate state, an indeterminate state arises, not by way of jhāna condition. Dependent on one constituent (khandha) associated with the fivefold sense-consciousness, three constituents arise," and so forth. Although the jhāna condition is absent, they are pointed out in the second group (dutiya-rāsi) because of the presence of equanimity, etc., in feeling and the stability of mind (one-pointedness), and because there is no other place to state such states.

"Vatthupaṇḍarattā" (because of the brightness of the base) means that it has a bright nature by way of the physical base of sensitivity (pasāda) and the heart-base (hadayavatthu), which are naturally pure because they are not opposed to the dark (unwholesome) states. However, since this method is not applicable in the four-constituent realm (immaterial realm), the brightness of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and the unwholesome states arising from it would not occur there; therefore, the cause of brightness in that realm should be stated. Otherwise, this brightness is simply the inherent nature of the mind.

In the word "idampi," the particle "pi" is used in reference to the previously mentioned consciousness associated with doubt (vicikicchā), which is accompanied by mere stability. "Pakatiyā" means by not overstepping (the initial application/vitakka). That distinction also (arises from impact). "It strikes the body-sensitivity (kāyappasāda) and is resisted in the great elements (mahābhūta) which are the causes of sensitivity" means it reaches the avenue of the sense and strikes. Just as when it is said, "It arises depending on a form-object," there is no distinction of before and after between the taking of the object and the arising, so too should it be understood here regarding the striking and resistance. The analogy of the cotton and the anvil is also stated for the purpose of showing the impact on both, not for the purpose of showing a sequence of before and after in the striking of the dependent (sensitivity) and the base (elements). Here, the word "external" (bahiddhā) is a mere illustration. For an internal great element can also be an object. Alternatively, "external" is said in reference to the great elements other than those that are the base for body-consciousness. The friction of the impact is strong; therefore, when meeting with desirable tangible objects (iṭṭha-phoṭṭhabba) or undesirable tangible objects (aniṭṭha-phoṭṭhabba), the favoring and the agitation of the four elements, which are the causes of pleasure and pain, continue for a long time.

If it is asked: "Should not other consciousnesses also be considered mind elements (manodhātu) because they are inherently empty (suññata)?" The answer is: No, because of the presence of specific characteristics. For eye-consciousness and others, the specific characteristics are their dependence on the eye-base, etc., and their function of seeing, etc., in their respective spheres. For mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa), the specific characteristics are its being preceded by the mind (heart-base) without another dependence, its not being an immediately preceding condition for a consciousness with a different dependence, and its function of superior cognition because it is not the exit-door of the mind-door. Being devoid of such specific characteristics and being mere cognition...
126:
The mind element (manodhātu) refers only to the three-fold mind element (the five-door adverting and the two receiving consciousnesses), and not specifically to the mind that cognizes. Therefore, in this context, since the mind itself is the element, the word 'eva' (only) in the phrase 'manodhātu' should be understood as having the sense of 'mere' (matta). This is because the word 'eva' serves to exclude the specific function of cognition of the [mind-]consciousness. Because it is the exit-point from the mind-door and the entry-point into the mind-consciousness, it should be understood that the mind element lacks the specific function of cognition. For this very reason, it is not called 'mind-consciousness' (manoviññāṇa). Indeed, that consciousness, being the mind element, does not arise from the mind (bhavaṅga) to assist the mind, nor does it arise from the mind as a condition for the mind. Rather, it is a condition for seeing (dassana) and so forth, and having arisen because of that seeing and so forth, it is their precursor and follower.

The reason 'right intention' (sammāsaṅkappa) is not mentioned is that it is not similar to its progenitor [wholesome states] in the way the great resultants (mahāvipāka) are. In those great resultants, even when a two-rooted resultant arises from a three-rooted wholesome state, they are similar to the wholesome in being associated with roots through states such as right intention.

In this context of the 'stream of fivefold consciousness' (pañcaviññāṇasota), just as a person reciting a well-studied text might not notice certain sequences of words that fall into the stream of recitation, there is no such thing as the Buddha not noticing. The absence of jhāna factors in the stream of fivefold consciousness is also not the reason for not mentioning jhāna factors in this receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana). If the designation of what follows immediately after the fivefold consciousness were to be considered as falling into that stream, then the two mind-consciousness elements that occur after this receiving consciousness would not be able to fall into that stream. Therefore, it is called 'falling into the stream of fivefold consciousness' (pañcaviññāṇasotapatita) only because, like the fivefold consciousness, it is rootless (ahetuka), it lacks the nature of a path-condition (maggapaccaya), and although initial and sustained application (vitakka-vicāra) are present, the jhāna factors are weak and thus do not reach the count of jhāna factors, just as in the fivefold consciousness. For this very reason, the jhāna factors and powers (bala) are not extracted in the Summary Chapter (Saṅgahavāra) even for the three rootless functional consciousnesses. However, because there is the mere function of a jhāna-condition, the jhāna-conditionality of the weak initial application and so forth present in this receiving consciousness and others was taught in the Paṭṭhāna.

The investigating consciousness (santīraṇa), which arises by obtaining the proximity-condition (anantarapaccaya) with the same physical base, is stronger than the mind element. Therefore, when that investigating consciousness experiences the taste of the object according to the object, it is associated with joy (somanassa) in a desirable object because of the intensity of the experience, and it is associated with equanimity (upekkhā) in a neutral desirable object. For this reason, it was said: 'This [joy] arises only in a desirable object,' and so forth. Although the determining consciousness (votthabbana) is strong, it stops the occurrence of the resultant stream and performs a different function of attention (manasikāra) that produces a dissimilar mind [javana]; thus, it is not a mere experiencing like a resultant. Therefore, it is associated with equanimity in all objects. Likewise, the five-door adverting and the mind-door adverting are associated with equanimity because they are new [initial] by virtue of the function of adverting.

## The Explanation of Rootless Wholesome Resultants is Finished.
127:
## Explanation of the Eight Great Resultant Consciousnesses

In the phrases such as 'Non-greed is an indeterminate root' (alobho abyākatamūlaṃ), first, in the definitions of non-greed and non-hatred on the wholesome side, it is stated: 'What on that occasion is non-greed? The non-greed, non-longing... non-greed is a wholesome root' (Dhs. 32), and 'What on that occasion is non-hatred? The non-hatred, non-resenting... non-hatred is a wholesome root' (Dhs. 33). Therefore, here on the indeterminate side as well, in the definitions of non-greed and non-hatred, it is appropriate to say: 'Non-greed is an indeterminate root' and 'Non-hatred is an indeterminate root.' However, in the definitions of the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) and so forth, it is stated on the wholesome side: 'The jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, investigation of states, right view' (Dhs. 34, 37), but it is not stated: 'Non-delusion is a wholesome root.' Therefore, here on the indeterminate side as well, it would seem that the text 'Non-delusion is an indeterminate root' should not exist. Nevertheless, it should be understood that this is stated for the purpose of showing that non-delusion, like non-greed and non-hatred, is also an indeterminate root.

'Because of not producing intimation' (aviññattijanakatō) means it performs the prevention of the doors of bodily and vocal action. 'Because of not having the nature of result' (avipākadhammatō) means it also performs the prevention of the door of mental action. This is because the doors of action are mentioned only for wholesome states which have the nature of producing results. Likewise, 'because of not occurring' (appavattitō) means it does not occur in the form of bases of meritorious action (puññakiriyavatthu) such as giving (dāna). By this statement, only the variety of the bases of meritorious action is excluded.

'Because of strong conditions' (balavapaccayehi) means because of conditions such as the object which are accomplished without [present] effort (payoga). Among the unprompted (asaṅkhārika) and other consciousnesses, when kamma is accumulated by any mind, the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) that arises when the kamma, the sign of kamma (kammanimitta), or the sign of destination (gatinimitta) appears without prompting and without effort is unprompted. The rebirth-linking that arises when kamma and so forth appear with prompting and with effort is prompted (sasaṅkhārika). The life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and death (cuti) are just like the rebirth-linking. The registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) should also be understood as unprompted and prompted, like the wholesome and unwholesome. To analyze the strength and weakness among these minds, he said: 'Therein, all the Omniscient Bodhisattas,' and so forth. 'It changes by the power of time' (kālavaseṇa pana pariṇamati) means that in a time when kammas leading to a short life are abundant, it changes by the power of the conditions of semen and blood produced in the continuity [of beings] associated with that kamma, and by the power of uneven conditions such as climate (utu) and nutriment (āhāra) produced by the uneven revolution of the moon and sun, which are rooted in that kamma.

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Extraction of Resultants

The 'Discussion on the Extraction of Resultants' (Vipākuddhārakathā) is begun to show from which kamma, how much of a result arises, and in which place it matures. 'Right here' (ettheva) means only when kamma is accumulated by a single volition. By the power of two-rooted rebirth-linking, the twelve-fold division also...
128:
It means that there is also a result of twelvefold variety. By way of rootless rebirth-linking (ahetuka-paṭisandhi), the group of eight rootless results also occurs. The second elder (Mahādatta Thera), not desiring the mixing of prompted (sasaṅkhārika) and unprompted (asaṅkhārika) results of prompted and unprompted wholesome kamma, said "twelve" and so on. For, according to the intention of the former elder, the state of being prompted or unprompted occurs due to the cause (the cause such as being strong or weak at the time of the process); however, according to the intention of the other elders, it occurs due to kamma. The third elder (Mahādhammarakkhita Thera), not desiring the occurrence of a double-rooted (duhetuka) result from a triple-rooted (tihetuka) kamma, said "ten" and so on.

In this context of extracting results (vipākuddhāra), they took up the Sāketa problem to define kamma and rebirth-linking. They mentioned "ussada" (preponderance) to show that the result has the nature of having various qualities and defects as its cause by the power of kamma. The mention of roots (hetu) here is stated according to the intention of the first elder (Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga Thera). I shall state the distinctions in the views of the second elder and others in their respective places. Because knowledge (ñāṇa) is the opposite of delusion, which is the cause of failure (vipatti) such as being blind from birth (jaccandha), even if a triple-rooted kamma is very weak, if it pulls a rebirth-linking, it should pull only a double-rooted one; therefore, it is said, "rootless rebirth-linking does not occur."

However, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi, the Venerable Sāriputta, showing rebirth-linking with roots (sahetuka) along with the excellence of destination (gatisampatti), excluding rootless rebirth-linking in the failure of being blind from birth or deaf from birth in a happy destination (sugati), stated: "In the excellence of destination, when there is rebirth-linking associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta), by the condition of which eight roots does rebirth-linking occur?" By this statement, it is shown that rebirth-linking associated with knowledge cannot occur due to kamma dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta). Otherwise, the statement "rebirth-linking occurs by the condition of seven roots" should also have been said.

That this is so is like what was answered regarding rebirth-linking associated with knowledge: "In the excellence of destination, when there is rebirth-linking associated with knowledge, by the condition of which eight roots does rebirth-linking occur? At the moment of impulsion (javana) of wholesome kamma, three wholesome roots are conditions by way of conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya) for the volition (cetanā) arisen at that moment. Therefore, it is said that formations (saṅkhāra) also occur with wholesome roots as condition. At the moment of attachment (nikanti), two unwholesome roots are conditions by way of conascence condition for the volition arisen at that moment. Therefore, it is said that formations also occur with unwholesome roots as condition. At the moment of rebirth-linking, three indeterminate (abyākata) roots are conditions by way of conascence condition for the volition arisen at that moment. Therefore, it is said that consciousness (viññāṇa) occurs with mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) as condition, and mind-and-matter occurs with consciousness as condition."

Thus, while the occurrence of rebirth-linking associated with knowledge from kamma dissociated from knowledge exists, it would be possible to provide an answer in the same manner as stated before in other places by saying: "In the excellence of destination, when there is rebirth-linking associated with knowledge, by the condition of which seven roots does rebirth-linking occur? At the moment of impulsion of wholesome kamma, two wholesome roots occur."
129:
Just as rebirth-linking associated with knowledge cannot occur due to kamma dissociated from knowledge because it is not stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pāḷi as "by the condition of seven roots in the case of one associated with knowledge," so too, it follows that rebirth-linking dissociated from knowledge cannot occur due to kamma associated with knowledge because it is stated only as "in the excellence of destination, rebirth-linking occurs by the condition of six roots in the case of one dissociated from knowledge," and it is not stated as "by the condition of seven roots."

Actually, here too, it is not impossible to associate three and two roots at the moment of performing kamma and the moment of attachment (nikanti), and two roots at the moment of rebirth-linking; it is possible (though not so stated). However, the intention of this elder (Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga) might be: "This text is taught as an incomplete (sāvasesa) teaching because of the desire to show a result similar to the kamma." If one argues: "Does the text here, 'by the condition of eight roots in the case of one associated with knowledge,' also fall into being an incomplete (sāvasesa) teaching?" No, it does not, because weak double-rooted kamma is incapable of giving a result associated with knowledge. It should be noted that just as triple-rooted kamma can produce a rootless result, it also has no obstruction to its capability in producing a double-rooted result.

The statement "feeling should be changed by the object" is said with reference to investigating (santīraṇa) and registration (tadārammaṇa). Because of the inability to distinguish the excellence of the object, the eye-consciousness and others are only accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā-sahagata) towards desirable and neutral-desirable objects. Body-consciousness is only accompanied by pleasure (sukha-sahagata) due to the specific nature of the impact.

To show the occurrence of the resultant consciousness by way of a special time having all impulsions (javana) which are the condition for registration, it is said: "for one who has attained... in restraint and non-restraint," because at other times there is no occurrence of complete resultant consciousness such as the fivefold sense-consciousness. By the words "crab... descending into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)," this meaning is shown: just as after filling the fields with water, one might descend into the river by a non-path like a crab's track without entering the canal which is the path to the river; so too, after the mind has run through the impulsion, it descends into the life-continuum without the path of registration when that registration, which is the path for entering the life-continuum, has not arisen.

Among these three void cases (moghavāra), the second should be accepted after investigation. If it were taught in the section on the condition of dependence (paṭiccavāra) of the Triad of Feeling in the forward order (anuloma) as "by way of repetition condition (āsevana-paccaya), not two in the path (magga)" and "not by way of path condition, two in repetition," then that second void case would also be obtained. If determining (votthabbana) were also a repetition condition, it would also be a repetition condition for the wholesome and unwholesome. For there is no state which, being fit to receive the repetition condition, is not stated as a repetition condition when it is a state that becomes a repetition condition. However, it was not taught that determining (votthabbana) acts as a repetition condition for the wholesome and unwholesome.
130:
“Dependent on a wholesome state, a wholesome state arises not by way of repetition condition (āsevana-paccaya); dependent on an unwholesome state...” and so forth. By this statement from the Paṭṭhāna, the status of determining consciousness (votthabbana) as a repetition condition is already rejected. If it were argued that “This was stated by way of dissimilar feelings (vedanā),” even so, just as it is stated that “Adverting (āvajjana) is a condition for wholesome aggregates and unwholesome aggregates by way of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya),” it should also be stated that “it is a condition by way of repetition condition.” If it is argued that “It is not stated because of the difference in class (jāti),” then just as a sense-sphere state, though different by way of plane (bhūmi), acts as a repetition condition for fine-material-sphere states and so on, it should be stated that the repetition condition exists even for states of different classes. Furthermore, by way of states of the same class, just as it is stated that “Adverting is a condition for rooted aggregates by way of proximity condition,” it could also be stated that “it is a condition by way of repetition condition,” yet it is not so stated. Therefore, in the Triad of Feeling (Vedanā-tika) as well, when the count is extracted in the summary as “One state not associated with the path condition due to the repetition condition, and one state not associated with the repetition condition due to the path condition,” the second void case (moghavāra) of the aforementioned manner should be examined, as there is no repetition condition status for determining consciousness (votthabbana).

Determining consciousness (votthabbana) is called adverting (āvajjana) because it turns the continuity of the process resultants (bhavaṅga-continuity), and it is called attention (manasikāra) because it produces an impulsion (javana) that is dissimilar to that resultant continuity. For this reason, in the Paṭṭhāna, it is not stated that “Determining consciousness is a condition for wholesome aggregates by way of proximity condition,” but rather it is stated only as “Adverting.” Therefore, an object such as a visible form, which is unable to be an object-prenascence condition (ārammaṇa-purejāta) for the four or five impulsions (javanas) following determining consciousness, cannot be a condition for adverting and so on. This is the inherent nature of that object. Thus, it is appropriate to show the second void case by way of the incompleteness of impulsions (not reaching seven times); this method should also be carefully investigated as it does not appear in the Commentaries. Because the bhavaṅga follows the impulsion, it is stated as “registration (tadārammaṇa) is bhavaṅga.” In the Paṭṭhāna, it is also stated: “A rooted bhavaṅga is a condition for a rootless bhavaṅga by way of proximity condition,” and “A rootless bhavaṅga is a condition for a rooted bhavaṅga by way of proximity condition.” The resultant (vipāka), which is merely the fruit of wholesome and unwholesome deeds as pleasure and pain, does not differentiate between desirable and undesirable objects. However, the impulsion (javana) performs the differentiation of desirable and undesirable objects by way of lust, aversion, and so on. Therefore, it is stated: “Only the impulsion experiences the taste of the object.”

To show how the process occurs in the form of adverting and so on when there is no creator (kāraka), the ancient teachers have adopted the fivefold natural law (niyāma). A natural law is simply the specific power of the inherent nature, function, and conditionality of phenomena. “Giving a result corresponding to such and such” means giving its own...
131:
...giving of a corresponding result. The term “sadisa-vipāka-dāna” (giving a similar result) also has the meaning of giving a corresponding result. The designation “idaṃ vatthu” (this story) in the singular is made because it is the subject matter of a single verse. “Jagatippadesa” refers to a region of the world other than the three types already mentioned. This is because an evil deed obstructed by time (kāla), destination (gati), physique (upadhi), or effort (payoga) may not produce its result, but there is no evil deed that fails to produce its result simply because it is obstructed by a geographical region; it will certainly produce its result (thus such a region does not exist). The natural law (Dhamma-niyāma) is the fixed nature of phenomena such as the rebirth-linking that is the proximate cause for omniscience, which causes the shaking of the ten thousand world systems. This Dhamma-niyāma is what is intended here; it shows the meaning that the state of adverting and so on occurs by the power of this natural law, and not by the power of a creator.

“In this place” refers to the section explaining the sixteen types of resultant consciousness. The simile of the sugarcane press (nāḷiyanta) worked by twelve men is not stated by way of the twelve types of consciousness performing a function together at a single door and single object, but rather by way of the twelve types of consciousness merely performing their respective functions at a single door. Intending to show the rootless registration (ahetuka-tadārammaṇa) immediately following impulsions similar to those that produce rootless rebirth-linking, it is said: “Of any impulsion among the four double-rooted wholesome consciousnesses... it establishes.” For a person with rootless rebirth-linking, when a triple-rooted impulsion occurs, the arising of a rootless registration is not prohibited by the kamma that gives the rebirth-linking result. Likewise, for one with double-rooted rebirth-linking, it should be understood that a double-rooted registration following a triple-rooted impulsion is not prohibited. Since this clarification of resultants by way of the kamma that produces rebirth-linking with sixteen complete resultants is merely an illustration of the occurrence of registration, the sixteen resultant consciousnesses and so on of a single triple-rooted kamma that has results in the course of existence (pavatti) should also be applied according to the stated method. Therefore, when many registrations occur due to any single kamma, because there is no distinction in the kamma, those registrations follow the causes known as impulsions; they are distinguished by the distinction of those causal impulsions. Thus, this determination of registration is stated by way of the impulsion, and not by way of being produced by various kammas. Having considered this, it is stated in the Paṭṭhāna: “One contemplates rooted aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. When the wholesome or unwholesome impulsion has ceased, rootless resultant arises as registration,” thus showing rootless registration immediately following knowledge (insight). It is also stated: “When the wholesome or unwholesome impulsion has ceased, rooted resultant arises as registration,” showing rooted registration immediately following an unwholesome impulsion. It should be understood that this does not mean a prohibition was made by thinking, “This was not shown by this Elder.”
132:
The statement regarding (defining registration) by impulsion (javana) is made considering that unwholesome impulsion does not have a similar resultant (registration/tadārammaṇa) as wholesome impulsion does. Regarding the determination of prompted (sasaṅkhārika) and unprompted (asaṅkhārika) states, it should be noted that even in unwholesome states, this statement is not inappropriate (it is appropriate). The phrase "This is not the case" refers to the absence of determining properly or improperly when the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is turned properly or improperly by means of determined factors, etc. "It is prohibited" is said considering that the Buddha's silence itself constitutes a prohibition. It should be understood that registration (tadārammaṇa) does not occur in those (sublime or supramundane) objects because a kamma born of sensual craving cannot produce a resultant (registration) that experiences sublime or supramundane objects. When an object comes into range, the life-continuum inclined towards that object gives rise to adverting (āvajjana); therefore, adverting arises because of its inclination towards the object. However, since the life-continuum is always inclined towards its own object, even though it serves as a condition for consciousness with a different object (adverting), it arises without adverting due to its inclination towards its own object in the absence of that (adverting).

"Due to being practiced" means it has frequently arisen before without adverting. "Due to frequent occurrence" means it has been frequently produced before in both the object that has come into range and the rebirth-linking object. Alternatively, "due to being practiced" refers to the state of being cultivated by the person. "Due to frequent occurrence" refers to the state of occurring frequently by itself. The statement "The immediate condition for cessation (nirodha) is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" is made referring to the attainment of cessation immediately after that (sphere), not as an immediate condition for cessation in the same way as for the immaterial aggregates. The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception does not arise without preliminary (parikamma) impulsion. Since the adverting of the preliminary impulsion is the adverting for that (sphere) itself, this (sphere) must also be accompanied by adverting, just like other (jhanas).

Here, this meaning should be understood: In the state of being the immediate condition for cessation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, inclination (ninna), etc., are not seen elsewhere. It arises even in the state of preliminary work that does not have that cessation as its goal. Nevertheless, that (sphere) is the immediate condition for that cessation, and it arises in that way. Similarly, the aforementioned mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu) arises without adverting even though inclination, etc., are absent in the arising without adverting. For this reason, the example "the Noble Path consciousness and the Fruition consciousnesses immediately following the Path" is stated. If this were said referring to the absence of adverting with Nibbāna as its object, then change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) and cleansing (vodāna) would be the only appropriate examples, as the absence of adverting for these (Path and Fruition) could be established by them alone. Also, at the time of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), "the adaptation (anuloma) with a limited object or a sublime object..."
133:
According to the (Paṭṭhāna) Pali text, "Conditioned by way of proximity condition for the attainment of fruition," the fruition consciousnesses of the attainment of fruition should not be excluded when saying "fruition consciousnesses occurring immediately after the Path," because they lack adverting with the same object. Although change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) and cleansing (vodāna) have not frequently occurred (ciṇṇasamudācāra) in the object of Nibbāna, they have indeed frequently occurred in other objects. The fruition consciousnesses of the attainment of fruition are not taken (as examples) because there is clearly preliminary work (parikamma) for the sake of that attainment of fruition after (above) the Path-process (and thus they are already habituated to Nibbāna). The fruition consciousness occurring immediately after adaptation (anuloma) is already habituated. However, the fruition consciousness occurring immediately after the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (upon emerging from cessation) is not habituated because there is no preliminary work for the sake of that fruition consciousness, unlike the fruition consciousness immediately after the Path. Therefore, the illustration "of one emerging from cessation (the fruition consciousness)" is shown. The statement that it cannot arise without an object was made to elicit the question "What object does it have?" and to specifically point out the object, because this (equanimity-investigating) consciousness does not have a sublime object.

In that (discussion on resultants), the illustration of the person born blind (jaccandha) and the cripple (pīṭhasappi) is shown to demonstrate that resultant consciousness cannot occur without its physical base (vatthu-rūpa). The term "grasping the object" (visayaggāha) is used to show the resultant consciousness such as eye-consciousness, etc., by means of the sensitive bases like the eye, etc., grasping their respective objects. The phrase "by way of strong dependence and purpose" (upanissayamatthaso) is used to show that same resultant by way of strong dependence (upanissaya) and by way of the purpose (attha) such as seeing, etc., of the eye and so on. "Only the heart-base" means that while preceding consciousnesses depend on the heart-base and also follow the sensitive bases and have other objects (objects other than kamma, sign of kamma, or sign of destiny), the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is not like that. It means that the life-continuum arises depending solely on the heart-base, free from other bases and objects. In this context, "having the heart-materiality as base" (hadayarūpavatthuka) should be understood to mean that (adverting) follows other bases. Just as a spider's climbing depends on the thread, the consciousness (fivefold consciousness) having a sensitive base arises. Just as moving, etc., by the thread, the remaining consciousnesses that follow that sensitive base arise. Because it is shown that the impact on the sensitive base and the vibration of the life-continuum occur simultaneously, like the striking of the thread and the movement of the spider, it is also shown that "each... comes."

The phrase "the time of turning the life-continuum" is stated considering that the state of being an immediate condition—similar to the giving of a signal by the adverting (consciousness), which is like a foot-massager, to the eye-consciousness, etc., which are like doorkeepers—is itself the turning of the life-continuum. It should be understood that the performing of receiving, etc., without seeing (the object) by the resultant mind-element, etc., is stated by way of similarity to (the child in the simile) merely grasping firmly, merely knowing the flatness and squareness, merely knowing it is a coin, and merely handing it over for the mother's work. It is not intended that the receiving consciousness (sampaṭicchana), etc., are identical to the state of not seeing the coin by the child who grasps it firmly, etc.
134:
By the statement "This thing is white," it should be understood that eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) alone accomplishes the function of seeing, as it is common to the perception of white forms. In the same way, this should be applied to the ear-door (sotadvāra) and so forth, by way of hearing and so on. One who is habituated to making molasses by boiling [sugarcane juice] well, or one whose benefit is molasses, is called a "Gōḷiyaka."

The word "upanissayato" is not intended to refer to the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). Rather, it means that in the absence of which a certain effect cannot arise; that cause is what is intended here by "upanissaya." The phrase "ālokasannissitaṃ" (dependent on light) also refers to the manifestation of eye-consciousness when light is present, and not to the state of being a decisive support condition. The life-continuum (bhavaṅga) that occurs by itself without reaching the state of being a condition for functional consciousness (āvajjana) is called "mandathāmagata."

"Seeing the fault in unprompted (asaṅkhārika) and prompted (sasaṅkhārika)" means seeing the fault in unprompted kamma having prompted results, and prompted kamma having unprompted results, thinking that a resultant (vipāka) should not have a nature contrary to the kamma. Since rootless resultants (ahetuka-vipāka), which have functions such as merely falling upon visible objects and so forth, do not have a nature contrary to prompted kamma, they do not have the state of being unprompted. Likewise, because they do not have a nature contrary to unprompted kamma, they do not have the state of being prompted. Thus, because they are not contrary to both prompted and unprompted kamma, it is acknowledged that these rootless resultants arise from both types of kamma.

"Citta-niyāma" (order of consciousness) refers to the fixed law of registration (tadārammaṇa). By the phrase "kiriya-to pañcā" and so forth, it is stated that registration also arises immediately after functional impulsion (kiriya-javana). However, in the Paṭṭhāna, it is stated: "When wholesome (kusala) and unwholesome (akusala) states have ceased, the resultant arises as registration," thus mentioning registration only immediately after states that have the nature of producing results. In the Wholesome Triad (Kusala-tika) also, by saying "Trainees (sekha) or worldlings (puthujjana) [contemplate] wholesome states as impermanent..." and so forth, registration is mentioned only after wholesome and unwholesome impulsions (javana), not after the indeterminate (abyākata), nor is registration seen mentioned anywhere as following functional impulsion. There is no reason for not mentioning registration if it indeed existed after functional impulsion. Therefore, this view of Mahādatta Thera should be carefully examined. For it is appropriate to say that the life-continuum follows an active impulsion like the river current follows a boat; but registration does not follow the peaceful functional impulsion of an [Arahant] who possesses six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā), just as the river current does not follow a leaf-cup.

"Piṇḍajavanaṃ javati" (it runs as a collective impulsion) means that wholesome, unwholesome, and functional impulsions are spoken of collectively. Or, it means the impulsions that run are shown as being grouped in a single registration. The Thera who speaks of this collective impulsion takes only the four equanimity-associated states from the unwholesome, and speaks as if grouping the twelve equanimity-associated impulsions. In the Paṭṭhāna, however, it says: "One relishes and delights in the wholesome; based on that wholesome, lust arises. Wrong view..."
135:
...doubt (vicikicchā), restlessness (uddhacca), and displeasure (domanassa) arise. When the unwholesome has ceased, the resultant arises as registration." Because of this teaching, the two states of consciousness associated with doubt and restlessness that occur in other desirable objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa) should also be grouped in the wholesome-resultant registration. However, immediately after those states, only rootless-resultant registration should occur, and since that rootless resultant is already taken as investigation (santīraṇa), there is nothing new to be taken. And because it is considered that they should not be grouped in the rootless resultant, they are not grouped.

In this second view, "at the end of triple-rooted impulsions," it is said to be "appropriate" to show that triple-rooted registration (tihetuka-tadārammaṇa) is suitable, because it is similar in nature to the impulsion and because no other registration is obtainable. For one who asserts that rootless registration occurs after the unwholesome (as mentioned by the first Thera) and that rooted registration occurs after the wholesome, there is no reason to say that triple-rooted kamma, which produces rebirth, does not produce a triple-rooted resultant immediately after a triple-rooted impulsion, even if it produces double-rooted or rootless resultants. Therefore, even if not explicitly stated, it should be accepted as appropriate; this is the meaning. Or else, in the respective views of the Theras, whatever intention was used to state the arrangement of prompted and unprompted and so forth, that arrangement should be accepted as appropriate according to that intention alone; one intention should not be confused with another. "Hetusadisameva" means it is exactly similar to the root of the productive kamma (janaka-kamma). "It will be clear in the Mahāpakarana" means that the arrangement of the arising [of these states] will become clear through the Pali text found in the Paṭṭhāna.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Sense-sphere Wholesome Resultants is finished.

## Explanation of the Discourse on Fine-material and Immaterial Sphere Resultants

"Anantarāyena" means due to the absence of the causes for decline (the hindrances/nīvaraṇa). "Paṭipadādibhedo" refers to the difference in practice (paṭipadā) and object. Indeed, for one who produces a jhāna with painful practice and slow intuition (dukkha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā) and enters it repeatedly, that jhāna remains as having that specific practice. If that jhāna does not decline, its resultant, when it arises, should also have that same practice.
