The state of having predominance of desire (chandādhipati) and so forth, however, occurs because of the state of desire etc. being the predominance condition (adhipati-paccaya) present at that moment, not by way of the mode of arising [of the jhāna]. This is true: even a single jhāna can have different predominances at different moments. Even the fourth jhāna alone can be developed as the four bases of power (iddhipāda). Therefore, predominance of desire and so forth are not taught by way of the jhāna that is the cause of the resultant.
136:
Even a single jhāna can have different predominances at different moments. The development of the fourth jhāna itself occurs by way of the four bases of power (iddhipāda); therefore, predominance of desire (chandādhipateyya) and so forth are not mentioned by way of the occurrence of the resultant jhāna.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Fine-material and Immaterial Sphere Resultants is finished.

## Explanation of the Discussion on Supramundane Resultants

Just as the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) is accumulated, so too mundane kamma, conditioned by craving and so forth, is said to be "accumulated" (upacita). However, supramundane resultant is not like this, as it is not conditioned by craving and so forth; thus, it is not so called. "Suddhāgamanavasena" (by way of pure occurrence) means: by way of being unmixed, because in showing how the name "void" (suññata) is given to the fruition, the "with-attribute" (saguṇa) objects—which give the names "signless" (animitta) and "desireless" (appaṇihita) and are clearly present—are not taken. The Path, which possesses the names "void" and "desireless" by way of the occurrence of insight, stands at the moment of the Path's occurrence and is associated with giving the three names to its own fruition; the same should be applied to the other (the Path with the name "signless"). This is merely showing the method. It should be noted that the Path occurring immediately after the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), which has three names due to "with-attribute" objects, also stands at the moment of the Path's occurrence and is not prevented from giving the three names to its own fruition.

In the case of the "attainment of fruition for use" (valañjanaka phala-samāpatti) obtaining a name by way of insight, it would not obtain the name "signless" like the Path. However, just as there is a distinction of jhāna and practice (paṭipadā) in the attainment of fruition for use, just like the fruition immediately following the Path, when it obtains names such as "void", it also obtains the name "signless". "Avūpasantāya" is said with reference to the proximity condition (anantara-paccaya) of such faith... wisdom, because this state is not obstructed by any other state. By this statement, it is shown that predominances such as desire (chanda), being predominances that produce similar desire and so forth in their own immediate succession, produce only resultants that are themselves predominances.

The Path, such as Right View (sammā-diṭṭhi), which has the nature of leading out (niyyānika) and completely cutting off defilements, must have its fruition—in which defilements are stilled—also possess the nature of leading out. Therefore, even in the fruition, it is called "path factor" (magganga) and "included in the path" (maggapariyāpanna). Because of this, in the Magga-vibhaṅga, the eight-factored path and five-factored path are extracted for the fruitions as well; likewise, the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga) are also extracted. "Maggaṃ upādāya" is said with reference to the meaning of being called "path" because of its similarity to the Path.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Supramundane Resultants is finished.
137:
## Explanation of the Discussion on Unwholesome Resultants

Just as there is a distinction of investigating consciousness (santīraṇa)—namely, investigating consciousness accompanied by joy and that accompanied by equanimity—in desirable and moderately desirable objects, there is no such distinction of investigating consciousness in undesirable and moderately undesirable objects. However, the undesirable object itself is spoken of in two ways: as the extremely undesirable and the mildly undesirable.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Unwholesome Resultants is finished.

## Functional Indeterminate

## Explanation of the Mind-Element Consciousness

"Vātapuppha" (wind-flower) refers to a sterile flower that does not bear fruit. Such a flower does not bear fruit even if the tree is not cut. But the flower of a cut tree would have borne fruit if the tree had not been cut. Similarly, the two types of adverting (āvajjana) which occur in the continuity of a person whose root of existence (ignorance and craving) is not cut, but which do not produce resultants, are like the wind-flower. The functional impulsion (kiriya-javana) occurring in the continuity of another (an Arahant) is like the flower of a cut tree. This is because that functional impulsion would have produced resultants if the root of existence had not been cut.

## Explanation of the Functional Mind-Consciousness-Element Consciousness

By the words "loluppataṇhā pahīnā" (craving for greed is abandoned), the previous occurrence (functional impulsion) which is the cause of this (smile-producing) consciousness is shown. Since this consciousness is devoid of investigative wisdom, it occurs in the continuity of an Arahant, producing merely joy without being associated with knowledge. This should also be understood in instances such as worshipping a stupa (cetiya-pūjā) and so forth.

"Vattaṃ karonto" (performing duties) is said with reference to the occurrence of consciousness at the body-door regarding a tangible object while performing a duty. Because it is said, "With this consciousness, one becomes joyful," in various doors, referring to this very occurring (smile-producing) consciousness which is obtained following the five doors, or which is the cause for reviewing the abandonment of craving for greed and so forth in the five doors themselves, it is said, "Thus it is first obtained in the five doors."

Having spoken of the knowledge that is unobstructed in objects such as those of the past, the statement "This (smile-producing consciousness) arises for the Blessed One" should be examined in light of the words: "All bodily action of the Blessed One, the Buddha, who is endowed with these three qualities, follows after knowledge," and so forth.

Because rootless (ahetuka) consciousness lacks roots (hetu), it lacks firm stability, and thus the state of being a "power" (bala) is incomplete. Therefore, in the summary section (uddesa-vāra), it was not said, "The power of concentration (samādhi-bala) arises, the power of energy (vīriya-bala) arises." For that very reason, in the classification section (saṅgaha-vāra) of rootless consciousnesses, the jhāna factors were not extracted. Because of this, in this pair of rootless consciousnesses as well, the powers are not shown in the summary section nor included in the classification section. However, because energy (vīriya) is clearly present...
138:
The smile-producing consciousness (hasituppāda) is more powerful than the remaining rootless (ahetuka) types of consciousness. This is because, just as initial application (vitakka) and so on are merely jhāna-conditions in this smile-producing consciousness, concentration and energy are also merely powers (bala). Therefore, in the Section of Detailed Exposition (niddesavāra), it is stated as "the power of concentration" (samādhibala) and "the power of energy" (vīriyabala). However, because this consciousness is neither wholesome (kusala) nor unwholesome (akusala), it should be understood that it is not spoken of as "right concentration" or "wrong concentration", nor as "right effort" or "wrong effort". If that were the case, it should also not be so called in the great functional consciousnesses (mahākiriyacitta); yet it is so called. Therefore, it should be noted that concentration and effort, which do not reach the state of path-condition (maggapaccaya) because they lack the nature of leading out (niyyānika)—whether right or wrong—are not spoken of in that way (as "right" or "wrong") in this smile-producing consciousness.

The knowledge of the higher and lower faculties (indriyaparopariyattañāṇa), the knowledge of tendencies and latent dispositions (āsayānusayañāṇa), omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa), and unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa), which arise immediately after this mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana); as well as the knowledge of the Twin Miracle (yamakapāṭihāriyañāṇa) and the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇāsamāpattiñāṇa), which arise immediately after the preliminary work (parikamma) that occurs immediately after this mind-door adverting—all these proceed only upon the object adverted to by this adverting. Intending this, it is said, "They take the six...". Because it has a vast object, it is called "Great Elephant" (mahāgaja), being as great as a royal elephant.

## Description of Fine-Material and Immaterial Sphere Functional Consciousness

Now, the connection should be made thus: "Those functional consciousnesses that have arisen should be known." Individual existence (attabhāva) refers to the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā).

## End of the Description of the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness.
139:
## 2. Rūpakaṇḍa (Section on Matter)

## Description of the Summary (Uddesa)

Now, after having analyzed the resultant (vipāka) and functional (kiriyā) indeterminates in detail, indeterminate matter (rūpa-abyākata) should be analyzed in detail. Furthermore, it is not possible to analyze that indeterminate matter by defining the occasion (samaya) through any particular state. It is true that it is not possible to define the occasion of matter by the arising of consciousness. This is because matter that is not mind-produced (produced by temperature, nutriment, or kamma) is clearly present; because mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna) arises due to many types of consciousness; because among the consciousnesses that produce matter, some consciousnesses cannot produce matter in certain planes or moments, thus there is no definition; and because matter, excluding the two types of intimation (viññatti), does not have the nature of arising together with consciousness.

It is also not appropriate to define the occasion by "attaining and abiding" in matter, as one does with the sublime (mahaggata) and immeasurable (appamāṇa) jhānas. This is because matter does not have the nature of being "attained and abided in". It is also not appropriate to define the occasion by derivative matter (upādārūpa). This is because those derivative types of matter do not exist in the capacity of a co-nascent condition (sahajātapaccaya) and so on. It is also not appropriate to define the occasion by the great essentials (mahābhūta). This is because some great essentials arise without certain derivative types of matter, and because matter of different times is present.

It cannot be said, "At the time when the earth element (pathavīdhātu) arises, at that time the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) arises." This is because the eye-base does not exist together with the earth element which is the support for the ear and so on, nor with the earth element produced by consciousness and so on. This should be applied in the same way to the ear-base (sotāyatana) and so on.

It also cannot be said that intimation (viññatti), integration (upacaya), and so on, which are not of the same time as the great essentials, arise at that time. At one single time, many thousands of material groups (rūpakalāpa) arise and persist. Unlike mental states (nāmadhamma), there is no co-existence of only two material groups. Even while one group persists, the cessation of another and the arising of yet another occur. Therefore, in every way, it is not possible to analyze indeterminate matter by defining the occasion.

However, it is possible to analyze it by methods such as the "single" (ekaka) method, and by its nature such as being "without root" (ahetuka) and so on. To analyze it in such a way, and to show that there are still unanalyzed indeterminates in the Chapter on the Arising of Consciousness (cittuppādakaṇḍa); and because it is inappropriate to conclude by showing only a part when teaching by the nature of indeterminates alone without defining the occasion; and wishing to include all states, both analyzed and unanalyzed, the Lord said: "Which states are indeterminate? Wholesome... the unconditioned element (asaṅkhatadhātu). These states are indeterminate." For it is appropriate to analyze only after showing the unanalyzed states that ought to be analyzed, in order to generate the desire to know. Here, the resultant and functional indeterminates...
140:
Since resultant (vipāka) and functional indeterminates (kiriya-abyākata) have already been analyzed, they are not analyzed in detail here. The unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) is also not analyzed in detail because it lacks diversity. Among these indeterminates, because matter (rūpa-abyākata) possesses diversity and has not yet been analyzed in detail, the Buddha, wishing to analyze it, said: "Among these, what is all matter?" and so forth. This is the grammatical connection of the meaning of the Pali text in this context.

In the phrase "showing the method," taking the resultants mentioned below is itself the showing of the method. Because that showing of the method was already performed and understood regarding resultants, it was omitted and not taken regarding functional indeterminates. Alternatively, showing the functional indeterminates that should be taught as belonging to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), etc., is called showing the method; since that showing of the method has already been stated by taking "kāmāvacara," etc., it has been omitted. "25 types of matter" refers to the ten bases (āyatana) and fifteen types of subtle matter (sukhuma-rūpa) mentioned in the Pali. Alternatively, if integration (upacaya) and continuity (santati) are treated as one and the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) is included, there are also 25 types. "96 types" refers to the seven decads (dasaka) such as the eye-decad (70), the three octads (aṭṭhaka) such as those produced by temperature (24), and the two types of sound matter produced by temperature and consciousness. The groups of matter that arise as clusters (kalāpa) are called "parts of matter" (rūpa-koṭṭhāsa) because they are components of a group of matter. "Koṭṭhāsa" means parts or limbs. Alternatively, "koṭṭha" means the body, and the parts of that body such as hair, etc., are called "koṭṭhāsa"; other parts besides hair, etc., are also called "koṭṭhāsa" because they are similar to those parts. That Nibbāna is taken "without remainder" (nippadesato) means that although it is distinguished by terms such as "with remainder of grasping" (saupādisesa), "without remainder of grasping" (nirupādisesa), "destruction of lust" (rāgakkhaya), and "unconditioned" (asaṅkhata), it is taken in its entirety. In terms of ultimate meaning, the unconditioned element is only of one kind.

"All" refers to the entire universe (cakkavāḷa). "Circular" means having a circular shape, and in terms of circumference, it means there are 3,610,350 yojanas. Here, the roundness is called "circular." "Four nahutas" means 40,000. "Named Naga" means the tree named Naga, which is called "Naga."

Regarding devas, dānavas, and others, they appear greatly by power of their bodies which are three gāvutas or more in size. In this context, the word-definition (vacanattha) is: the great forms that have appeared and arisen are called "Great Essentials" (mahābhူta). Because he shows many wonders and many unreal marvels, a magician is a great being (bhūta), thus he is called a "mahābhūta." Ogres (yakkha) and others are "mahābhūta" because they are great beings by their very birth. Alternatively, this term "mahābhūta" should be understood as a conventional (nirūḷha) term for those magicians and ogres. The elements such as earth (pathavī), however, are called "mahābhūta" because they are like those [magicians and ogres]. Since the word "bhūta" has both genders, it is used here in the neuter gender. In the phrase "due to great maintenance (parihāra)," intending to state the word-definition, he said: "By great forms..."
141:
Alternatively, because they are beings with great maintenance (parihāra), they are called 'Great Essentials' (mahābhūta). Between these two meanings, in the latter, the word 'parihāra' is elided from the preceding term 'mahāparihāra' to form 'mahābhūta'.

'Accimato' is a name for fire. One hundred thousand crores is called 'koṭisatasahassekaṃ'. All those hundred thousand crores of universes are treated as one and called 'the universe' (cakkavāḷa) by power of the field of authority (āṇākhetta). It dissolves in salt water. 'Vikīrati' means to be destroyed. Wishing to show the transformation in matter that is grasped (upādinnaka-rūpa), he said 'patthaddho' (stiffened) and so on. In the phrase 'kaṭṭhamukhena vā', the word 'vā' (or) has the sense of a comparison. Just as a body bitten by a Kaṭṭhamukha snake becomes stiff and rigid, so too, due to the disturbance of the earth element, that body becomes stiff as if it had entered the mouth of a Kaṭṭhamukha snake.

In another way, the word 'vā' is used in the sense of 'eva' (only/certainly). This meaning should be understood by bringing it after the phrase 'pathavīdhātup-pakopena'. In that sense: 'Even a body bitten by a Kaṭṭhamukha snake becomes stiff only because of the disturbance of the earth element; therefore, that body, which is inseparable from the earth element, is at all times like one that has entered the mouth of a Kaṭṭhamukha snake.' In another way, the word 'vā' has an indefinite (aniyama) sense. In that sense: 'A body bitten by a Kaṭṭhamukha snake may or may not become stiff depending on the power of mantras and medicines; however, due to the disturbance of the earth element, that body, being without mantras and medicines, certainly becomes stiff as if it had entered the mouth of a Kaṭṭhamukha snake.'

'Pūti' means having a foul smell. 'Mahāvikārāni bhūtāni' means arisen forms that have great transformations, or it means forms that are clearly present. Here too, the word 'vikāra' is elided from the preceding term 'mahāvikāra' to be spoken of as 'mahābhūta'.

Although elements like earth are well-known in the entire world, when they are grasped according to their true nature by abandoning distorted perceptions, they cannot be grasped without great effort. Therefore, although they are well-known, they are called 'great' (mahanta) because their nature is difficult to understand. Indeed, one who remains thinking that these Great Essentials are 'easy to understand and not great,' when he sees the difficulty in grasping them, realizes, 'Oh, these things are indeed wonderfully great!'

Regarding the word 'upādāya' (derived), it is called 'pavattarūpa' (occurring matter) with reference to its occurrence in the subsequent period as understood by this term. In this way, by the word 'upādāya', the state of being dependently originated is stated. Alternatively, it is called 'upādāya' because it depends (nissayati); matter that is itself dependent is 'upādā-rūpa' (derived matter). This is a designation for matter that is absolutely dependent on another support. To show that this matter does not belong to a 'being', nor to 'feeling' (vedanā) and so on—since it exists even in their absence—he said 'catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ' (of the four great essentials) and so forth. Indeed, the state of being a master (sāmibhāva) belongs to the supporting matter.
142:
## Explanation of the Threefold Summary of Matter

Among the miscellaneous dyads (pakiṇṇaka-duka), excluding the internal dyad (ajjhattika-duka), other dyads do not reach the state of being combined as triads (tika) with all other dyads. Since the intimation dyad (viññatti-duka) also does not reach such combination, the Blessed One taught the triads by taking only the internal dyad, which is the first among the dyads that can be combined with all others, and combining it with the remaining dyads. Indeed, by this method, one can understand the combination as triads of other dyads besides the internal dyad, which are obtainable through other dyads.

## Explanation of the Fourfold Summary of Matter, etc.

In the tetrads (catukka), because mind-produced matter (cittasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) is certainly of the nature of the two intimations (viññatti), the mind-produced dyad (cittasamuṭṭhāna-duka) follows the same course as the intimation dyad (viññatti-duka) and others. Therefore, the Blessed One did not teach the tetrad (catukka) that could be obtained by combining that mind-produced dyad with the derived matter dyad (upādā-duka). Similarly, He did not teach the tetrads obtainable by combining the visible dyad (sanidassana-duka) and others with that mind-produced dyad, nor those obtainable by combining that mind-produced dyad with the gross dyad (oḷārika-duka) and the distant dyad (dūra-duka). Alternatively, the Blessed One, who knows the intrinsic nature and functions of phenomena (dhamma) and the manner in which they should be understood by persons to be taught, did not perform the combination of those two intimations with other dyads, nor that of other dyads with those two intimations. What is the use of searching for a reason in this matter? It should be certainly understood that such a combination should not be made because the Blessed One did not make it.

As for other miscellaneous dyads, it is appropriate to combine them with other miscellaneous dyads, and they are indeed so combined. Among the base dyads (vatthu-duka) and others, excluding the ear-contact object dyad (sotasamphassārammaṇa-duka) and others, tetrads can be obtained by combining the clung-to dyad (upādinna-duka) and the clung-to and subject to clinging dyad (upādinnupādāniya-duka) with other object dyads (ārammaṇa-duka), external base dyads (bāhirāyatana-duka), and so on. Tetrads can also be obtained by combining the mind-produced dyad with all object dyads, external base dyads, and so on. It should be understood that tetrads cannot be obtained by combining those clung-to dyads and others with the remaining dyads, nor by combining other derived matter dyads and others with all base dyads and so on.

## The Explanation of the Summary is finished.

## Analysis of Matter

## Explanation of the Exposition of Single Items

The showing of the absence of divisions in matter, which cannot be further analyzed, is itself called 'niddesa' (exposition) because it can make a determination. Therefore, the Blessed One made the exposition with the word 'eva' (only/certainly), which defines the absence of divisions, through the Pali text such as "All matter is certainly not a root (na hetu)," and so on.

The meaning of the term 'hetu-hetu' is either the root cause (mūla-hetu) or the root which is the root-condition (hetupaccaya-hetu). This same meaning of "the great essentials are causes (hetū)" is also taught by the text "the great essentials are conditions (paccayā)." Since the words 'hetu' and 'paccaya' have the same meaning, the condition itself is called 'hetu'; therefore, it is called 'paccaya-hetu' (condition-cause).

It is taught that the great essential which is the cause of the matter aggregate (rūpakkhandha) is also the cause for the designation of that matter aggregate. This is because if that cause, the great essential, does not exist, the matter aggregate also does not exist.
143:
The Blessed One gave the detailed exposition using the word 'eva' (only/certainly), which defines the absence of further divisions to be analyzed. 'Hetu-hetu' means the root cause (mūla-hetu) or the condition-cause (hetupaccaya-hetu). This same meaning of "the great essentials are causes (hetū)" is also taught by the text "the great essentials are conditions (paccayā)." Since the words 'hetu' and 'paccaya' have the same meaning, the cause itself is called 'hetu'; therefore, it is called 'paccaya-hetu' (condition-cause). It is taught that the great essential which is the cause of the matter aggregate (rūpakkhandha) is also the cause for the designation of that matter aggregate; this is because if the great essential, which is the cause, does not exist, the matter aggregate also does not exist.

In the fruition of past, future, and present undertaken kammas, although there are other causes such as ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā), the Blessed One taught wholesome and unwholesome [actions] as 'hetu' (cause) because they are predominant in determining desirable (iṭṭha) and undesirable (aniṭṭha) results. Similarly, desirable and undesirable objects (ārammaṇa) arising from the fulfillment or failure of destination (gati), substrate (upadhi), time (kāla), and effort (payoga) are called 'hetu' because they are predominant like kamma. In this sense, kamma and objects are called 'uttama-hetu' (supreme causes). "Destination, substrate, time, and effort are the basis for fruition; kamma is the cause," will be taught later. In this Section on Matter (Rūpakaṇḍa), however, because it is predominant like kamma, the object also deserves the word 'hetu'; therefore, it is called 'uttama-hetu'. Ignorance (avijjā) is called 'hetu' because it is the common cause for meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and others. 'Pharati' means it goes or reaches. The phrase 'paṭikkhepa-niddesa' (exposition by negation) is said by way of rejecting the roots and so on that appear in the Matika. In this Section on Matter, the Blessed One taught the inclusion of matter under the term 'na-hetu' (non-root) and others because it has those respective natures; He also taught the state of being defined by the word 'eva' because it has no nature other than the 'na-hetu' nature.

In the material dyad (rūpī-duka), the word 'rūpī' itself is called 'rūpa' in this Section on Matter. Therefore, it is evident that the terms 'rūpī' and 'rūpa' have the same meaning, because only matter that possesses the characteristic of being deformed (ruppana-lakkhaṇa) has the state of being 'rūpī' and the state of being 'rūpa'. By the Pali "uppannaṃ chahi viññāṇehi viññeyyaṃ" (arisen, to be known by the six consciousnesses), the Blessed One shows the nature of matter which is the opposite of the mental (arūpa). This is because the mental, which is present (paccuppanna), cannot be known by the six consciousnesses in the same way as matter. Therefore, by distinguishing it from the mental, He defines this nature of being known by the six consciousnesses only in matter, saying "Present matter is known by the six consciousnesses; the mental is not." He does not define matter [only] by this nature. For past and future matter exist, and that matter does not have the nature of being known by the six consciousnesses. This very definition is again defined by the word 'eva': "The stated definition exists only in matter; it is not that it does not exist as it is in the mental." Alternatively, 'sabbaṃ rūpaṃ' (all matter) refers to elemental matter (bhūta-rūpa) and derived matter (upādā-rūpa) as 'all' without considering the distinction of time. To exclude past and future matter, which have a knowable nature similar to the mental, He qualified it with the text 'uppanna' (arisen/present). The meaning is that all such present matter is certainly to be known by the six consciousnesses.

If this is so, does it not follow that the visible object base (rūpāyatana) can also be known by ear-consciousness (sotaviññāṇa) and others? It does not; by way of showing the certain characteristic of matter by grouping all matter together...
144:
It is because of showing the nature of being cognizable by the six consciousnesses, which is contrary to mental phenomena (nāma), by taking it as a single entity. Although there is a restriction such as "only present form is cognizable by the six consciousnesses," in the phrase "all form" (sabbaṃ rūpaṃ), this restriction regarding the state of being cognizable is not stated. Rather, in the term "present" (paccuppannaṃ), the restriction of the definite characteristic of all form would not be shown. In the Pāḷi text as well, the word 'eva' is used as "viññeyyameva" (only cognizable), not as "uppannameva" (only arisen). Therefore, there is no arrival at a restriction regarding the state of present form being cognizable by mind-consciousness; thus, what benefit would there be in it falling into the stream of the five consciousnesses? Therefore, the meaning should be applied only in the manner already stated.

"Kathaṃvidhaṃ" means "how is it well-established by qualities?" Knowledge itself is called the basis of knowledge (ñāṇavatthu). The inclusion of those of the same class, or alternatively, inclusion by way of the same class, is called inclusion by same class (sajātisaṅgaha). They are well-born in this arising of consciousness; therefore, it is called "sañjāti" (birth). Inclusion by way of birth is called "sañjātisaṅgaha." It means inclusion by way of the place of birth (sañjātidesa). By the power of mutual assistance and by non-separation, states such as right mindfulness (sammā-sati) and others that arise in the sphere of concentration are included in the aggregate of concentration (samādhikkhandha). In whichever arising of consciousness the performance of its own function by concentration accompanied by mindfulness and so on occurs, that arising of consciousness is called the sphere of concentration (samādhidesa). Through the state of absorption (appanā) of right intention (sammā-saṅkappa), a function similar to penetration (paṭivedha) occurs; therefore, by way of a similar function of penetration, right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) and right intention are included in the aggregate of wisdom (paññākkhandha).

## The explanation of the Description of the Single Items in the Analysis of Form is finished.

## Description of the Dyads

## Explanation of the Discussion on the Classification of Derived [Form]

The knowledge that perceives the assembly of beings who have little dust of defilement and so forth is called the Buddha-eye (buddhacakkhu); among the six unique knowledges (asādhāraṇañāṇa), it should be understood as the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyattañāṇa). The knowledge that perceives all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is called the All-seeing eye (samantacakkhu). The knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana) that proceeds in such a manner as "The truth of suffering is to be fully understood, has been fully understood," and so forth, is called the Eye of Knowledge (ñāṇacakkhu); that Eye of Knowledge, like the previous two eyes, is of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). The knowledge that perceives the Four Noble Truths is called the Eye of Dhamma (dhammacakkhu). The series of forms produced by the four causes, which exist as supporters of the sensitive eye (pasādacakkhu), are called the constituents (sambhāra). Because it exists together with the constituents, it is called "sasambhāra" (the eye with its constituents). The water element (āpodhātu) itself, which is well-produced in the state of origin, is called "origin" (sambhava). The base of color (vaṇṇāyatana) itself, which exists as shapes such as circularity and so forth, is called "shape" (saṇṭhāna). This is a separate mention of the water element and the base of color, whether they exist in the manner of origin and shape or not.
145: This is because the water element and the color-base are clearly present in the aforementioned lump of flesh. In fact, the lump of flesh consists of fourteen components (sambhāra). The state of the fluid (sambhava), which is stated along with the matter dependent on the four great elements, should be understood as being dependent on the three elements. Or, because the water element and the color-base themselves are not the fluid and the shape, they are mentioned separately; thus, the fact of being dependent on the four great elements is not contradictory. One who perceives that lump of flesh by its whiteness, etc., does not perceive the sensitive eye-organ (cakkhu-pasāda). Intending to speak of the distinction such as expansion (patthinnatā), it is said again even though it was already said, 'Earth also exists', etc.  ## Sarīrasaṇṭhānuppattidesabhūte’ti: By this phrase, the remaining black circle (pupil) is excluded. Like oil, it exists pervading the seven layers of the eye, assisted by the four great elements which are its support, protected and surrounded by life (āyu), color (vaṇṇa), etc., which depend on those elements, and supported by the three types of continuity produced by temperature (utu), mind (citta), and nutriment (āhāra). By saying it pervades the seven layers of the eye, it shows that the sensitive eye-organ exists in many clusters (kalāpa). Saying that in size it is only the size of a louse's head (ūka-sira) is because it occurs in a place the size of a louse's head. In the phrase 'rūpāni manupassati', the letter 'ma' is a euphonic particle (sandhi) connecting the words. Or, 'manu' refers to a being (macca). There is the sensitive organ (pasāda) cherished by the supporting great elements. Speaking figuratively (pariyāyena), it is appropriate to call the sensitivity of the four great elements the sensitivity of one or two among them. Just as the wealth of people with equal wealth is called the wealth of one person, it is spoken of by this figurative method. The body (sarīra) is just the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). Because striking is itself friction, it is called 'striking-friction' (paṭighaṭṭanānighaṃsa). Or, it is called striking-friction because of the friction born from striking, which is known as the arrival of eye-consciousness at its support by being directed towards a visible object.  The term 'parikappavacana' (hypothetical statement) refers to words spoken by conceiving an antecedent action (hetu-kiriya) such as 'If it should come into the range of the sense-base' and a consequent action (phala-kiriya) such as 'one would see'. Here, although the antecedent action is not stated because it is manifold, it should be understood that it can be known. By the words 'one would see', it includes the sensitive eye-organ that has not yet reached the state of being a support for eye-consciousness in the three periods of time. The meaning of 'dassana-pariṇāyaka' (leader of seeing) is the state of being a leader in seeing. Just as a lord, saying 'Do this and that', directs and leads his people in various tasks, so too this eye, by being the support for eye-contact (cakkhu-samphassa), etc., is called 'eye' (cakkhu) because it leads those states as if commanding them in the task of seeing. It is called 'cakkhu' because it leads. According to the method already stated, it means it points out and leads (eye-contact, etc.). Or, it is called 'cakkhu' because it points out or makes manifest visible objects that are even or uneven. Because states are well-produced in this eye, it is called 'sañjāti'. Which states are produced?
146:
States such as contact (phassa) arise well in this eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda). Likewise, it is called 'convergence' (samosaraṇa) because it is the meeting place of states such as contact. It exercises the sense of lordship (indaṭṭha) by making eye-contact (cakkhu-samphassa) and others follow its own state of sharpness or dullness. Although it may be grasped as permanent, stable, or a self, it is called 'world' (loka) because of the sense of crumbling and disintegrating in various ways. Through this eye, states such as contact are used or entered; therefore, it is called 'resort' (valañjana). It is called a 'door' (dvāra) because it is the cause for the usage of states such as contact that arise at that eye-door.

The term 'parikappo' (conception) mentioned previously has the same meaning as 'vikappana' (conceptualization). 'Ghaṭṭayamānameva' means reaching the distinction of the sensitivity being directed [towards the object].

By the statement describing the arising of eye-contact and others based on visible form (rūpa), the arising of those [eye-contacts] and other states such as the five-door adverting (pañcadvārāvajjana) associated with that eye-door based on visible form is also stated. With the intention of showing by which causal force (paccaya-satti) the visible form assists eye-contact and others, [the teacher] said 'By this' (iminā), etc. In that context, by the phrase 'of contact and others having eye-sensitivity as their physical base' (cakkhu-pasāda-vatthukānaṃ phassādīnaṃ), it should be understood that the arising of the mind-element (manodhātu) and others—which have the same visible form as their object and are similar to those having eye-sensitivity as their base—is shown through the pre-nascence condition (purejāta-paccaya). To show the distinction in causal force among certain groups of states such as contact, [the teacher] said 'of those included in the eye-door javana process' (cakkhudvāra-javana-vīthi-pariyāpannānaṃ), etc. Indeed, those states such as contact included in the eye-door javana process, which occur by giving weight to the visible form and consist of intense enjoyment and delight, as well as their associated states, arise through object-predominance (ārammaṇādhipati) and object-decisive support (ārammaṇūpanissaya) conditions. Other states such as eye-contact not included in the eye-door javana process arise only through the object-pre-nascence condition (ārammaṇa-purejāta). Thus, the word 'based on' (ārabbha) indicates the state of assisting through causal forces other than the object-condition, while the word 'object' (ārammaṇa) indicates only the object-condition force. This is the distinction between these two terms, ārabbha and ārammaṇa.

'He hears' (suṇāti) means he hears by way of being the support for ear-consciousness. Considering that the action of taking the taste known by the word 'tongue' (jivhā) is 'tasting' (sāyana), [the teacher] said 'in the sense of tasting' (sāyanaṭṭhena). It is called 'body' (kāya) because it is the place of arising (āya) for states such as contact associated with 'contemptible' (kucchita) painful feeling. Or, it is the place of arising for 'suffering-suffering' (dukkha-dukkha) and 'suffering-due-to-change' (vipariṇāma-dukkha). Because the body-base (kāyāyatana) is pervasive throughout the body where there is kamma-born matter (upādinnaka-rūpa), the presence of body-sensitivity (kāya-pasāda) also exists within the eye-sensitivity. This is because that body-sensitivity interpenetrates and is associated with the eye-sensitivity. If it were not so, pervasiveness throughout the entire body would not be possible, yet that pervasiveness has been stated by the Commentator. Therefore, an objection (codanā) is raised regarding the confusion of characteristics: that the appearance of the tangible object would occur in the eye-sensitivity, and the appearance of the visible object would occur in the body-sensitivity. [The teacher] said 'one does not exist in the other' because eye-sensitivity and body-sensitivity have different supports and belong to different material groups (kalāpa). The mention of visible form, taste, etc., is to show that even visible form and taste, which share the same support of great elements (mahābhūta), do not assume each other's nature and thus do not exist in one another; what then need be said about eye-sensitivity and body-sensitivity which have different supports?
147:
Because it is capable of being struck by visible forms and it is the sensitivity of the great elements, it is called rūpābhighātārahabhūtappasāda. That which has such a characteristic is the eye (cakkhu). Rūpābhighāta means either the striking of the eye-sensitivity upon the visible form or the striking of the visible form upon the eye-sensitivity. The second method, stated for all sensitivities, is that sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā) and craving for fine-material existence (rūpa-taṇhā), which are the root causes of the kamma that produces an individual existence (attabhāva) with complete or incomplete sense-bases (āyatana), deserve the designation 'desire to see' (daṭṭhukāmatā) and so forth, because of the longing for an existence possessing those sense-bases. In the context of 'desire to see' and so forth, they are called daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhāna because they are originated by kamma that has the craving known as 'desire to see' as its root cause. That which has the characteristic of clarifying the great elements of such a nature is the eye. Alternatively, this sensitivity of the great elements is called daṭṭhukāmatānidānakammasamuṭṭhāna-bhūtappasāda. That which has such a characteristic is the eye. Its function (rasa) is to draw the person or consciousness towards visible forms.

What is the distinction in saying, "The body is the sensitivity of all great elements"? Is it not the case that the sensitivities of the great elements where fire (tejo) and so forth are predominant are also sensitivities of all the great elements? This is true. However, the word 'all' (sabbesaṃ) indicates the meaning 'equal' (samānānaṃ). This is stated to exclude the predominance of any single part that might follow. Regarding the phrase 'the qualities of fire and so forth,' it means that in both the former and latter views, as appropriate, the qualities of the respective great elements—such as the light (visible form) of fire in the form of a lamp, the sound of air, the smell of earth, and the taste of water in the form of saliva—are supported by those qualities and thus assist in the apprehension of visible forms and so forth. Regarding the statement 'because of seeing the predominance of visible forms and so forth,' the first proponent says, 'Visible forms and so forth are the qualities of those great elements,' because one sees the brilliant color in fire, the naturally heard sound in air, the good smell and so forth in earth, and the sweet taste and so forth in water, which are associated with special potencies. To that teacher, the answer was given starting with 'If we should desire,' and so forth. By this same method, the second proponent is also refuted.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the third view, the doctrine of the teacher Kaṇāda—who asserts that the eye and so forth are made of fire, space, earth, water, and air, or by their specific qualities like visible form—is brought forward, and the passage beginning with 'If they should say' is stated to refute it. If it is argued that the smell found in liquor is different from that in cotton because it is the smell of earth associated with water, and thus the smell of cotton cannot be considered predominant? This should not be said, because it is not overwhelmed (by water). In liquor, the earth associated with water is overwhelmed by water, but the earth in cotton is not overwhelmed. Therefore, the smell of that cotton-earth alone must be predominant. Since fire associated with hot water is found in abundance, its color should also be seen as brilliant, just like the touch of that hot water. If that were the case, the color of cold water, which is not connected with fire, would be inferior to the color of hot water. Therefore, because both of these do not exist (there is no inferiority). Because of the absence of both, the status of visible forms and so forth as the specific qualities of fire and so forth is denied. By this denial, this argument for fire and so forth is refuted; thus, it is said that the sequential absence of both is the reason for setting aside the speculation on the distinctions of the great elements.
148:
Indeed, the state of being a specific quality of the fire element and so forth for visible form and so forth has been refuted. By that refutation, this reason—"because of the state of not being grasped by visible form and so forth, which are qualities of the fire element and so forth"—is also refuted. Thus, with the intention that the absence of both in succession is the cause for abandoning the conception of a distinction among the great essentials (mahābhūta), he said "Tasmā pahāyethetaṃ" and so forth. Even in a single kalāpa (group), visible form, flavor, and so forth are dissimilar; what more need be said that in various kalāpas, the sensitive organs such as the eye are dissimilar, even though there is no distinction in the underlying great essentials? To show this, he spoke by pointing out visible form, flavor, and so forth.

If there is no distinction among the great essentials, what then is the cause for the distinction of the sensitive organs such as the eye? To answer that question, he said "Yaṃ aññamaññassa" and so forth. It should be understood that even a single kamma, being accomplished through the aspiration for an individual existence with five bases (āyatana), is the cause for the distinction of the eye and so forth; therefore, it is stated as "unshared with one another" and as "distinction of kamma." Truly, that kamma is the cause for the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) due to a certain specific potency; by that same specific potency, it cannot be the cause for the ear-sensitivity (sota-pasāda), because that would result in the absence of a different faculty from the eye. By the statement, "At the moment of rebirth-linking, a single sublime (mahaggata) volition is a condition by way of kamma-condition for the kamma-born forms," it is understood that for all kamma-born forms existing at the moment of rebirth-linking, a single volition is the kamma-condition. If there were various volitions in the arising of the faculties at that time of rebirth-linking, then kamma-born form produced by both small and sublime kamma would occur. However, since it is established that a single rebirth-linking cannot be produced by many kammas, it follows that many faculties arise from a single kamma.

That whose support of great essentials is not attached is called "anallīnanissaya" (unattached support); this refers to the objects known as visible form and sound. The supporting great essentials of smell and taste attach to the supporting great essentials of the nose-sensitivity and tongue-sensitivity; therefore, those objects are "attached" by way of their support. The tangible object (phoṭṭhabba) itself attaches to the supporting great essentials of the body-sensitivity, because it consists of the triad of [great] essentials. Even though it is situated far away and is distinct, it is called "reached" (sampatta) only because it causes impact and friction; this is the view of the teacher of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. As for sound, it comes like wind through a succession of elements, attaches to the supporting great essentials of the ear-sensitivity by way of its support, and having struck the ear-sensitivity, it reaches the state of definition; thus it is said to reach definition gradually. If this were so, sound-object produced by the mind could never be an object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) for ear-consciousness. This is because the arising of form produced by the mind does not occur outside the body.

Why is this statement "it would be heard after a long time" made? Is it not that the sound of washermen and so forth, who are situated far away, is heard after a long time? No, it is because of the distinction in the cognitive process (vīthi) of grasping the sound that has become manifest to those far and near. Just as when the sound of speech becomes manifest to those far and near, there is the non-grasping and grasping of specific syllables due to the distinction in the cognitive process of grasping; likewise, in the sound of washermen and so forth, whether it is manifest to the one nearby from beginning to end in succession, or in the middle, or manifest as a produced mass, it is perceived as being heard quickly or heard after a long time due to the distinction of the processes that grasp by way of decision occurring after the ear-consciousness process. That sound arises in whichever place; depending only on that place, it reaches towards the ear-sensitivity at the moment of its own manifestation. However, although it reaches towards it at that moment of occurrence, the sound situated far away...
149:
...when the sound of a washerman and so forth is manifest to one who is far away, either at the end or in the middle, or manifest as occurring in a mass, because of the distinction of the deciding cognitive processes occurring after the ear-consciousness process, there is the conceit (perception) that "it is heard quickly" or "it is heard after a long time." But that sound, depending only on the place where it arose, comes into the range of the ear at the moment of its existence. It should be understood that a sound situated far away is the cause for the arising of an echo elsewhere and for the movement of vessels and so forth, just as a magnet is the cause for the movement of iron.

Or else, just as the great elements that follow the striking of a bell are the support of the resonance and have the nature of impact, so too the great elements that arise following an impact and reach as far as the ear-sensitivity have the nature of impact. Therefore, the sound depending on those great elements is said to reach the stage of being delimited gradually, having struck through a succession of elements by the power of the support. It cannot be known as "from such and such a direction." Why? Because the sound is grasped only at the location of the ear-sensitivity.

Because it desires an uneven object, it is called "visamajjhāsaya" (inclined toward the uneven). Although it lacks conscious inclination (ajjhāsaya), the eye is called "visamajjhāsaya" because it tends toward uneven objects, as if it had such an inclination. Or, the eye of a person who has sight is called "visamajjhāsaya" by way of that person's inclination.

Because it occurs only in the cavity of the ear-hole and because it is the cause for grasping the object, it is said to "make an inclination" only there. That ear-sensitivity assists in the hearing of sound by being the support for ear-consciousness. If one wishes to state the meaning of the phrase "the open space (ajatākāsa) is also suitable" according to the intention of the Commentary, one says "inside a cave," and so forth. If one wishes to speak according to one's own intention, one says "What is the use of this natural law?" and so forth.

Because it has smell as an object which has wind as its strong support, it is called "vātũpanissaya-gandhagocara." Here, wind is the strong support (upanissaya) in the grasping of smell; by that usage, smell is called "vātũpanissaya." Or else, wind itself is the strong support; for what? For nose-consciousness. That wind is called "vātũpanissaya" because it exists in the smell as another type of co-operating cause (sahakārħ-paccaya), and the smell is the condition (paccaya).

The water element, such as saliva and so forth, is also another type of co-operating cause. Likewise is the earth element. Indeed, the earth element which is the foundation of the tangible object being pressed, and the earth element which is the foundation of the supports of the body-sensitivity being pressed by the tangible object, should be understood as the strong supporting cause for grasping the tangible object.
150:
It should be understood as the strong dependence (upanissaya) for the apprehension of tangible objects at all times. Even in the apprehension of tangible objects without pressure, the earth element (pathavī), which is the support of the body base (kāyāyatana), should be regarded as the strong dependence. And the status of that earth element as a strong dependence is indeed appropriate at all times.

The phrase "five colors" (pañcavaṇṇānaṃ) serves the purpose of showing the diversity of the threads (sutta) which are the substrata of those colors. Threads of five kinds are the five colors. This word "ekantato" (exclusively) is stated to exclude those intervening material groups (kalāpantara-rūpa) which cannot be separated by pressure at all times due to their presence in each material group. For those intervening material groups are not absolutely inseparable because they exist within each material group.

By the term "vaṇṇanibha," only the visible base (rūpāyatana) is indicated. Therefore, with reference to that visible base itself, the neuter designation "sanidassanaṃ" (visible) is made. For that reason, because blue and other colors, which are the visible objects in the primary sense, cannot be known by touching, and because length and so on can be known by touching, "length" is not the visible base in the primary sense. "Depending on this and that" (taṃ taṃ nissāya) means depending on the collection of primary elements (bhūta) which are assembled in the form of length and so on. "Standing thus and thus" (tathā tathā ဌိတံ) means that the visible base itself, which is a collection of colors existing in the form of length and so on, is spoken of by the designation "length" and so on. They are distinguished from one another because one color does not exist in another. The distinction of the spheres of objects (visayagocara) is the non-existence in other objects and the frequent occurrence of eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa) only in that visible object.

Since the sound of drums and so on are sounds produced by striking, it says "the remaining sounds already mentioned." By the term "speech of non-humans" (amanussavacana), it is intended to include not only other beings besides humans but also wood and so on; thus it says "all the rest as well." Even though it is so, although it does not appear in the Pāli text by way of praising a specific object, it should be praised in that way; this is the meaning of the phrase "or otherwise" (ye vā pana).

"Vissagandha" refers to the foul smell of rotting meat and so on. "Lambilam" refers to the sweet and sour taste.

Because one knows well by this, it is called "sañjānana" (recognizing); it is indeed a marking (upalakkhaṇa). Female characteristics (itthilinga) and so on, which arise due to their respective causes such as kamma and consciousness (citta), arise with such and such modes when they occur in the body together with the faculties. Therefore, they are said to "arise depending on the female faculty (itthindriya)." The faculty-nature of this state is stated because of its dominance over female characteristics and so on. This is because, in a continuity (santāna) possessing the faculties, the material causes having the modes of female characteristics and so on cannot arise in any other way, and because of the fact that those material forms are the cause for the apprehension of the concept "woman." However, since the female faculty does not produce, nor protect, nor support the material forms even in the female-decad (bhāva-dasaka), nor the material forms in other groups (kalāpa), therefore, that female faculty, like the life faculty (jīvitindriya), towards the material forms in its own group...
151:
Alternatively, it is not stated that the femininity faculty (itthindriya) assists the matter in its own group (kalāpa) or in other groups through the conditions of faculty (indriya-paccaya), faculty-presence (indriya-atthi), and faculty-non-disappearance (indriya-avigata), in the same way that the nutriment-matter (āhāra-rūpa) assists the matter in other groups. This same principle applies to the masculinity faculty (purisindriya). Regarding the matter characterized by gender (liṅga) and so forth, since the visible-base (rūpāyatana) is cognizable by eye-consciousness, it is said that gender and so forth are also cognizable by eye-consciousness.

The statement "The two faculties are established due to wholesome [kamma]" should be understood as referring to the happy destinations (sugati). This is because rebirth in the woeful destinations (duggati) occurs only through unwholesome [kamma]; therefore, the gender-matter (bhāva-rūpa) arising at that time, both at the moment of rebirth and during the course of existence, would also arise only through unwholesome [kamma]. Since these two faculties cannot exist together in the same continuum of a being, according to the words of the Yamaka Pali: "If the femininity faculty arises for someone, does the masculinity faculty also arise for that person? No," it is stated that even in a hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka), only one faculty exists.

Indeed, to demonstrate the occurrence of the term "body" (kāya) in bodily intimation (kāya-viññatti), the supporting sutta "Restraint of the body is good" is cited. Making one's intention known or clearly manifesting it is called copana (movement). The mode of support of the great elements (mahābhūta) in which the air element (vāyo-dhātu) is predominant is understood as intimation (viññatti). Just like the upward-going winds and so forth, in a group where the air element is predominant, the mode of intimation of the great elements occurs. Therefore, intimation is described through the function of the air element: "It is called thambhanā (stiffening) because it supports the body and makes it rigid." For this reason, the mode of the air element can be called bodily intimation, and similarly, the mode of the earth element (pathavī-dhātu) can be called vocal intimation (vacī-viññatti), as it arises from the specific mode of the great elements where the earth element is predominant.

"Speech that has reached distinction" means reaching distinction through words such as "Tissa" or "Phussa." Alternatively, speech that is grasped by the verbal formations (vacī-saṅkhāra)—namely, initial and sustained application (vitakka-vicāra)—and is not yet distinct because it has not reached the range of ear-consciousness, is called "vocal breaking" (vacī-bheda) when it is brought into the range of that ear-consciousness.

"They also support the postures" means supporting the postures as they normally occur. This is because when the undisturbed life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occurs, the limbs seem to sink or withdraw. However, this does not happen when the active consciousnesses, described as "thirty-two" or "twenty-six," are occurring. When those [consciousnesses] occur, the limbs are braced and proceed according to the normal postures.

Although specifically mentioned as "the death-consciousness of Arahants," [it should be understood as:] "At the moment of the final consciousness of beings in the sense sphere, and at the moment of the consciousness immediately preceding the final consciousness of beings in the sense sphere, for those in the fine-material and immaterial spheres who are in their last existence, and for those who, having been reborn in the fine-material or immaterial spheres, will attain final Nibbāna, for them..."
152:
According to the words of the Pali (from the Saṅkhāra Yamaka): "The verbal formation of those who are passing away will cease, but their bodily formation will not cease," it is understood that the death-consciousness of others also does not produce matter. Indeed, there is no failure to produce the bodily formation—namely, in-breathing and out-breathing—due to the absence of causes like entering the womb (gabbha-gamana) which would otherwise obstruct the in-breaths and out-breaths of the mind-produced matter. It is not appropriate to say both "he passes away and his mind-produced matter occurs." Furthermore, there is no Pali text stating "the death-consciousness produces matter."

"Na kassati" means it is not scratched or drawn. "Gataṃ" means it is understood. "The four great elements do not touch [it]" means that the boundary (space) of the elements in a particular group of matter is not touched by those very elements. Even though the elements of one group may touch the elements of another group, the boundary of the groups of matter, which is the space void of those respective elements, is not touched by those elements. Otherwise, there would be no distinction between the groups, as the elements of those groups would become pervasive and mixed. The non-pervasiveness of the great elements is the very nature of the untouchability of space.

It has been stated that lightness (lahutā) and the other [characteristics] are difficult to distinguish because they arise together without abandoning one another. Therefore, to demonstrate the specific differences through those respective predominant transformations (vikāra), the [sub-commentary] teacher says "Even so," and so forth. The aforementioned causes are stated because they are the specific conditions (visesa-paccaya) for those respective transformations. In reality, however, without distinction, all causes are generally the conditions for all types of matter.

Accumulation at the beginning is called ācaya; it is the first arising. Further accumulation is called upacaya. Uninterrupted occurrence is called santati (continuity). In that context, although ācaya is not explicitly mentioned in the brief summary (uddesa), it is understood through the word upacaya itself; thus it is said: "That accumulation of the bases (āyatana) which arises again and again is the upacaya of matter." In the Pali, the prefix upa- can mean both "first" (initial) and "above" (subsequent); therefore, the meaning should be understood as: "Initial accumulation is upacaya, and subsequent accumulation is santati." Otherwise, if only the meaning of "subsequent" were taken, the first arising known as ācaya would not be mentioned.

What is meant by the description "That which is the accumulation of the bases," and so forth? The term "base" (āyatana) is used to describe accumulation (ācaya). Since accumulation (ācaya), growth (upacaya), and continuity (santati) are all essentially accumulation in terms of the nature of arising (nibbattibhāva), accumulation is described through the bases because accumulation and the others are manifested by the bases. By speaking of the accumulation of the bases, the bases themselves are the things that have the nature of accumulation and the nature of arising. Thus, through the term "accumulation," those bases which have the nature of arising are described.
153:
The bases (āyatanas) that have such a nature of arising have been taught. In truth, arising (uppāda) is merely a characteristic; it is not actual matter (rūpa-rūpa). For this very reason, [the author of the Compendium] says, "Only the base (āyatana) has been taught." The Blessed One, in teaching the characteristic of accumulation (ācaya), is said to have taught only the bases (āyatanas) that possess that characteristic. Even so, what is meant by this? By teaching only accumulation (ācaya) or only the bases (āyatanas) through the accumulation of bases or the bases of accumulation, what meaning is taught by the Blessed One—who did not mention only this term "ācaya" in the brief exposition (uddesa) or the detailed explanation (niddesa), but instead specified growth (upacaya) and continuity (santati) and explained them by way of the bases and the teaching of accumulation? This is the intention of the Commentator. By the Pali term "ācaya," growth (upacaya) is meant; and by the Pali term "upacaya," continuity (santati) is meant. Wishing to explain both of these in order, he said, "Arising (nibbattī) and increase (vaḍḍhi) have been taught." Since growth (upacaya) and continuity (santati) are identical in essence, they are just accumulation (ācaya). Therefore, by explaining the brief exposition of growth and continuity, the meaning is that the distinction in the modes of accumulation—namely arising (nibbattī) and increase (vaḍḍhi)—is taught through the teaching of accumulation by way of the bases. To clarify this very meaning, he said, "In essence (attato hi)," and so on. Since both of these are also names for the materiality of birth (jāti-rūpa), it should be understood that among the specific characteristics of the materiality of birth, such as accumulation and so on, and in its occurrence (pavattī) and so on, that which has the characteristic of accumulation and so on is growth (upacaya), and that which has the characteristic of occurrence and so on is continuity (santati).

"Pakatiniiddesā" refers to the words that point out the nature of producing effects such as the waning of the life-span (āyusaṃhāni). Alternatively, the effect itself, such as the waning of the life-span reached through decay (jarā), is called "natural" (pakati). Broken teeth (khaṇḍicca) and so on are not the only forms of decay. From the time of the embryonic stage (kalala), the subsequent materialities that arise at the moment when the preceding materialities reach decay arise in accordance with the matured preceding materialities, becoming more and more matured. Therefore, in due order, when they arise at the time of the waning of the highly matured materialities (the decade of decline, hāni-dasaka), they arise with the nature of broken teeth and so on. Because those materialities arise in the matured materialities—which are called the "path of decay" (jarā-gata-magga), like the breaking of grass and trees in water-channels and so on—they are merely called the "path of decay"; they are not actual decay. The imperceptible, immediate decay is called "uninterrupted decay" (avīci-jarā). Its function is to lead towards death.

"Taṃ patvā" means that having reached that nature, which is called its own exhaustion and passing away, matter is exhausted, passes away, and breaks up. Just as one who is struck and fallen down has no strength, must depend on others, and remains lying in bed, so it is for one oppressed by decay; thus, decay is like a striker.

"Kattabbato" means by way of the nature of what is to be done. It is called "subtle" because of the absence of hardness, like horns or stones moistened by the saliva of snakes or scorpions, and because of the absence of poison. In this context, "ojālakkhaṇo" (the characteristic of nutriment) refers to the essence of taste that follows the major and minor limbs, which performs the function of supporting and strengthening, and is a specific kind of matter—derived matter (upādā-rūpa)—dependent on the primary elements (bhūta-rūpa).

The explanation of the Section on Derived Matter (Upādābhājanīyakathā) is finished.
154:
It is called "subtle" because it does not occur with poison. In the phrase "ojālakkhaṇo," it should be noted that the essence of taste that follows the major and minor limbs, which performs the function of supporting and strengthening, and is a specific kind of matter dependent on the primary elements, is called nutriment (ojā).

## The Commentary on the Section on Derived Matter (Upādābhājanīyakathā-vaṇṇanā) is finished.

## The Commentary on the Section on Non-Derived Matter (No-upādābhājanīyakathā-vaṇṇanā)

646. "Na upādiyateva" means it does not only depend; rather, it both depends and is depended upon.

647. The phrase "purimā pana" is said by way of the initial pointing out of the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), water element (āpo-dhātu), fire element (tejo-dhātu), and air element (vāyo-dhātu) in the fivefold summary (pañcavidha-saṅgaha). Alternatively, it means the water element taught in the initial brief exposition (uddesa) of the earth element and so on, which were taught in the explanation of the base of tangibles (phoṭṭhabbāyatana-niddesa). Or, it should be understood that the posteriority of the already taught base of tangibles is stated because it is past, and the priority of the water element is stated because it is future. "Āyū" refers to the life-faculty (jīvitindriya). Fire born of kamma (kammaja-tejo) is called "heat" (usmā). "Yaṃ kiñci dhātūm...pe... nuppajjati" means that in a single moment, it does not arise simultaneously in the many various earth elements that have come into range; likewise, it does not arise [simultaneously] in the fire and air elements. When many objects converge, the arising in one particular object first is shown by way of attention (ābhujita) and by way of the excellence of the object and the sensitive material (pasāda); however, arising in other objects certainly exists. To make known the means by which the transition from one object to another occurs, he asks, "How does the mind transition from one object [to another]?"

651. In iron balls (ayopiṇḍa) and so on, if the earth element were not bound by such a water element, it would scatter; therefore, it is said, "The water element, having bound those earth elements, makes them solid." Just as a suitable amount of water binds particles of dust and keeps them as a lump of clay, so too in iron balls and so on, it should be understood that the water element arising right there due to corresponding causes binds them and keeps them so.

"Aphusitvā patiṭṭhā hoti" (it is established without touching) is said because the water element is not a tangible object (aphoṭṭhabba); likewise, it is said, "It binds without touching." The meaning is that there is no mutual dependence between the tangible elements and the non-tangible water element in the way there is mutual dependence through the touchable nature of the three tangible elements. It is impossible to deny the mutual dependence among the great primary elements (mahābhūta) which do not arise separately from each other and which arise as conditions for one another. It should be noted that it is not appropriate to scrutinize "touching" or "not touching" in materialities that arise together as a single group. By the text "na... jhāyati," only the nature of fire is negated; it does not [necessarily] allow for the state of being cold.
155:
Since the water element (āpodhātu) is not a tangible object, it should be understood that mutual dependence through the nature of being touched does not exist between the tangible elements (phoṭṭhabbadhātu—earth, fire, air) and the non-tangible element (āpo). Just as it is impossible to prevent mutual dependence among the great elements (mahābhūta) that occur inseparably as causes for one another, it is also inappropriate to analyze touching and non-touching among material phenomena that have arisen together as a single unit due to their inseparability.

By the statement "it does not burn because it is hot," only the nature of the fire element (tejo) is negated; it does not mean that coldness is being affirmed. By negating the nature of the fire element, coldness is also negated. The fire element itself is called "cold" because its quality of maturing (pari pācaka) is seen in coldness during times such as snowfall. Since cold and heat are opposites, it is appropriate that another distinct great element called "cold" does not occur along with heat. The non-occurrence of cold in a group (kalāpa) where heat is excessive, and the non-occurrence of heat in a group where cold is excessive, is appropriate in the specific state of the fire element because the two are mutually opposite.

Bhāvaññathatta (alteration of state) refers to the arising of the earth element etc., with inferior or superior intensity due to specific conditions, such as solids like molasses becoming liquid or soft, and liquids like sugarcane juice becoming solid. Lakkhaṇaññathatta (alteration of characteristic), which is the abandoning of characteristics like hardness, does not exist in these elements. The meaning is that only bhāvaññathatta, known as inferiority or superiority, exists.

In the descriptions of "definitely not-clung-to" (ekanta-anupādinna), "definitely mind-produced" (ekanta-cittasamuṭṭhāna), etc., it means that [decay and impermanence] are included. By the phrase "whatever else also" (yaṃ vā panaññampi), it shows that preceding material phenomena also lack the nature of being owned by karma (kammassakatatta), etc. Since the terms "not-clung-to" (anupādinna) etc., and "not-owned-by-karma" (nakammassakatatta) etc., have the same meaning, if one should not be stated, the other should also not be stated; if one should be stated, the other should also be stated. Therefore, it should be noted that because they are included only in "definitely not-karma-born" matter, they are not included in "indefinite" (anekanta) matter.

They are evident depending on the great elements that are "definitely mind-produced," because they are a specific mode of those great elements. Since it is non-concretely produced matter (anipphanna-rūpa), the meaning is that it is impossible to describe the arising (uppāda) of that intimation (viññatti) in any way.

## The Commentary on the Description of the Dyads is finished.

## The Commentary on the Description of the Tetrads

This refers to the latter term, "cognized" (viññāta). Since all matter is included in "cognized" (matter to be known), it should not be differentiated. Because there is no "seen" (diṭṭha), "heard" (suta), or "mutually sensed" (muta) matter other than "cognized" matter, the answer is given without a question. This is because it is impossible to ask "Which matter is seen?" apart from "cognized" matter.
156:
The meaning is that it is [unnecessary] to ask "What is seen?" (diṭṭha). Because the term "cognized" (viññāta) includes all matter, there is no distinction to be made; thus the answer is given without distinguishing "cognized matter" and "non-cognized matter." Since there is no "seen," "heard," or "mutually sensed" matter other than "cognized" matter, one should not ask "Which is the seen matter?". For example, when two terms are summarized, one might ask "Which is that derived matter?" referring to its distinctness from non-derived matter. Similarly, when the four terms starting with "seen" are summarized, one might ask "Which is that seen matter?" referring to its distinctness from the other three, such as "heard." Since such distinctness does not exist, the question is not asked. The same applies to "heard" and so on. However, the Tetrad (group of four) is stated because of the distinction in the way they are apprehended, such as through seeing, and because "cognized" matter exists as something distinct from "seen" etc.

## The Commentary on the Description of the Pentads

"Gone to the state of fire" (tejobhāvaṃ gataṃ) means matter that has reached the state of fire by its very nature. The inclusion of matter already mentioned, but through a different method, should be understood here as "method-establishment" (nayakaraṇa). This method-establishment should also be applied to the Tetrad term "cognized" (viññātaṃ). The existence of the divisions of tangible matter is the method in the Octad collection (aṭṭhaka-saṅgaha).

## The Commentary on the Miscellaneous Discussion

By the statement "there are no hindrances," the abandoning of the hindrance of torpor (middha) is stated. However, materiality (rūpa) is not to be abandoned. And it cannot be said that the Sage (the Buddha) has no illness of the physical body (rūpakāya), because of the statement: "My back is aching, I will stretch it" (M. Ni. 2.22). "Sound with consciousness" (saviññāṇakasadda) refers to sounds like the sound of speech produced by consciousness. The statement "these things do not arise" is made with the intention that decay (jarā) is the maturing of matter that is maturing, and impermanence (aniccatā) is the destruction of matter that is being destroyed; thus these are merely modes of matter and do not possess an intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of their own. Similarly, birth (jāti) is the arising of matter that is arising, and that birth is also merely a mode of matter and does not possess an intrinsic nature of its own; thus it is said, "In the ultimate sense, birth does not arise."

Because the cause of those material phenomena is the cause of this birth, it is called "conditioned by that" (tappaccayā). The state of having such a condition is "the state of being conditioned by that" (tappaccayabhāva). The designation that occurs by way of being conditioned by that is "the designation of the state of being conditioned by that" (tappaccayabhāvavohāra). It acquires that designation. "In the moment of the produced phenomenon" (abhinibbattitadhammakkhaṇasmiṃ) means in the arising moment (uppādakkhaṇa) of the phenomena being produced. Since it is not that those phenomena do not arise at that moment, it is appropriate to say that the nature of arising itself is birth, and that it is produced by karma etc., and originated by them. However, at that arising moment, those phenomena do not decay or perish. Therefore, it is not appropriate to say that the states of decaying and breaking of those material phenomena are produced by mind etc., or originated by them. If it is argued: "Even so, the word upādinna (clung-to) speaks of being taken by karma accompanied [by craving and views], not of being produced. Therefore, the upādinna nature of the decay and destruction of upādinna-kammaja matter should be stated." No, it should not be stated. Because the word ādinna (taken/clung) signifies production (nibbattivācaka).
157:
In calling matter produced by kamma accompanied by craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi) as 'clung-to' (upādinna), this designation arises only by taking into account the moment when the conditions possess their functional power and the sense of production (nibbattī). It should be noted that this term does not apply to aging (jarā) and death (maraṇa) because they do not exist at that moment [of arising]. Since aging and death are the states of dependently arisen phenomena, aging and death occur when there is the arising (uppāda) of those phenomena, and do not occur when it is absent. Indeed, matter that has not yet arisen cannot undergo maturation or breaking. Therefore, with reference to the fact of having birth (jāti) as a condition, it is said: 'Aging and death are dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna).'

'Because of having an occurrence connected to a support' means that since they are merely the states of arising, maturing, and breaking of matter that is currently arising, maturing, and breaking, birth (jāti) and so forth are said to have an occurrence connected to the supporting matter that is currently arising and so forth. If this is so, then birth and so forth, which are the nature of the arising etc. of the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and other derivative matter (upādāyarūpa), would depend on that derivative matter. Therefore, if it is asked—just as the characteristics of matter depending on the great primaries (mahābhūta) are derivative matter, would not the characteristics of matter depending on derivative matter become 'derivative of derivative matter' (upādāyupādāyarūpa)?—it is not possible. This is because the characteristics of derivative matter connected to the great primaries do not deviate from the state of being connected to the original great primaries. Furthermore, because the material qualities included in a single group (kalāpa) arise simultaneously, the arising, presence, and dissolution for a single group occur only once each. Just as the life faculty (jīvitindriya) in a single group is called derivative matter that protects the group, so too birth and so forth, which are the nature of the arising etc. of the group, are called simply 'derivative matter'. In this same way, matter as alteration (vikārarūpa) and delimiting matter (paricchedarūpa) should also be applied.

Temperature-originated matter (utu-samuṭṭhāna) that is connected with kamma-produced matter is called 'kamma-conditioned' (kamma-paccaya) because it possesses distinctions such as beauty or ugliness, and good or bad shape, due to the particularity of the kamma. External temperature-originated matter, which is the cause for experiencing the results of kamma, is called 'temperature-originated matter with kamma as condition' (kamma-paccaya-utu-samuṭṭhāna).
