Therefore, it is said that such an object should not be spoken of in terms of being a 'limited object' (parittārammaṇa) and so forth. Similarly, based on what is grasped as a unity in the continuum of the group of aggregates, [it is said] "Spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta)..."
181:
The taking [of a person] as 'a person who is a bad friend' and the designation [thereof] occur. Because wholesome and unwholesome states arise for one who associates with the collection of aggregates—which is the basis for such grasping—with the perception of a 'person', it is stated in the Paṭṭhāna: 'A person is also a condition by way of decisive support condition.' However, what is called a 'person' is not a reality (sabhāva) that truly exists. Therefore, just as the earth element is found when the water element and others are distinguished by the mind, a person is not found when the aggregates such as form are distinguished. In the Puggalakathā, the view of a person (puggaladiṭṭhi) is also prohibited. The Bhikkhunī Vajirā also said to Māra:

'Māra, why do you believe in a "being"? You have a wrong view.
This is a mere heap of conditioned formations; no "being" is found here.'

To show the occurrence of the designation of the word 'being', that same Bhikkhunī continued:

'Just as the word "chariot" occurs due to the assembly of parts,
So when the five aggregates exist, the convention "being" occurs.'

If a person does not exist, how can the grasping of a person have an object (sārammaṇatā)? The answer is because even a non-existent object can be grasped. In truth, the mind arises only by taking an object that is either imagined, recognized in the world, or a truly existing reality; thus it is said to have an object. The word 'sārammaṇa' (having an object) merely indicates that mind and mental factors cannot occur without an object; it does not indicate whether the object grasped by them is existent or non-existent. This is the decision of the teachers who completely follow the negation of the existence of [concepts] which are distinct from the conditioned and the unconditioned.

'Nāmakaraṇaṭṭhena' means by the nature of making its own name by itself without depending on anything else. That which makes a name for another depends on that other, and thus it is a name-making that depends on another, not the nature of [intrinsic] name-making. Therefore, the masses, relatives, and qualities that create common names and so on do not reach the state of 'nāma' (mentality). A person whose name is given by others (e.g., King Mahāsammata) also does not have the nature of name-making and thus does not exist as 'nāma'. However, because states like feeling (vedanā) are established by their own nature, the names like 'feeling' have the nature of name-making and are thus called 'nāma'. The illustration of earth (pathavī) and so on is intended only to show how 'nāma' is established by its own nature, not to show a general similarity in being 'nāma'. Because the word 'nāma' is well-known only in regard to formless phenomena (arūpadhamma), it is used only for those states and not for the earth element and so on; thus they are not 'nāma'. In the Mātikā, too, regarding earth and so on...
182:
It has already been stated that material phenomena such as earth do not reach the state of 'nāma'. The reason is that, while material phenomena occur in the form of a collection with names like 'hair' after discarding names like 'earth', formless phenomena (arūpadhamma) do not occur in the form of a collection called by another name after discarding names like 'feeling'. Alternatively, material phenomena like the eye and visible objects are manifest without a name because of their nature as that which manifests and that which is manifested. Formless phenomena are not like that. They are called 'nāma' because they have the nature of being grasped in connection with a name, like designation-contact (adhivacanasamphassa). Impingement-contact (paṭighasamphassa) is also called 'nāma' because it is not manifest without a name, unlike the eye and so on. This impingement-contact is included in 'nāma' either because it is a formless phenomenon, or because it shares the nature of other mental phenomena, or because it shares the nature of other types of contact. Here, the etymological definitions 'it is rūpa because it manifests (rūpayati)' and 'it is nāma because it makes a name (nāmayati)' should apply to the subsequent material phenomena and the preceding mental phenomena respectively. 'Rūpayati' means it manifests itself even without a name. 'Nāmayati' means it makes a name that manifests itself because it is not manifest without a name. Regarding the state of being an object-predominance condition, although materiality can be an object-predominance condition, it is not a condition with the extraordinary nature of 'bending' [the mind] like Nibbāna, which is the ultimate relief; therefore, only Nibbāna is called 'nāma'.

'For the purpose of showing the occurrence of the roots of the round (vaṭṭa)' means for the purpose of showing ignorance (avijjā) and craving for existence (bhavataṇhā), which are the roots of the round for beings. In this context, 'samudācarati' means it occurs excessively or repeatedly; thus the root of the round itself is the occurrence (samudācāra). Since the occurrence of the roots of the round is shown by showing the roots themselves, it also means 'for the purpose of showing the occurrence of the roots of the round'.

Based on the specific grasping of each of the five aggregates as 'self' and 'world', it is said 'self and world'. Or, it is said 'self and world' by virtue of one who grasps one aggregate as self and another as the world which is his own utility, or one who grasps his own self as 'self' and another's self as 'world'. 'That will be' means the firm and wrong misapprehension that the five aggregates grasped in those two ways will exist.

The Dhamma to be practiced together is called 'sahadhamma'; the training rule (sikkhāpada) existing in that Dhamma is 'sahadhammika'. Because the word 'āyasam' is added to the word 'dovacassa' (which is in the sense of action/kamma) without any other meaning, it is said 'dovacassāyaṃ', meaning 'the act of one who is difficult to speak to'. Alternatively, the occurrence of being difficult to speak to is 'dovacassāyaṃ'. Speaking in opposition to what another has said is...
183:
Paṭāṇikagahaṇaṃ means taking up a position of contradiction against what others say. Living with respect and honor toward those worthy of respect due to virtues such as morality (sīla) is called garuvāsa. Living among those who are senior by birth, etc., and who should be listened to, is called sajeṭṭhakavāsa. Alternatively, those who should be feared are called garu, and those before whom one should feel shame are called jeṭṭhaka. The volition (cetanā) because of which one becomes difficult to speak to is considered to be dovacassatā (unruliness); thus, it is said, "it is only the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha)."

1333. A name associated with the word "du" is called dunnamā. With the meaning that practicing by imitating from afar even without approaching the one to be emulated is sevanā (association), it is said, "bhajanā means approaching (upasaṅkamanā)." Sabbato bhāgena means (associating) through body, speech, and mind, both openly and privately.

1336. Vinaya refers to the Vibhaṅga and the Khandhakas. Since there is no one who reaches an offense (āpatti) before or after the moment of transgressing the basis (vatthu), one distinguishes the offense along with its basis. Therefore, it is said, "along with the basis... is called āpattikusalatā (skill in offenses)." Saha kammavācāya means (being together) with the Abbhāna-kammavācā and Tiṇavatthāraka-kammavācā, and with words such as "Venerable Sir, I have fallen into such and such an offense." In truth, one distinguishes the emergence (vuṭṭhāna) from an offense only together with the formal act (kammavācā). Alternatively, since the cause of an offense is the basis (vatthu) and the cause of emergence from an offense is the formal act (kammavācā), it is stated as "along with the basis, along with the formal act" by way of knowing the effect together with its cause.

1338. This same meaning is stated here as "saha parikammena." Vuṭṭhānakapaññā refers to the preparatory wisdom (parikammapaññā) which is the cause for emerging from an attainment.

1340. All wisdom that takes the elements (dhātu) as its object is called dhātukusalatā (skill in elements). With the meaning that the wisdom knowing the acquisition and attention (uggahamanasikāra), which is a part of that wisdom, is manasikārakusalatā, the wisdom knowing the acquisition and attention is also mentioned in the preceding term. Alternatively, in the preceding term, the attention to the Pali text of the elements that has been memorized is called "manasikāra." Among those types of wisdom such as acquisition (uggaha), the wisdom that involves learning, attending, listening to the meaning of the Pali text of the elements, bearing it in mind by way of the text and the meaning, and knowing the definition by way of nature such as "this is called the eye-element" and by way of number as being eighteen, is called uggahapaññā, etc. In the subsequent term, those five kinds of wisdom are called "uggaha," and the attention by way of impermanence, etc., that occurs thereafter is called "uggahamanasikāra." Knowing that uggahamanasikāra means its occurrence. Alternatively, knowing the learning that has arisen as "this is such a learning" is called uggahajānana. Knowing the attention as "it should be produced in this way, and it has been produced in this way" is called manasikārajānana. Both of these...
184:
...is called manasikārakosalla (skill in attention). Both the knowledge of learning (uggaha) and the knowledge of attention (manasikāra) are meant by manasikārakosalla. Indeed, since learning is associated with attention, it is appropriate for it to receive the name "attention" (manasikāra). Both the object that should be attended to, such as the characteristic of impermanence, and the wisdom which is the means of attention, can be called attention. The knowledge that is skillful in these matters is called manasikārakusalatā (skill in attention).

By the words beginning with "tīsu pi vā," the state of that skill as learning (uggaha), etc., is stated. The wisdom of investigation (sammasanapaññā), when associated with the Path (magga), accomplishes the task of investigating by way of impermanence, etc., by abandoning the perception of permanence (niccasaññā), etc. Similarly, attention associated with investigation, when associated with the Path, accomplishes the task of attending by way of impermanence, etc. Therefore, it is said, "investigation and attention are a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane." Knowing the state of being a cause for the produced states such as mental formations (saṅkhāra) from ignorance (avijjā), etc., in the form of "this arises because of this cause," shows the skill in dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā).

Mango seeds and so forth are mentioned to show non-clung-to (anupādinnaka) inanimate objects. The eye-base (cakkhāyatana) and so forth, which are of a different nature, unsuitable, and unable to produce the ear-consciousness (sotaviññāṇa), etc., are called "dissimilar conditions" (visabhāgapaccaya). The ear-consciousness and so forth, which cannot arise because of those eye-bases, etc., are called "states produced by dissimilar conditions" (visabhāgapaccayasamuppannadhamma). Alternatively, it is a dissimilar condition because it is a condition for the eye-consciousness which is of a different nature from the ear-consciousness. A state produced by the ear-base, which is a condition dissimilar to the eye-base, is called visabhāgapaccayasamuppanna.

In the exposition of rectitude (ajjavaniddesa), "ajjava, ajjavatā" simply means uprightness or the state of being upright. In the expositions of rectitude (ajjava) and gentleness (maddava), while explaining uprightness and softness, the term "nīcacittatā" (lowliness of mind) is specifically mentioned in the exposition of gentleness. In that exposition of gentleness, the mention of "mudutā" (gentleness) again after "nīcacittatā" is for the purpose of qualifying nīcacittatā. This is because inferior pride (omāna) is also a form of lowliness of mind, but it is not gentleness (mudutā).

Without reacting against the bad deeds and bad words of others, they endure them by taking them upon themselves. "Cittassa sakamanatā" means the mind's own natural state which is not perverted. Alternatively, taking the mental continuum as a single unit, it refers to the state of the mind accompanied by joy (pīti) that arises within that continuum. Alternatively, a person who has his own mind is called "attamana," and the state of such a person is attamanatā. To prevent the view of a person (puggaladiṭṭhi) that this attamanatā is the state of a being (satta), it is stated as "of the mind" (cittassa).
185:
By not performing what should be done with body and speech, and by delighting in what should not be delighted in, such as gold and silver, one also acts with the mind. Alternatively, it should be understood that this is stated in terms of the destruction of virtue, such as the restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara).

On a tree with defects, lumps of resin or sprouted mushroom buds are called 'aṇḍaka'. Similarly, powder clumps or nodules that appear like eggs on a decaying tree with sapwood should also be understood as 'aṇḍaka'. Harsh speech that enters the ear like a lotus stalk rubbing against it should be regarded as 'kakkasā'. Speech that arises due to anger and is an accompaniment to that anger is called 'kodhasāmanta'. Just as a maiden grown up in a city is called 'porī', speech that is very delicate and soft like such a maiden is called 'porī'. In that word 'tattha', the connection of meaning can occur either with the verb stated as 'is spoken' or with that speech itself. By terms such as 'saṇhavācatā' (gentle speech), the volition (cetanā) that produces that speech is shown.

A hole caused by the non-attainment of material things (āmisa) is called an 'attainment-of-material-things hole' (āmisālābha-chidda). By the phrase 'dve yeva hi', only the two kinds of holes arising from the non-attainment of material things and the Dhamma, as previously mentioned, are intended. 'Gamanasabhāgena' means by a region suitable for the path to be traveled. 'Saṅgahapakkhe ṭhatvā' means that the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) should be taught only with the intention to benefit, not with the desire for gain and honor, etc. An action that must inevitably be done is called 'kicca'; other tasks to be performed are called 'karaṇīya'. Emergence from an offense other than the abbhāna (rehabilitation) is called 'vuṭṭhāna'.

'Sassambhārakathā' means a discourse together with the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda), which is the cause of seeing. Alternatively, a discourse concerning seeing together with its causal constituents is 'sassambhārakathā'. After saying 'because of the non-restraint of which eye-faculty', it is further said 'for the purpose of closing that eye-faculty with the door of mindfulness'; it is not said for the purpose of closing the 'non-restraint' (asaṃvara). This is stated with the understanding that the following of states such as covetousness (abhijjhā) due to the non-restraint of the eye-faculty is shown as occurring only because of an unrestrained eye-faculty. 'Yatrādhikaraṇaṃ' means because of which cause, namely the eye-faculty. Because of what kind of eye-faculty? Because of an unrestrained eye-faculty. What is unrestrained? Because of the non-restraint of which eye-faculty covetousness and so on follow; the meaning is connected as: for the restraint of the eye-faculty characterized by that following.

Since there is no desire to repeat the statements about immorality (dussīlya) occurring at the moment of impulsion (javana), everything is stated here only in relation to the eye-door; it should be applied accordingly to the six doors. This is because there is no immorality consisting of bodily and verbal misconduct in the five [sense] doors. By the words 'yathā kiṃ' and so on, just as if the city gate is not guarded, the houses and so on connected to that city gate are not protected, so too if the javana is not restrained, the doors and so on connected to that javana are not protected. Thus, the analogy is shown only for the similarity that if the city gate and the javana are restrained, the other houses and doors are protected. It does not indicate a similarity of before and after, or a similarity of internal and external.
186:
Just as when there is no restraint at the city gate, there is no protection for the houses and so on connected to it, so too when there is no restraint in the javana, there is no protection for the doors and so on connected to it. Thus, it only illustrates the similarity that when there is restraint of one (the city gate and javana), there is restraint of the others (houses and doors). It does not illustrate a similarity of before and after, or a similarity of internal and external. Alternatively, while the door-subconscious (dvāra-bhavaṅga) and so on exist, the javana that arises again is treated as if it were external and is said to be like a city gate, while the remaining door-subconscious and so on are said to be like the gates inside the city. Or else, when non-restraint arises in the javana, because it becomes the cause for the non-restraint of the door-subconscious and so on thereafter, it should be understood that thieves such as immorality (dussīlya) enter through the javana, which is like a city gate, and commit theft by destroying the goods of merit in the door-subconscious and so on.

The state of being purposeful through this nutriment, which has the benefit of crossing over [suffering], is called 'idamatthikatā'. Non-contentment occurring at the moment of consuming nutriment is 'āhārapari-bhoge asantussanā'. It means the desire for playing and so on. Here, non-contentment (asantuṭṭhitā) is greed (lobha), while not knowing the measure (amattaññutā) and non-reflection (appaṭisaṅkhā) are delusion (moha). These two states should be known as 'immoderation in eating' (bhojane amattaññutā).

'I am superior' and so on is indeed 'mānamada'. Conceit arising based on the ability to practice the ways of the ignoble, or passion (rāga) itself, is 'purisamada'. Food cooked thickly by mixing sugar, ghee, milk, etc., is called 'piṇḍarasa-bhojana'. Alternatively, food mixed with meat juice and so on is 'piṇḍarasa-bhojana'. 'Manda' means little. 'Ṭhitiyā' means for the sake of endurance. Because one who eats for the sake of that endurance eats with the thought 'I will make the body endure', it is said 'for the sake of maintenance' (ṭhapanatthāya). This qualifier 'abhuṭṭapaccayā uppajjanakā' (arising from the cause of not eating) has the purpose of showing that hunger (khudā) which can be prevented by food. By the term 'sakalaṃ sāsanaṃ', it includes the Dhamma of the Pali texts as well as all wholesome states. What is the difference between the feeling (vedanā) that arises because of the cause of not eating and the feeling that does not arise because of the cause of eating? The former is the feeling caused by hunger as it normally occurs. That arises in one who does not eat by way of occurring excessively. The latter is also caused by hunger, but it is the feeling of burning in the limbs, piercing pain, etc., which has not yet arisen. That feeling, because of eating, will not arise, having not arisen previously. The difference between these two feelings is the fact of having the cause of affliction (vihiṃsā).

'Yātrā' means maintenance (yāpanā). It was said previously as 'yāpanāya'. What is the difference here? Previously, 'yāpanāya' meant for the sake of maintaining the life-faculty (jīvitindriya), but here, maintenance consisting of the non-interruption of the four postures is called 'yātrā'; this is the distinction here.
187:
The distinction is: acceptance without knowing the measure of the donor and the gift, or the measure of oneself as the recipient; or acceptance for the purpose of causing the destruction of alms-food given in faith; or acceptance by which one would incur an offense—this is unrighteous (adhammika) acceptance. Consumption without reflection is unrighteous (adhamma) consumption. By consuming a blameless and irreproachable requisite, one makes oneself blameworthy and reproachable. "There will be blamelessness" means knowing the strength of one's own natural digestive fire and so forth, and eating food in the proper measure, thinking, "By eating in this way, I shall be beyond reproach."

Living with comfortable postures is living at ease. In the phrase "having eaten this much... they proceed," eating and drinking are the causes for the comfortable proceeding of the postures; because the postures are taken as the cause, it is figuratively stated as if it were accomplished by those postures themselves. Some write, "Drink water without eating," but the reading is actually "having eaten." Furthermore, by way of allowing only a small amount:
"If that robe is allowable and can cover what should be covered, this requisite robe is sufficient for living at ease."
"If the rain does not wet the knees of one sitting cross-legged, that dwelling is sufficient for living at ease," so it was said.

Bhojanānisaṃsa (the benefit of food) means the benefit of living at ease and being beyond reproach through eating food endowed with the aforementioned eight factors. Knowing the measure of suitable and faultless food is called yuttappamāṇajānana.

One whose mindfulness is lost due to destruction, or confused due to being overwhelmed by opposing states, is called naṭṭhamuṭṭhassatī. The state of such a person is naṭṭhamuṭṭhassatitā.

Visuddhippatta (attainment of purity) refers to virtue (sīla) associated with the Path and Fruition. Lokuttaradhamma refers only to supramundane states such as supramundane mindfulness and so forth. Since the perfection of virtue (sīlasampadā) does not exist in the fine-material and immaterial spheres, it should be applied only to those that are possible (the sense sphere and the supramundane).
188:
It is called 'sabhoga' because it exists together with the requisites of enjoyment. 'Catunnaṃ saccānaṃ anulomaṃ' means [insight knowledge] that is in conformity with the knowledge penetrating the Four Truths. Indeed, by the word 'saccānaṃ' (of the truths), the Path knowledge that penetrates the truths to be penetrated is meant. Alternatively, it means the insight knowledge which is the strong decisive support for the knowledge penetrating the Four Truths, being in conformity with the Four Truths that are to be penetrated.

Alms-food given after requesting, "Please enter for alms making my house the first/priority," is called 'dhurabhatta'. Alternatively, alms-food given by oneself taking the lead and also directing others to give regular meals (niccabhatta) and so forth is called 'dhurabhatta'.

'Paṭivāseti' means to cause to turn back or to cause to retreat.

By the term 'pubbe nivutthakkhandhā', it refers to the aggregates included in the continuity of aggregates in previous births. 'Khandhapaṭibaddha' refers to things connected with the aggregates, such as clothing, ornaments, vehicles, villages, and countrysides. By the term 'khayasamaya', the Path moment (magga-khaṇa) is meant.

'Adhimuccanaṭṭhena' is due to the sense of proceeding according to one's wish, which is described as plunging into [the object] without being restrained.

The state of completion which is the end of the exhausted defilements is 'khīṇanta'. Alternatively, the initial time of the exhausted defilements is 'khīṇanta'. At that end of the exhausted defilements, or at that initial time which is the end of the exhausted defilements, it is called 'khīṇanta'. In terms such as 'niruddhanta' and so forth, it should be understood in this same manner.

## The Commentary on the Summary of the Dyads is finished.
## The Commentary on the Chapter of the Summary is finished.
189:
## 4. Section on Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa)
## Explanation of the Summary of the Triplets (Tika-atthuddhāravaṇṇanā)

'Nayamagga' refers to the sequence of proceeding through (understanding) the Suttanta-bhājanīya etc., and the sequence of proceeding through the Anuloma etc. This is because in this Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa, when the meanings are determined, that Nayamagga can also be easily harmonized. 'Pañhuddhāra' is the extraction of answers obtained in the forty-nine, forty-nine questions, and in the nine, nine questions. Placing the numbers obtained in those very questions is called 'Gaṇanācāra'. 'Atthuddhāra' is the extraction and showing that "these meanings such as the arising of consciousness (cittuppāda) etc. are wholesome (kusala) etc."

'Kaṇṇikaṃ kaṇṇikaṃ' means combining and stringing together the dhammas analyzed and expanded in the Cittuppādakaṇḍa and Rūpakaṇḍa by way of groups, such as "wholesome [consciousness] in the four planes, twelve unwholesome arisings of consciousness," etc. The words 'Ghaṭa' and 'Gocchaka' are just synonyms of 'Kaṇṇika'. In this text, the indication of "wholesome [consciousness] in the four planes" in the singular (ekavacana) is because wholesome contact (phassa) etc. occurring in the four planes reach a state of unity in being wholesome. This Atthuddhāra teaching is undertaken for the person who has understood the dhammas by way of the arisings of consciousness etc. in the four planes in the Cittuppādakaṇḍa and Rūpakaṇḍa. Therefore, whatever wholesome [dhammas] were analyzed in the four planes in those Cittuppādakaṇḍa etc., the meaning is that all those understood dhammas are wholesome.

Although the detail of the Wholesome Triplet (Kusala-tika) was understood previously, in that Cittuppādakaṇḍa, the dhammas were analyzed and understood distinctly by way of occasion (samaya) and by way of nature such as contact (phassa) etc., but they were not understood as unified in a single characteristic. Therefore, excluding the distinctions of occasion etc. taught in that Cittuppādakaṇḍa, for the purpose of making known the wholesome [dhammas] which are distinct in all ways by unifying them in a single characteristic such as "wholesome", the exposition (niddesa) of the Wholesome Triplet is analyzed again in this Aṭṭhakathākaṇḍa. And here, the reason for indicating "wholesome" in the singular and concluding in the plural has already been stated. If it is true that the dhammas reach unity in being wholesome, why was the question (pucchā) not also asked in the singular? In the summary (uddesa), because the word 'kusala' is an adjective (visesana) of the word 'dhamma', and because the dhammas having that adjective are asked, and because those dhammas have a specific number that has not yet been extracted (it is not asked in the singular). In the exposition (niddesa), however, because the wholesome [dhammas] are shown specifically by way of the four planes already understood in detail, it is appropriate to teach by bringing them into unity as "wholesome in the four planes". This is because in this exposition, the term 'kusala' is primary; and that term 'kusala', without depending on the dhammas to be qualified (visesya), occurs by taking only the mode of wholesomeness established in its own nature, and thus occurs by way of unity alone, not by way of distinction.
190:
In the phrase "twelve unwholesome arisings of consciousness" (dvādasa akusalacittuppādā), the first unwholesome arising of consciousness is also taught by bringing it into unity in the state of an arising of consciousness associated with wrong view and accompanied by joy, without considering the distinctions by way of occasion, contact, etc. Thus, up to the twelfth, it is said "twelve unwholesome arisings of consciousness." In this same way, it should be applied as appropriate to terms such as "resultant (vipāka) in the four planes," etc.

In the term 'cittuppāda' (arising of consciousness): it arises in this (collection of mental factors), therefore it is 'uppāda' (arising). What arises? Consciousness (citta) arises. The place where consciousness arises (the collection of mental factors) is 'cittuppāda'. Thus, the meaning is possible by way of characterizing the whole (consciousness and mental factors) by its part (mental factors). In this way, the meaning that the group of consciousness and mental factors is 'cittuppāda' is established. In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, the term 'citta' is taken as "consciousness itself is the arising (uppāda), thus cittuppāda," for the purpose of excluding matter (rūpa) which also arises. The term 'uppāda' is taken to exclude the state of consciousness not arising. Or, in the Cittuppādakaṇḍa, because the state of consciousness arising is evident in the phrase "consciousness has arisen," it is said "consciousness itself is the arising." It should be understood that the term 'uppāda' is taken because of the existence of consciousness that does not arise, which must be excluded. This meaning should be seen as an expanded indication that makes consciousness primary, as in "the two sets of fivefold consciousness" (dvepañcavijñāṇāni) etc.

In the phrase "in the six doors" (chasu dvāresu), there is nothing special to be said regarding the five doors. In the mind-door (manodvāra) also, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) known as the registration (tadārammaṇa) follows after the impulsion (javana) having a limited (paritta/sense-sphere) object. For that registration is the result (vipāka) of limited kamma. And result is the nature of experiencing desirable or undesirable objects. Since result occurs in accordance with kamma, the result of limited kamma is the experience of a limited object only. Therefore, all registration is called "having a limited object (parittārammaṇa)." If so, does it not follow that the sublime (mahaggata) result also experiences only a sublime object? No, it does not. Because the result of sublime kamma—which is characterized by concentration (samādhi), has reached absorption (appanā), and has an object (concept/paññatti) occurring by way of perception (saññā)—must have an object similar to that kamma. Therefore, that result, which is the experience of the bliss of concentration, should be understood as having the object of the kamma in accordance with that kamma. Precisely because it is in accordance with kamma, the registration, although having a limited object, does not follow after a sublime impulsion. For that same reason, the sense-sphere result (kāmāvacaravipāka) which functions as rebirth (paṭisandhi) etc., takes only a limited object as the kamma-sign (kammanimitta), not a sublime or an immeasurable (lokuttara) object. Because it is stated (in the Paṭṭhāna): "A dhamma with a sublime object is a condition for a dhamma with a limited object by way of kamma-condition; a dhamma with an immeasurable object is a condition for a dhamma with a limited object by way of kamma-condition." And there is no sublime result or immeasurable result that has a limited object. In this (Atthuddhāra-kaṇḍa) also, only the state of having a limited object is stated for all sense-sphere results. Therefore, in accordance with kamma...
191: If sense-sphere kamma (kāmāvacara kamma) which has mahaggata or appamāṇa (supramundane) objects gives rise to rebirth (paṭisandhi), it gives only a rebirth that has kamma-object or gati-nimitta-object. It should be understood that even the resultant (vipāka) occurring during the course of existence (pavatti) has only sense-sphere objects (parittārammaṇa) such as visible forms. The smiling of Arahants, which occurs without mindfulness due to the force of habitual tendencies (vāsana), arises only regarding sense-sphere objects (paritta), not regarding others (such as mahaggata). This is because there is no cause for such smiling in Arahants who are free from defilements. Therefore, it is said that this hasituppāda consciousness has sense-sphere objects (parittārammaṇatā). The lack of care (ādarakaraṇa) in the giving of Arahants, etc., should be understood as a lack of concern (nirussukkata), not as a result of unwholesome states like laziness (kosajja). For those noble persons have stilled all anxieties. Their lack of care should be understood simply as being free from concern. The word 'ati-paguṇānaṃ' (of those very well-mastered) shows the object of the knowledge-disconnected reviewing consciousness (ñāṇa-vippayutta paccavekkhaṇā) that is without care; it does not restrict the object to that consciousness alone. Indeed, for knowledge-associated consciousness (ñāṇa-sampayutta), very well-mastered jhānas can even more easily become objects. Just as one reciting a very familiar text might not notice that two or three lesson-sequences have passed because of reciting with knowledge-disconnected mindfulness, so too, in very well-mastered jhānas, knowledge-disconnected reviewing can occur; thus it is said 'ati-paguṇānaṃ', etc. By the phrase 'kasina-nimittādi paññatti', all derivative designations (upādā-paññatti) shown previously are meant. Teachers say that these derivative designations have non-existent (avijjamāna) and existent (vijjamāna) meanings, like matter (rūpa), etc. In conventional truth (sammuti-sacca), things like kasina-nimitta are called designations (paññatti) only by way of verbal usage (vacana-vohāra), being merely the basis of speech. Since the speech that makes this conventional truth known is a non-existent designation (avijjamāna-paññatti), the non-existence (avijjamānatta) of that conventional truth is stated in the Commentary. Even though it is non-existent, in the perception (saññā) that arises taking that conventional truth as if it were existent, one cannot say 'this specific dhamma is the object' among sense-sphere dhammas (paritta), etc. This is because, although it arises based on those paritta dhammas, it does not stay upon them. Therefore, it is said that such perception, along with its associated states, should not be called as having paritta objects, etc. The phrase 'navattabbārammaṇā' (having inexpressible objects) refers to the inexpressibility of the object of perception as it is grasped. The Commentary states 'navattabbārammaṇā' by forming a compound with another word's meaning (aññapadattha-samāsa), meaning 'these consciousness-arisings (cittuppāda) have inexpressible objects'. It occurs in fifty-five kāmāvacara dhammas by way of fifty-four consciousness-arisings and matter (rūpa). 'Kevalaṃ' means 'without grasping (parāmasana)'. 'Aniṭṭhangatavasena' means 'by way of not reaching a decision'. Or, a consciousness-arising that is undecided or split in two is called 'aniṭṭhangata'. Occurrence in that manner is called 'aniṭṭhangatavasena pavatti'. The scattering of the mind among various objects is distraction (vikkhepa). Lack of steady calmness is unpeacefulness (avūpasama). Taking change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) and purification (vodāna) together as 'gotrabhū', it is said 'at the time of gotrabhū'.
192: 'Sabbattha-pādaka-catuttha' (the fourth jhāna as a basis for all): Here, the word 'sabbattha' should be understood in the possessive sense (sāmi-attha). Alternatively, it is called 'sabbattha-pādaka' because it is the foundational cause for all states such as insight (vipassanā). This is a description by way of the object of the result. 'Ākāsa-kasiṇa-catuttha' refers to the fourth jhāna of the limited-space kasina. That jhāna belongs only to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), not to the other (sense-sphere). It is said to have twenty-four varieties because there are twelve types by way of wholesome (kusala) and twelve by way of functional (kiriya). By combining wholesome and functional, it is said 'sabbattha-pādaka' with the meaning 'it is also a basis for the round (vaṭṭa)'. Since functional jhāna is not a basis for the round, he speaks words that might cause doubt (as to whether wholesome jhāna is also not a basis for the round). 'He merges it into the mahaggata mind': This means that, taking the well-known foundational jhāna mind (pādaka-jhāna-citta) mentioned in the method 'when his mind is thus concentrated,' etc., by means of preliminary work (parikamma), he merges the material body (rūpa-kāya) into the mind by way of the mind of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-citta). 'He merges the foundational jhāna mind into the material body': This also means that, taking the aforementioned foundational jhāna mind as an object, he merges the mental continuum into the material body, making it follow that material body, and determines it. These two types of determination bring about the state of an invisible body and a visible body. By the power of the preliminary work of the desire to go, the perception associated with that preliminary work becomes a perception of ease (sukha-saññā) and a perception of lightness (lahu-saññā), and thus it should be understood that it also accomplishes the act of going. 'The mind of a Stream-winner (Sotāpanna)': This should be understood as the specific Path-mind and Fruit-mind of a Stream-winner. Since it is said that Māra and others know the mind of the Blessed One, why would one who has attained the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) not know a mind that is accompanied by taints (sāsava)? 'Chinna-vaṭumaka' (those whose path is cut) refers to the Buddhas who have cut the round of saṃsāra. 'Also because of reviewing Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna': Here, the reviewings of Path and Fruit occur after the Path and Fruit have first been known through the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbe-nivāsānussati-ñāṇa). The reviewing of Nibbāna occurs after the immeasurable states (appamāṇa-dhamma) that have Nibbāna as their object have been known. Therefore, it should be understood that the reviewings of the Path, etc., accomplish the state of having immeasurable objects for the knowledge of recollecting past lives. For it is said: 'Immeasurable aggregates are a condition for the knowledge of recollecting past lives by way of object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya),' but Nibbāna is not mentioned. Therefore, although the task of reviewing Path and Fruit is mentioned as being done by the knowledge of recollecting past lives, it cannot be said that it can review Nibbāna. However, in the Commentary, the state of that knowledge having Nibbāna as an object is seen to be permitted. 'Will be reborn in the sense-sphere': This refers to knowing the aggregates that will be reborn. 'Will attain parinibbāna through the Nibbāna-element': This means he will attain parinibbāna through the Path and Fruit which have Nibbāna as their object and which constitute the final quenching of defilements.
193:
## Meaning of the phrase beginning with "Asahajātattā"

"Asahajātattā" means because of being dissociated (unassociated). This is because for mental phenomena (nāma-dhammā), there is no other co-existence (sahajāta) with other mental phenomena apart from association (sampayoga). Although it is said "when taking other phenomena as object," even when taking the Path (magga) as an object, if one does not give weight to it, one should consider that it cannot be called "navattabba" (indeterminable) by way of path-predominance (maggādhipati).

"Niyogā" is said with the meaning of "niyamena" (certainly), referring to the sense of constant association. Alternatively, those phenomena that have constant association are called "niyogā," meaning they are fixed (niyata). This is because among the arisings of consciousness mentioned in the section on the arising of consciousness (Cittuppādakaṇḍa), there is not a single one that has an exclusively future object.

Although it is said "in the occurrence of taking kamma or the sign of kamma (kammanimitta) as object, it has only a past object," the fact that rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) has a present object when taking the sign of kamma as object will be explained in the commentary on the Paṭiccasamuppāda Vibhaṅga. Therefore, this statement should be understood as referring to the past sign of kamma that has come into the focus of the mind-door at the time of death in the mind-door. Regarding the rebirth-linking occurring in the sign of destiny (gatinimitta) which remains for five mind-moments of the death-consciousness (cuti) accompanied by registration (tadārammaṇa), it refers to the four life-continuum (bhavaṅga) moments having a present object; in other cases (where registration does not occur), it refers to six life-continuum moments, saying "and also at the time of the life-continuum thereafter."

Indeed, if death-consciousness occurs before registration arises when an impulsive consciousness (javana) having the sign of destiny as object has occurred—as in the case of a being from the fine-material or immaterial sphere being reborn in the sense-sphere—then the six life-continuum moments following rebirth-linking have a present object. Enjoyment (assādana) etc. by consciousness associated with wrong view should be regarded as being accompanied by misinterpretation (parāmāsa).

By the phrase "at the time of the preceding [consciousness] of the impulsive consciousnesses having concepts (paññatti) or Nibbāna as object," it shows the method by way of those impulsive consciousnesses whose preceding mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana) cannot be said to have a past object etc. (i.e., it is navattabba). Even at the time of the preceding [consciousness] of impulsive consciousnesses having Nibbāna as object, that mind-door adverting cannot be so described (as past etc.), but it is not exclusively "indeterminable," because in the cognitive processes of the Path and Fruition, that mind-door adverting does not have Nibbāna as its object.

Regarding the phrase "these scents," isn't it that present scents are taken? How then does it have a future object? To this, it is replied: because of the occurrence of the thought "May they not dry up for two hundred years beyond eighteen years." The meaning is that it occurs by taking future scents as object, thinking "May they not dry up in the future."

One who bends the body by the power of the mind takes as object the body that is actually present and manifest at that time; thus the determined mind (adhiṭṭhāna-citta) has a present object. Similarly, it should be applied to the performance of other miracles and the making of one's own body long, short, small, thick, blue, etc.
194:
It should be applied. In the phrase "one or two sequences (ekadvesantati-vāra) should be known in this interval," it means the turns of the material continuity and mental continuity occurring in this interval should be known as "one or two sequences." Or, sequences arising from temperature (utu) etc. of a very brief nature are called "one or two sequences." "Both are present" means both these occurring as "duration-present" (addhā-paccuppanna) exist. "Saṃhīrati" means it is pulled by the delights (abhinandana) of craving and views.

Some teachers (Abhayagirivāsins) say this. Since those teachers do not accept the static phase (ṭhitikkhaṇa) of consciousness, it would be improper to say "one penetrates [the mind of another] at the static phase." Likewise, for those teachers who say "the consciousness of the person with psychic power and the consciousness of the other person arise at the same moment," the statement "one penetrates at the static phase or the dissolution phase (bhaṅgakkhaṇa)" is inconsistent. Because the consciousness arising in those two phases cannot be said to arise at the same moment as the other's consciousness. Consciousness arising in the static and dissolution phases would partly have a present object and partly a past object. Also, in the statement "when the minds of many people are adverted to by way of a group, thinking 'I will know the minds of others'," since "many people" (mahājana) here refers to many individuals other than oneself, one should say the occurrence of adverting is "I will know the minds of others." However, even if "of another" could mean "of many people," it is not appropriate to penetrate a single mind after adverting to a group of minds of that person. Because adverting to a group is not adverting to a part. Therefore, those teachers should not say "when the minds of many people are adverted to," etc.

Regarding their statement "Because the consciousness of the person with psychic power and the consciousness of the other person arise at the same moment," the intention would be this: One who has attained the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), wishing to know another's mind, enters and emerges from the basic jhāna (pādaka-jhāna). Without making distinctions such as past etc., he performs the preliminary work (parikamma) by way of the general nature of mind (citta-sāmañña), thinking "I will know this person's mind." Again, he enters and emerges from the basic jhāna, adverts to the mind by way of its general nature, and immediately after three or four preliminary impulsive moments, he penetrates and clarifies the other's mind with the knowledge of penetrating others' minds, just as one sees a visible form clearly with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). Thereafter, the delimitation of "with lust" (sarāga) etc. occurs by way of sense-sphere consciousnesses, just like the delimitation of blue etc. In that delimitation, the adverting that adverts to the mind of the being who is present and whose heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) is seen with the divine eye, adverts to the mind by taking the manifest, existing mind as object. The preliminary impulsive moments also occur by taking that manifest mind as object only by way of its general nature.
195:
Taking (the mind) as an object, the preliminary impulsions (parikamma-javanas) that know the mind arise. However, the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), while penetrating and clarifying the existing mind, arises at the very same moment as that mind which is its object.

In that case, because of grasping the mental continuum as an object, by the power of oneness (ekatta), the advertence (āvajjana) and others arise taking only the mind as an object. The object clearly known by the knowledge of penetrating others' minds is also the mind itself. Therefore, because of occurring in a similar manner, except in the undesired cases of the path-process (magga-vīthi) and fruition-process (phala-vīthi), there is no diversity of objects for the advertence and impulsions in other places. The fact that the preliminary impulsion with a present object supports the knowledge of penetrating others' minds with a present object by way of repetition condition (āsevana-paccaya) is established. If the momentary present (khaṇa-paccuppanna) is taken as the present in this way, the triad of the past (atīta-ttika) will also remain consistent with the Paṭṭhāna Pali.

Otherwise, if the present of continuum (santati-paccuppanna) and the present of duration (addhā-paccuppanna) were called 'present' here, then past and future states might also become present. If that were so, it should have been stated as 'A present state is a condition for a present state by way of proximity condition (anantara-paccaya),' and so forth. However, it was not so taught. According to the words of the Pali text, 'A past state is a condition for a present state by way of proximity condition; preceding past aggregates are a condition for succeeding present aggregates by way of proximity... conformity (anuloma) for change-of-lineage (gotrabhū)...' and so forth, even within the present of duration and the present of continuum, the four aggregates that have passed away immediately prior are known as 'past.' It is nowhere taught in the Pali that the meaning of the term 'present' found in the Abhidhamma Matika refers to the present of duration or the present of continuum. Therefore, those teachers stated that the knowledge of penetrating others' minds has a present object because the mind of the possessor of psychic power and the mind of the other person arise simultaneously.

However, when one attends, 'I shall know such a mind of this person that has already occurred,' or 'I shall know such a mind that will occur,' and enters the basic jhāna (pādaka-jhāna) and so forth, then the advertence, preliminary, and the knowledge of penetrating others' minds have only past or future objects. This is because the distinction as past or future has already been made by the advertence itself.

Certain teachers, relying on the statement: 'The possessor of psychic power, desiring to know another's mind, adverts; the advertence takes the momentary present as an object and ceases together with that object; thereafter, four or five impulsions arise. For the sense-sphere impulsions other than the final superknowledge mind, that very mind which has ceased is the object. These minds do not have diverse objects because they have a present object by the power of the present of duration,' [argue that] just as there is no diversity of objects for the advertence and impulsions even when they have present and past objects, so too when adverting to future minds that have not yet arrived by one, two, three, four, or five mind-moments, although the advertence and impulsions have future, present, and past objects as may be the case, the diversity of objects...
196:
...would not occur. Therefore, they say that when adverting to a future mind that has not yet arrived by four or five mind-moments, immediately after the preliminary impulsions which have a future object, the knowledge of penetrating others' minds which takes the momentary present as an object is established. The doctrine of those teachers is not tenable, both because these questions—'A state with a future object is a condition for a state with a present object by way of repetition condition; a state with a present object is a condition for a state with a past object by way of repetition condition'—are not brought forth and taught (in the Paṭṭhāna), and because in the enumeration (gaṇanā-vāra), it is taught only as 'three in repetition condition.' This is because there is no wholesome (kusala), functional (kiriya), or sublime (mahaggata) state that does not receive the repetition condition.

The basis of this doctrine cannot be established by the statement that the advertence and impulsions have a past object which was a momentary present that has ceased. This is because that statement was made with the intention that when taking the mind in general without specifying 'the mind that has occurred' or 'the mind that will occur,' the advertence does not grasp a future object, and because it does not grasp a future object, the impulsions also do not grasp a present object. At that time, immediately after the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga-calana), the advertence arises taking only the mind that has become manifest as its object. If the knowing superknowledge mind also had a present object, it would lead to the fault of the advertence and the superknowledge mind occurring simultaneously (co-existing). Furthermore, in adverting to a group of minds and penetratingly knowing a portion of that group, or in adverting to and knowing objects as they arrive, it would lead to the fault of diversity of objects for the advertence and impulsions in inappropriate places. Therefore, rejecting the statement 'The momentary present mind is the object of the knowledge of penetrating others' minds' as improper, and seeing that there is no diversity of objects because they have objects of the present of duration or the present of continuum by way of a time that does not lead to the aforementioned faults, (the commentator) stated that the advertence and impulsions have a present object and a past object that has ceased. Even that statement would not be accepted by the former proponents (Kecivādins). For if there were such objects of the present of duration or the present of continuum, then because of the provision of the proximity condition for a present state included under another term—as in the Pali passages 'Advertence is for wholesome states...' and so forth—it should have been stated: 'Advertence with a present object is a condition for aggregates with a past object by way of proximity condition.' However, it was not so taught.

Why then is the present-object nature of the knowledge of penetrating others' minds investigated in this way? In the analysis (vibhaṅga) of 'A past state is to a present state, a future state is to a present state by way of object condition,' it is shown that 'Past aggregates are a condition for the advertence of the knowledge of the modes of psychic power, the knowledge of penetrating others' minds, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and the knowledge of faring according to deeds by way of object condition,' and 'Future aggregates are a condition for the advertence of the knowledge of the modes of psychic power, the knowledge of penetrating others' minds, and the knowledge of the future by way of object condition.' Also, in the triad of the arisen (uppanna-ttika), 'Unarisen aggregates...'
197:
"Presently arising aggregates are a condition for the adverting (āvajjanā) of the knowledge of psychic powers (iddhividhañāṇa), the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa), and the knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsañāṇa) by way of object condition (ārammaṇapaccaya)." Taking the knowledge of others' minds [into account], in the analysis (Vibhaṅga) of this phrase "A present state is a condition for a present state," it is stated: "Present aggregates are a condition for the adverting of the knowledge of psychic powers by way of object condition." Also, in the Triad of the Arisen (Uppannatika), it is stated only this much: "Arisen aggregates are a condition for the adverting of the knowledge of psychic powers by way of object condition." Therefore, is it not to be understood that "the knowledge of others' minds does not occur regarding a present mind"? If it did occur, then just as in the preceding phrases, the knowledge of others' minds should have been included in the other phrases as well. It is true that it should be included; however, it can be understood from other Pali passages that this knowledge of others' minds is taught in brief by way of demonstrating the method (naya).

In these analyses (Vibhaṅga): "A state with a past object is a condition for a state with a present object by way of object condition; a state with a future object is a condition for a state with a present object...; a state with a present object is a condition for a state with a present object," it is stated: "Through the knowledge of others' minds, one knows the mind of one who possesses a present mind with a past object. Present aggregates with a past object are a condition for the adverting of the knowledge of others' minds by way of object condition." And, "Through the knowledge of others' minds, one knows the mind of one who possesses a present mind with a future object... pe... Through the knowledge of others' minds, one knows the mind of one who possesses a present mind with a present object. Present aggregates with a present object are a condition for the adverting of the knowledge of others' minds by way of object condition." Thus, the occurrence of the knowledge of others' minds regarding a present object is indeed taught. For this very reason, it should be understood that this investigation has been made.

Regarding the word "tesaṃ" (of them), it is a genitive case used in the sense of specification (niddhāraṇa), meaning "among those two knowledges" (knowledge of past lives and knowledge of others' minds). If it is said that the plural usage "kusalā khandhā" (wholesome aggregates) is a reference to the knowledge of psychic powers, the knowledge of past lives, and the knowledge of the future, and not a reference to the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of beings passing away according to their kamma (yathākammūpagañāṇa), then the fact that those knowledges can have the four mental aggregates as their object would not be established. This is not so. Because in other Pali passages it is stated: "Aggregates that are without initial thought and with only sustained thought (avitakkavicāramatta), and sustained thought (vicāra), are a condition for the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and the knowledge of the future by way of object condition," and "Aggregates that are with initial and sustained thought (savitakkasavicāra), and initial thought (vitakka), are a condition for the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and the knowledge of the future by way of object condition." Thus, it is evident that the plural reference also includes the knowledge of others' minds.
198:
Even if the knowledge of others' minds is considered in this way, if it is argued that the status of the knowledge of beings passing away according to their kamma (yathākammūpagañāṇa) having the four aggregates as its object is not established because it is not mentioned in Pali passages such as "aggregates that are without initial thought and with only sustained thought, and sustained thought," this is not so. The absence of mention in that Pali passage is due to another reason. In fact, through the knowledge of beings passing away according to their kamma, the four mental aggregates associated with kamma are known primarily through the kamma itself. Just as the knowledge of others' minds, by the power of preliminary work (parikamma) performed beforehand, distinguishes a mind as having initial thought, etc., or as having lust, etc., the knowledge of beings passing away according to their kamma does not distinguish in such a detailed manner. Rather, it distinguishes the group of aggregates only by the power of kamma. Therefore, in the classification such as "aggregates that are without initial thought and with only sustained thought, and sustained thought," that knowledge of beings passing away according to their kamma is not mentioned; it is not because it does not have the four aggregates as its object. This is the reason for the lack of mention. Some teachers, however, do indeed recite in that Pali passage: "of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, of the knowledge of beings passing away according to their kamma, and of the knowledge of the future." Indeed, it is not that this knowledge is unable to know kamma with distinctions such as having initial thought, etc., just as it distinguishes between wholesome and unwholesome. For the very distinguishing of the nature of misconduct and good conduct is the distinguishing of the specific associations with lust, etc., or non-lust, etc.

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of the aspect of being internal to oneself (niyakajjhatta)," because it is a natural phenomenon (sabhāvadhamma) that cannot be internal to oneself by any method, it is taught as "exclusively external (ekantabahiddhā)" solely because it is external in every way. It is not that it is not external because it is not a natural phenomenon; it is because, like the kasinas, etc., the mere state of being internal to oneself is impossible. Indeed, because it is not a natural phenomenon, there is no ultimate reality (paramattha) that is an internal state such as the kasina-concept, etc.; thus, it is not mentioned in the Triad of the Internal (Ajjhattatika). All those, such as the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), should be connected to the statement in the Triad of Past Objects as "indescribable object (navattabbārammaṇa)." Here, "vuttaṃ" (stated) means it has been clearly shown by reasons such as being permitted (anujñāta) and being spoken (vacana).

Now, with the word "taṃ" (that), he refers back to the sphere of nothingness meditative absorption mentioned as "this sphere of nothingness." Regarding the meaning stated here: "Although only the sphere of nothingness is mentioned here, because it is stated as an indescribable object for the sense-sphere wholesome states, etc., in the Triad of Past Objects with reference to their having the same object as that sphere of nothingness, here too, it indicates their status as indescribable objects. Thus, when that sphere of nothingness is mentioned, those states are also considered mentioned; therefore, they are not mentioned separately"—other teachers do not accept this. Such allusive speech (lesavacana) does not exist in the Commentary section (Aṭṭhakathā-kaṇḍa). If it did exist, then in the Triad of Small Objects, after stating the status of having small objects, etc., and the status of being indescribable for those states with the same object, then in the Triad of Past Objects, only one of them would be mentioned and the others would not need to be mentioned. Similarly, in the Triad of Feeling, for those states with the same feeling, the status of being associated with pleasant feeling...
199:
The state of association has been taught. Among those states, having spoken only one in the exposition of those accompanied by happiness (sukhasahagata-niddesa) in the Triad of Joy (pīti-ttika), the others should not be spoken. In this same way, it should be applied and understood in the exposition of those accompanied by equanimity (upekkhāsahagata-niddesa) and so on.

However, because the summary of meanings (atthuddhāra) is presented in the Commentary Section (Aṭṭhakathā-kaṇḍa) not merely in part but in full, although states such as the sensuous-sphere wholesome (kāmāvacara-kusala) are also of the nature of being 'indescribable' (navattabba) in the Triad of Internal Objects (ajjhattārammaṇa-ttika) just like the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), those states are not taught as 'indescribable'. Therefore, although they are similar in having a non-existent (paññatti) object, the sphere of nothingness becomes 'indescribable' when it arises by way of the final occurrence (niṭṭhappavatti) of that non-existence; because such an occurrence does not exist for the sensuous-sphere wholesome and others, they are not taught as 'indescribable'. Indeed, since the kasiṇas and so on, which are created by a specific mode of apprehension, do not exist by way of individual essence (sabhāva), the consciousnesses having those kasiṇas as objects are taught as having external objects (bahiddhārammaṇa) by virtue of apprehending the external. The sphere of nothingness, however, does not occur by way of apprehending the external, nor does it occur by way of apprehending the internal; therefore, it is taught as 'indescribable'.

In whatever mode of apprehension the sphere of nothingness occurs, even Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) cannot occur in that same mode. If it were to occur so, that Omniscience itself would become the sphere of nothingness. For example, although Omniscience knows all the objects and specific modes of occurrence of the defilements, it does not apprehend them in the way those defilements apprehend; for if it did, Omniscience itself would fall into the state of being a defilement. Likewise, Omniscience, which knows the mode of occurrence of the sphere of nothingness as it really is, does not apprehend the object as the sphere of nothingness does; how then could any state other than Omniscience do so? For this reason, the 'indescribable' nature of sensuous-sphere wholesome states is not taught. This is the decision of the teachers who do not accept that 'there is a single entity called departure (apagama) which is the object of the sphere of nothingness'.

Regarding the statement that a resultant (vipāka) does not become the object of anyone, it means that the resultant sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-vipāka) does not become the object of any jhana among the spheres of infinite consciousness. Likewise, the sphere of nothingness does not become the object of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Just as in the Triad of Resultants (vipāka-ttika), in the questions having 'states with resultant nature' (vipākadhamma) and 'states that are neither resultant nor of resultant nature' (neva-vipāka-na-vipākadhamma) as roots, it is taught: 'Wholesome sphere of infinite space is a condition for wholesome sphere of infinite consciousness by way of object-condition; wholesome sphere of nothingness is a condition for wholesome sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and likewise for the resultant and the functional. Functional sphere of infinite space is a condition for functional sphere of infinite consciousness; functional sphere of nothingness is a condition for functional sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by way of object-condition' (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.406, 410).
200:
In the states having the root of resultant nature (vipākadhamma-mūla), it is not taught that 'the resultants of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of nothingness are a condition by way of object-condition for the resultants, wholesome, and functional states of the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.' This is because there is no possibility of directing (abhinīhāra) the mind after emerging from a resultant state; it means there is no directing towards the higher paths, fruits, or jhanas by making the resultant an object.

In the phrase 'one's own aggregates etc.', 'aggregates' (khandhā) refers to the mental aggregates, and the word 'etc.' (ādi) includes matter (rūpa). Alternatively, the concept of 'I' (ahaṃ-paññatti) taken within the internal continuity is included by the word 'etc.' This same method applies to the apprehension of the aggregates etc., of others. Again, by the apprehension of 'concept' (paññatti), it refers to the concepts not bound to faculties (anindriyabaddha-paññatti) such as kasiṇas and the divine abidings (brahmavihāra), and derivative concepts (upādāya-paññatti). Or, by the word 'etc.' in the apprehension of the concepts of 'self' and 'others', it refers to all derivative concepts. Among kamma and so on, kamma is internal (ajjhatta), the sign of kamma (kamma-nimitta) is both, and the sign of destiny (gati-nimitta) is external (bahiddhā). Even the sign of destiny for one who is to be reborn as a worm in one's own body could be internal.

Because Mallikā the young girl offered barley gruel and would obtain the position of the chief queen of King Kosala; because the Great Minister Santati, while on the back of an elephant, would reach Arahantship; and because Sumana the florist, by worshipping with a handful of flowers, would realize Paccekabodhi-knowledge—on account of these, the Blessed One manifested a smile.

Regarding the statement 'they obtain the opportunity in this triad', those states which are 'indescribable' (navattabba) because they do not obtain the opportunity in the Triad of Limited Objects (parittārammaṇa-ttika) and the Triad of Past Objects (atītārammaṇa-ttika), are not 'indescribable' here; it means they obtain the state of having a single object among the internal and so on. This is because the five fourth jhanas—the universal-basis (sabbattha-pādaka), the space-kasiṇa, and the light-kasiṇa—are states with external objects (bahiddhārammaṇa) due to having kasiṇas as objects; the fourth jhana of the divine abidings is so due to having a concept as an object; and the fourth jhana of mindfulness of breathing is so due to having a sign (nimitta) as an object. 'One's own body and mind' is expressed as 'sakāya-cittānaṃ'; since there is no benefit for oneself through that knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), it is not intended as an internal object (ajjhattārammaṇa). In the phrase 'or of matter not bound to faculties', the words 'or of the three concepts' should also be brought in by the word 'or' (vā), or this should be seen as an illustration of the method. At such a time, it is a state with an external object (bahiddhārammaṇa).

## The Explanation of the Summary of Meanings of the Triads is finished.
201:
## Commentary on the Summary of the Dyads

Regarding the statement "Conceit (māna) ... is of only one kind," this is said by way of showing a distinction that has not yet been mentioned. In another way, conceit should be said to be of two kinds because it arises together with the fetter of sensual lust (kāmarāga-saṃyojana) and the fetter of ignorance (avijjā-saṃyojana). This method is the same for the lust for existence (bhavarāga) and so on. Likewise, in the Pali text concerning skeptical doubt (vicikicchā), the meaning of the word "likewise" is "of only one kind."

Regarding the phrase "in prompted (saṅkhārika) consciousness," this should be understood merely as showing the place where the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa) arises together with the three hindrances (sloth and torpor, restlessness, and ignorance). It is not intended to show the arising of that hindrance of sensual desire with those hindrances as a rule, because sloth and torpor (thina-middha) is an inconstant (aniyata) mental factor. The phrase "by way of the lower limit" means that since restlessness (uddhacca) arises in all unwholesome consciousness, in the arising of consciousness associated with restlessness, there are two hindrances (restlessness and ignorance); in other consciousnesses devoid of sloth, torpor, and remorse, there are three hindrances (one of sensual desire, ill-will, or skeptical doubt, along with restlessness and ignorance) that arise as a lower limit; thus it is said "two or three." To the extent that hindrances arise together, the meaning "there are hindrances as well as states associated with hindrances" is possible; to show them by way of the lower limit, it is said "two." To show that this meaning is also possible in occurrences higher than those two, it is said "three." Since "two or three" is an indefinite indication meaning "either two or three," it should also be understood as "either four or five." Alternatively, it is merely to show the characteristic that wherever there is co-arising, there are hindrances as well as states associated with hindrances. In the arising of consciousness where four or five arise, this meaning is also accomplished. Having considered this, it is also said "two or three" in the Cluster of Defilements (Kilesa-gocchaka). Indeed, by way of showing the characteristic, defilements as well as states associated with defilements are mentioned, but not by way of showing all possible defilements in their individual forms.

If restlessness arises in all unwholesome consciousness, why is it said, "The hindrance of restlessness arises in the arising of consciousness associated with restlessness"? It is said for the purpose of showing the specific domain of restlessness when it is devoid of other hindrances among the five hindrances taught in the Suttas. In the Abhidhamma, however, the sixth hindrance (ignorance) arises together with the others; therefore, there is no specific domain for that hindrance of ignorance when it is devoid of other hindrances. Because there is no place of arising apart from the hindrances that arise with it, and because there is no arising of consciousness characterized by that hindrance of ignorance alone, there is indeed no specific domain. Therefore, that hindrance of ignorance is said to "arise in all unwholesome consciousness." But the aforementioned arising of consciousness associated with restlessness is the specific domain of restlessness, characterized by restlessness because the remaining states follow the lead of restlessness. Therefore, restlessness which arises in all unwholesome consciousness is generally...
202:
Even when taking it as "the hindrance of restlessness," in order to make it clear by its own specific domain, He said, "It arises in the arising of consciousness associated with restlessness." Such an explanation should be understood as being made to show the sixth hindrance (ignorance) by way of its pervasiveness, after defining the five hindrances in the specific domains of consciousness associated with greed, displeasure, prompted consciousness, skeptical doubt, and restlessness.

Some teachers, however, say regarding the term "associated with restlessness" (uddhacca-sahagate) that by taking restlessness found in all unwholesome consciousness in a general sense as "restlessness," it means "in the arising of consciousness (all unwholesome consciousness) associated with that restlessness." However, this meaning is not accepted by many teachers, because all unwholesome arisings of consciousness are not characterized by restlessness in the same way as the twelfth arising of consciousness; and if they were so characterized, He should have taught it by assigning a number as "in the twelve [consciousnesses] associated with restlessness," just as in "in the eight [consciousnesses] associated with greed" and so on, to exclude other arisings of consciousness. Since all unwholesome states are not characterized by restlessness, this hindrance of restlessness should have been taught as "arising in all unwholesome states" like the hindrance of ignorance, but it was not so taught; therefore, the meaning should be understood only by the method already stated. And because the hindrance of restlessness, like the hindrance of ignorance, arises in all unwholesome states, it is said in the Summary Section (Nikkhepa-kaṇḍa), "The hindrance of sensual desire is both a hindrance and associated with a hindrance through the hindrance of restlessness," and so on. Therefore, the intention should be sought without taking it literally that the hindrance of restlessness arises only in a single arising of consciousness.

In the Cluster of Defilements (Kilesa-gocchaka), the ten bases of defilement (kilesa-vatthu) such as greed and so on come in this order only in this Abhidhamma. Therefore, because there is no specific domain for the defilement of restlessness—which is taught in this very Pali text—when it is devoid of the defilements taught together with it, it is taught as "Restlessness, shamelessness, and fearlessness of wrongdoing arise in all unwholesome states," without showing it by way of a specific domain. In the explanation of the term "defilements and defiled" (kilesā ceva saṅkiliṭṭhā), because the term "defiled" (saṅkiliṭṭha) does not have the same meaning as the term "associated with defilement" (kilesa-sampayutta) but merely indicates the state of being tormented and afflicted by the stain of defilement, He did not provide an explanation identical to the term "associated with defilement," but said, "Those defilements are both defilements and are defiled."

Regarding the phrase "two or three defilements," some teachers say that "two or three" is said by way of conventional usage (rūḷhī) through the influence of the terms already taught in the Cluster of Roots (Hetu-gocchaka) and so on. If it were said by way of conventional usage without regard for the meaning, then in the Cluster of Ties (Gantha-gocchaka) also, [it would say] "where two or three ties..."
203:
It should be said, "The ties (ganthas) arise together." As for the statement, "In the cluster of ties (ganthagocchaka), because the meaning that two or three ties arise together with other states is possible, the word 'together' (ekato) is meaningful in the cluster of defilements (kilesagocchaka); however, in the cluster of roots (hetugocchaka) and so on, it is not meaningful because the meaning can be understood even without that word 'together'"—that statement is also not correct. Even in the cluster of roots and so on, the word 'together' is used because it has the meaning of preventing the inclusion of roots and those associated with roots, etc., when they arise separately. Therefore, excluding the attribution of conventional usage (ruḷhī) or literal meaning (anvattha), the meaning should be understood only in the manner already stated. By showing the arising of greed (lobha), aversion (paṭigha), and delusion (moha) together with other defilements through the statement beginning with "Greed is sixfold" (lobho chadhā), it should be understood that it also implies the arising of those other defilements together with greed and so on. The remaining text is clear in meaning.

## The Explanation of the Section on the Commentary is finished.

Four thousand padas, and again three hundred padas—these are the padas that illuminate the obscure meanings (līnattha) of the Aṭṭhasālinī.

Having been respectfully requested by the monk named Dhammamitta, the wise one named Ānanda composed these texts.

## Thus ends the explanation of the obscure meanings of the Aṭṭhasālinī Commentary.

## The Mūlaṭīkā on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī is completed.
